    On this site · Read a hand

    Pot odds, with the assumptions visible.

    Price calls and raises, distinguish draw probabilities from equity, and test the assumptions behind a bluff or call.

    Read matching section

    Searchable article text, without exercise answers

    Workshop / Calculation After-play study. All scenarios are fictional. The calculations describe stated models, not recommended actions or solved ranges.

    A useful hand review has two different jobs: reconstruct the money and decide what the opponent could have. Do them in that order. You can be certain that a call costs five big blinds while remaining uncertain whether the hand has enough equity to call. Keeping those two levels of confidence separate is more useful than an impressive-looking percentage with missing assumptions. This workshop builds on the viewer's poker-math guide . Work in chips or big blinds, but use the same unit throughout one calculation. Put earlier contributions inside the pot. Do not charge yourself for them a second time.

    Let P be the pot already in the middle when it is your turn, including the opponent's latest bet. Let C be the additional amount you must call. If your call closes the action and all of that pot is available to you, the final pot is P + C. The break-even equity is C / (P + C) . Here, equity means your expected fraction of that final pot, including your share of ties. With no future betting, no deductions and no tournament-prize adjustment, the value of calling relative to folding is equity × (P + C) − C . This is a chip-value calculation. Tournament equity asks a different question. A half-pot river bet There are 20 BB before the opponent bets 10 BB. Now P = 30 and C = 10. The final pot would be 40 BB, so 10 / 40 = 25% . At an assumed 30% equity, calling is worth 0.30 × 40 − 10 = +2 BB relative to folding. The 30% is an input, not a finding. Change it to 20% and the same call becomes −2 BB. The arithmetic does not tell you which assumption is credible. Heads-up bet into a 12 BB pot, with no further betting or deductions Opponent bets Final pot after calling Break-even equity 3 BB 18 BB 16.7% 4 BB 20 BB 20% 6 BB 24 BB 25% 9 BB 30 BB 30% 12 BB 36 BB 33.3% 24 BB 60 BB 40%

    Start the street with 10 BB in the pot. You bet 4 BB. The opponent raises to 14 BB. The current pot contains 10 + 4 + 14 = 28 BB. You already contributed four on this street, so calling costs 14 − 4 = 10 BB. The final pot is 38 BB and the threshold is 10 / 38 = 26.3% . Dividing 14 by the final pot would charge yourself twice for part of your original bet. Treating a raise to 14 as a raise by 14 changes the hand entirely. In a reconstructed vlog hand, write the word to next to the amount before building the graphic.

    Suppose exactly nine of 47 unseen cards would complete a particular draw on the turn. The next-card probability is 9 / 47 = 19.1% . If the same nine target cards remain relevant and you are guaranteed both remaining cards without another payment, the chance of hitting at least one is 1 − (38 / 47 × 37 / 46) = 35.0% . Neither number is automatically your showdown equity. A completed flush can lose to a stronger hand; a pair might already be ahead; an opponent can improve too. The simple counting model also changes when additional dead cards are known. Its purpose is to make the assumptions visible. A flop call that may face another turn bet does not buy a free river. Before using 35.0%, describe how the hand reaches showdown. Implied odds require an assumption about additional money won later. Reverse implied odds describe additional losses when you improve but remain behind. Neither should become an unexplained allowance that makes every call look attractive. Multiway pots need another line of bookkeeping. In a multiway hand, ask whether another player can raise after you call and which pots you are eligible to win. An all-in short stack cannot count someone else's side pot as a prize available to them. Refund uncalled excess before calculating the contested pot. Use the side-pot examples when the contribution levels differ.

    For a deliberately simplified heads-up river model, you bet B into a pot P. The opponent either folds or calls. You always lose when called, and there are no ties, deductions or tournament effects. The bluff breaks even when the fold probability equals B / (P + B) . Risk six to win ten Betting 6 BB into 10 BB needs 6 / 16 = 37.5% folds. If an assumed opponent folds 40%, the expected change is 0.40 × 10 − 0.60 × 6 = +0.4 BB . The caller's equity threshold against that bet is different: 6 / 22 = 27.3% . One calculation prices your bluff; the other prices their call. They should not match. This does not prescribe bluffing any particular hand. A hand with showdown value has an alternative in checking; a bluff that wins chips might still be worse than that alternative. An opponent's fold rate also depends on the actual range, board, size and history, not a universal population label.

    A useful final note reads: “The call costs 10 BB into a final pot of 38 BB. It needs 26.3% equity under the no-further-betting chip model. My unresolved question is whether the opponent's raising range gives this hand that equity.” That sentence separates a calculation from a strategic judgment and gives the next study session a specific job. Record the pot, incremental call, final eligible pot, assumed equity and the reason for that assumption. Then change one assumption. A conclusion that reverses under a small, plausible range change deserves a cautious explanation, not a confident verdict.

    PokerStars Learn: pot odds provides background on the call-price relationship. The examples and calculations here are independently constructed. Decimal percentages are rounded. Prepared with AI assistance. No actual hand, personal result or solver validation is claimed.

    On this site · Tournament study

    A short stack is a situation, not a chart.

    Study 10–20 BB live tournament decisions beyond push/fold: 15BB action choices, antes, raise sizes, a checkable ICM call and a private review sheet.

    Read matching section

    Searchable article text, without exercise answers

    At 15 big blinds, “What can I shove?” is only one question. You may be first in, facing a raise, completing the small blind or considering a call for your tournament life. Start by defining the available actions and what you are trying to maximize: chips or modeled prize equity. After-play study, not an at-table aid. This expanded guide focuses on 10–20 BB live tournament decisions. Calculated examples are fictional and show their assumptions. No personal hand, new solver run or universally correct range is claimed. Sources checked October 15, 2026. If you want the shortest route, record the situation , compare what changes at 20, 15 and 10 BB , then work through the chip-value versus ICM call . Use position and stack terminology if effective stacks are unfamiliar. The short-stack input record is for a private review after play. Two players can hold the same cards with the same nominal stack and face different decisions. A button entering an unopened pot is not in the same position as a big blind responding to a raise and a call. A useful chart matches the game being studied, including the actions that were allowed to happen.

    A decision tree describes what players can do and what can happen next. A push/fold model deliberately removes some branches. In HoldemResources’ heads-up example, the small blind can only shove or fold; the big blind facing a shove can only call or fold. That chart answers the restricted two-player game. It does not establish that a smaller raise or a limp would be worse if those actions were available. 1 Chip expected value , or chip EV, values outcomes in chips. ICM , the Independent Chip Model, estimates tournament prize equity from stacks and payouts. Changing the objective is separate from expanding the tree. HRC’s free Nash ICM calculator explicitly remains a push-or-fold calculation; its configurable tree documentation also describes broader preflop and postflop analysis. 2 3 Action tree and objective are separate choices Study model What changes What remains a limit Push/fold, chip EV Values the allowed outcomes in chips Smaller raises and limps may be absent Push/fold, ICM Values outcomes using a specified prize model Adding payouts does not restore omitted actions Multiple actions, chip EV Can compare the non-all-in branches actually configured Still needs stacks, ranges, sizes and later-play assumptions Multiple actions, ICM Adds a prize objective to a broader tree Remains conditional on the configured tree and payout model “The chart shoves” and “this other model raises small” need not be contradictory. First check whether the models offered the same choices. Then check whether they valued the results in the same units. Neither a mixed frequency nor a tool’s recommendation is a confidence score about an unknown live opponent. Check: does adding payouts add small raises?

    Write the blind level, ante type, seats dealt in, button location, action so far and stack convention. “15 BB before posting” differs from “15 BB behind after posting.” Keep the original chip counts so a conversion can be checked. Identify every opponent who can still enter the pot, not only the person whose action caught your attention. A smaller-stack contrast, retained from the original workshop: a player begins with 8,000 chips at blinds of 500/1,000 with a 1,000 big-blind ante. They are the big blind and can post both in full. The starting stack is 8 BB ; after posting the live blind and ante, 6,000 chips remain behind . The live blind counts toward a call. The ante does not. Short-posting and ante-priority procedures require the event’s rules. Effective stacks are opponent-specific. With 17 BB against players starting with 8 BB, 16 BB and 55 BB, the amounts initially contestable between you and each are 8, 16 and 17 BB, before accounting for forced contributions. Then account for dead antes and live posts. An opponent who started with fewer chips can cover your remaining live stake after you pay a big-blind ante; assess elimination risk from the actual post-ante state. In a multiway all-in, different contribution levels can create side pots; use the side-pot lab for refunds and eligibility. Separate three meanings of “players remaining”: players still to act in this hand, players seated at this table, and players left in the tournament. They affect different parts of the decision. Nine-handed under the gun has eight players behind; a six-handed first-to-act seat has five. The same position label does not make those situations identical. Tournament field size and payouts answer another question again.

    At a six-handed table with a 0.5 BB small blind, a 1 BB big blind and a 1 BB big-blind ante, the initial pot is 2.5 BB . Do not multiply that big-blind ante by six. With a 0.1 BB ante from each of six players instead, the initial pot is 2.1 BB . A nine-handed table using that individual ante would begin with 2.4 BB. At unchanged blinds, a player completing a full six-hand orbit pays 2.5 BB in the first structure or 2.1 BB in the second, assuming every obligation is posted in full. This is bookkeeping, not a survival clock: blinds rise, tables change and hands can win or lose chips before the orbit ends. Keep forced contributions in the ledger. An ante is money in the pot, not a live bet toward the amount to call. That distinction can alter an all-in price. The current Poker TDA rules also address big-blind-ante situations and restrict strategy tools at the table. Confirm the rules of your event and use these materials away from play. 4

    Fictional boundary model: nine-handed no-limit Hold’em; action folds to you in the cutoff; you start with 20 BB before forced bets and have posted none; all opponents start with at least 21 BB; blinds 0.5/1 BB; a 1 BB big-blind ante is fully posted by the big blind. No other contributions, bounty or deductions. The objective is chip EV. Compare a raise to 2 BB with a shove of 20 BB. For this calculation only, assume each action wins the initial pot when everyone folds and loses its entire additional investment whenever anyone continues. There is no showdown equity, later betting or refund in that losing branch. These artificial assumptions isolate risk and reward; they are not a model of how either action actually plays. The pot starts at 0.5 + 1 + 1 = 2.5 BB . Under this zero-equity model, the break-even joint fold probability is risk / (risk + reward) : Zero-equity fold thresholds in the fictional 20 BB setup Additional investment Joint folds needed to break even Raise to 2 BB 2 / 4.5 = 44.44% Shove 20 BB 20 / 22.5 = 88.89% The two actions will not necessarily receive the same responses. A small raise can face a call or reraise and a real shoving hand may retain equity when called. These numbers therefore do not select a preferred action. They show why removing the small-raise branch changes the question. Ante sensitivity, with a separate 15 BB starting stack: keep the same cutoff, opponents covering, 0.5/1 blinds and artificial losing-when-called model. A 15 BB shove needs 15 / 16.5 = 90.91% joint folds with no ante, versus 15 / 17.5 = 85.71% with a 1 BB big-blind ante. The nominal stack is unchanged while the immediate reward differs. If several opponents remain, the relevant event is everyone required to fold, not any one player’s fold rate. Responses are conditional on earlier actions and card removal. The multiway guide explains that calculation. Do not interpret these toy thresholds as measured live-player frequencies.

    Choose the decision family before consulting a reference Family What must match First-in decision All earlier players folded. Count everyone still to act and retain their stacks. Facing an open Record the opener’s total size, assumed range and the players behind. A rejam is a shove after someone has raised. Calling an all-in Count what is still owed and the relevant range. Calling cannot make the existing shover fold. Limped or multiway pot Prior contributions, more ranges and possible side pots create a different game. At 15 BB, “shove first in” and “call a shove” are different decisions even with the same cards. The opener can win immediately through folds. A caller needs an adequate expected share of the contested pot under the relevant objective. Neither a familiar hand name nor the fear of becoming shorter supplies the missing range.

    Treat the depths as study checkpoints, not switches that activate universal rules. Position, antes, opposing stacks and the prior action remain part of every checkpoint. Poker Academy’s September 17, 2026 article reports nine-handed, chip-EV, 1 BB big-blind-ante solutions with 2 BB opens, and a 2.5 BB small-blind raise option. Its examples show small early-position opens at 20 and 15 BB, both raises and shoves on the 15 BB button, and some small button raises even at 10 BB. It also includes small-blind limps. These are provider-reported examples, not new solves or recommended live-field frequencies. The public summary is not a complete export of every opponent stack and downstream setting. 5 At 20 BB, compare the branches you would lose by using push/fold. Can a small raise win the pot, get called by worse or induce a response you can profitably continue against? If you intend to fold to a shove, which ranges make that plan reasonable? A non-all-in raise is not automatically a mistake because you may later fold. Nor is raise/fold automatically appropriate with every playable hand. At 15 BB, start with the decision family and the players behind. An early-position first-in decision, a button open, a small-blind completion and a rejam over a raise are separate studies. A short blind can shove over your raise; a covering player can threaten your tournament life. Write the response plan before describing a smaller raise as “keeping options open.” It also creates new decisions. At 10 BB, shoving becomes a more prominent study option without becoming the only legal action. A 2 BB open uses one fifth of a 10 BB starting stack before forced bets are considered. That makes the remaining call price important, but it does not mean every hand is committed. Count the additional call and compare against an assigned range. Avoid turning a low threshold into proof that your hand reaches it. In the small blind, distinguish completing from opening elsewhere. If action folds to you, you already have a live half-blind invested in a standard 0.5/1 structure. Completing costs another half-blind and leaves the big blind an action. A cheap completion is not a free showdown. The range that reaches that decision and the big blind’s options matter. For a useful comparison, keep everything except the selected variable fixed. If the table, ante, stack convention and permitted sizes all change between two screenshots, the difference cannot be credited solely to moving from 20 to 15 BB.

    Complete fictional setup: four players remain in a standard no-limit Hold’em tournament. Finishing prizes are $50, $30, $20 and $0 . Starting stacks before posting, in the order small blind, C, you in the big blind, D , are 40, 30, 20 and 10 BB . Blinds are 0.5/1 BB with no ante . C and D fold; the small blind shoves. No bounty, deal, re-entry, satellite prize, deductions or other contributions apply. You posted 1 BB and have 19 BB left to call . The small blind covers your 20 BB contribution. Its excess 20 BB is uncalled and returned if you call; it is not part of the contested award. There are no further betting decisions after a call. The two-outcome calculation below explicitly assumes no ties. Your cards and the shover’s range are unspecified because we are calculating a required win probability, not assigning one to a hand. Chip EV: after calling, each player has contributed an effective 20 BB, making a 40 BB contested pot . Relative to folding now, the extra call costs 19 BB. The break-even win probability is 19 / 40 = 47.5% . Chips already posted are not charged again. Classic ICM: the Malmuth–Harville model assigns finish probabilities from chip shares, successively removing each possible higher finisher. It then weights those probabilities by the prizes. HRC identifies this as the algorithm used by its separate ICM equity calculator. This prize model does not forecast individual skill, future position or blind changes. 6 Four-player ICM branches with 100 BB conserved Choice or outcome Stacks in the stated order Your modeled prize equity Fold 41, 30, 19, 10 BB $22.946148 Call and win 20, 30, 40, 10 BB $33.603175 Call and lose 60, 30, 0, 10 BB $0, fourth place On a narrow screen, scroll this comparison sideways. The amounts are calculated for this fictional payout structure. The fold branch preserves the small blind’s 40 BB starting stack plus your surrendered 1 BB. Winning returns its uncalled excess and leaves you with the 40 BB contested pot. Losing transfers your full 20 BB to the covering player. All branches conserve 100 BB. With loss value zero and no ties, calling has modeled prize equity q × $33.603175 . It must match folding’s $22.946148. Using unrounded values gives q = 68.2857% , approximately 68.3% . A hypothetical 60% win probability would exceed the 47.5% chip threshold but fall below this particular ICM threshold. That is not a recommendation for any named hand. The exact hero finish probabilities are available in the reproduction script . It uses only Python’s standard library, enumerates the finish orders and prints the branch values, thresholds and chip-conservation checks. It is an arithmetic example, not a poker solver, range generator or at-table assistant. Changing the short stack, prizes, action or bounty can change the comparison. With a single winner-only residual monetary prize after a deal, classic ICM reduces that residual value to chip share; locked awards are constants. Do not import the usual payout ladder into a hand without checking the actual deal. Conversely, “ICM matters” does not establish a fold when the state is unspecified. Continue with tournament equity for another counted example. Check: is a 60% win chance enough here?

    PokerNews’ coverage of the May 2026 Triton Montenegro $50,000 seven-handed event reports that Thomas Muehloecker opened and called a Christoph Vogelsang ace-five shove with K♥ J♥ from a stack described as 15 big blinds. It also reports a three-handed deal with $100,000 and the trophy left to play for. This is an attributed public report, not Nolan’s hand or recollection. 7 The account does not supply a complete decision state: exact pre-hand stacks and positions, opening size, ante, whether the 15 BB describes the original stack or what remained, and opponent range assumptions. Its deal allocations also differ between the narrative and results table. Confirm the deal terms before assigning a payout objective. The supported conclusion here is a question list, not a grade for the K♥ J♥ call. For your own difficult short-stack hand, capture those missing details and what you actually thought at the time. Keep later analysis separate. A showdown supplies one holding; it does not verify the entire range that should have been assigned before the cards were shown. Use recording hands to preserve an honest record.

    Record table size and position convention; all relevant stacks and posting conventions; blinds and antes; prior action; the chip-value or prize-value objective; permitted actions; and the source or version. A prize-sensitive comparison also needs payouts, remaining-field information and other prize mechanics. A tool with postflop support still needs its postflop settings to match the study question. 3 Label the reference matching inputs , approximate with named differences , or not comparable . Matching inputs does not certify solution accuracy. A screenshot with missing settings cannot provide an exact reference. A six-max, no-ante, first-in 5 BB chip-value chart is not an exact answer for a five-handed 4.5 BB big-blind-ante spot near a payout jump. Likewise, shove/fold labels at 4 and 5 BB do not specify a 4.5 BB answer. Do not silently round a difficult spot into certainty or interpret a mixed frequency as confidence.

    Choose one family, such as a button first-in decision. Save a complete input record and predict which factor should matter before consulting a result. Change one variable: ante, one opponent’s stack, an allowed raise size or the payout objective. Record what changed and what stayed fixed. Finish with a sentence you can explain without the chart: “This comparison changes the posted pot while keeping stacks and actions fixed,” or “The chip-value reference omits the prize question I need to answer.” Identifying a mismatch is useful work even when the exact action remains unresolved. Download the short-stack input record , or copy the same blank text below. Keep completed records private. The sheet includes a short version for a limited-energy study session and a fuller model checklist. Check: does a 1 BB big-blind ante become 9 BB nine-handed?

    On this site · Tournament study

    When more chips are not enough.

    A checkable three-player ICM example explains prize equity, risk premiums and why gaining chips can lower expected payout.

    Read matching section

    Searchable article text, without exercise answers

    Workshop / Tournament value After-play study. This is a small, explicitly simplified model, not an actual tournament hand or an ICM strategy recommendation.

    A tournament chip cannot be cashed out at a fixed price. The same stack can have a different modeled prize value depending on the other stacks and the payout structure. That is why a chip-profitable gamble does not automatically improve your expected tournament payout. The Independent Chip Model, or ICM, translates stacks and prizes into a model of tournament equity. It is useful precisely because it asks a different question from a basic pot-odds calculation . It is not a forecast that knows each player's skill, future cards or future decisions.

    Imagine three equal stacks of 10 units each and a $100 prize pool paying $50, $30 and $20 . Under standard ICM, each equally sized stack has the same expected payout: 100 / 3 = $33.33 , rounded. The model assigns each player a one-third chance of each finishing position. Now consider a hypothetical choice between keeping those stacks unchanged and taking a gamble against one other player. Winning transfers their ten units to you; losing transfers your ten to them and puts you third. There are no blinds, antes, dead money, ties or intermediate outcomes in this benchmark. It is deliberately not a literal hand with a bet waiting in the pot. What is the doubled stack worth? If you win, the surviving stacks are 20 and 10. Standard ICM gives you a 20 / 30 = two-thirds chance of first and a one-third chance of second. Your modeled value is (2 / 3 × $50) + (1 / 3 × $30) = $43.33 . If you lose, you receive the third prize: $20 . The comparison is therefore a gain of $10 above your original value when you win, but a loss of $13.33 when you lose. Doubling the chips did not double their prize value. The fictional transfer gamble, with amounts rounded to cents Outcome Your chips Your modeled payout Keep the state 10 $33.33 Win the gamble 20 $43.33 Lose the gamble 0 $20.00

    Let q be your probability of winning this no-tie gamble. The expected prize value is q × (130 / 3) + (1 − q) × 20. Set that equal to the original 100 / 3 and solve: q = 4 / 7 = 57.14% . For a blind-posted call rather than this simplified transfer, audit a four-player 20 BB example . Its additional call costs 19 BB, with different chip and prize thresholds. For chip value, preserving ten versus winning twenty or losing everything has a 50% break-even threshold. In this constructed example, the prize model needs 7.14 percentage points more win probability. That difference is an example of a risk premium. It is not a fixed adjustment to attach to every tournament call. At a hypothetical 55% chance to win, the gamble has an expected 11 chips rather than ten, a gain of +1 chip . But its expected payout is 0.55 × (130 / 3) + 0.45 × 20 = $32.83 , which is $0.50 below preserving the state. The disagreement is about the objective, not a contradiction in arithmetic.

    The uninvolved player's stack remains ten units. After either decisive outcome, they face a 20-unit stack heads-up and are guaranteed at least second prize. Their ICM value is (1 / 3 × $50) + (2 / 3 × $30) = $36.67 . They gained approximately $3.33 in modeled prize equity without gaining a chip. This is a useful explanation for a viewer who sees someone benefit while two other players clash. It is also why an account of a tournament hand can need context about a player who folded before the action became dramatic. Changing the prizes changes the question. If the entire $100 were awarded to first place in this same model, ICM value would be proportional to chips. The equal-risk gamble would again break even at 50%. A flat-prize satellite creates a different incentive structure. Bounties introduce additional rewards that cannot be represented merely by changing an ordinary final-place payout label. These comparisons show why “near the money” is not a complete input. Prize structure, who covers whom, other short stacks and the decision's actual outcomes all matter. Do not infer a correct action from an event-stage label alone.

    Standard ICM uses stack sizes to assign finishing probabilities. It does not directly model differences in player skill, seating position, the next blind increase or how future hands will be played. A precise number can therefore be precisely conditional on a simplified model. Likewise, the absence of an immediate money bubble does not establish that chip-value and prize-value strategies coincide. The size of a relevant effect must be evaluated for the situation; it should not be assumed to switch on at one particular field size. A screenshot showing “ICM” does not settle a hand if the stacks or payouts are missing. Nor does a dollar-valued result certify the ranges used to calculate it. Keep the game state, model and range assumptions separately reviewable.

    Record the number of players remaining, available payout information, relevant stack distribution, who covers whom, blind and ante structure, bounty format if any, and the action up to the decision. Identify estimates and missing information instead of inventing precise stacks elsewhere in the field. Then write two questions: “What does the chip-value model say?” and “What changes when the prize objective is included?” Agreement is informative. Disagreement is a reason to inspect assumptions, not to select whichever answer better fits the eventual result.

    GTO Wizard: ICM basics describes the model and its limitations. Its bubble-factor explanation distinguishes risk premiums from a money-bubble-only rule. The three-player transfer example and its exact fractions are independently constructed here. Prepared with AI assistance. Model values are not promised payouts, financial advice or validated solutions to a real hand.

    On this site · Read a hand

    From possible hands to weighted ranges.

    Count physical combinations, remove known cards, weight betting frequencies and test a fictional river range.

    Read matching section

    Searchable article text, without exercise answers

    Workshop / Ranges After-play study. All hands, ranges and action frequencies below are fictional teaching inputs, not population data or solver output.

    “They can have ace-king or a missed draw” is a start, but it is not yet a range model. How many physical combinations remain? Which of them took the earlier actions? How often does each bet this river? A list of possible hands becomes useful only when those questions are kept separate. This workshop extends the viewer's introduction to ranges . The aim is not to assign a stranger a perfectly known strategy. It is to make a hand-review claim specific enough to examine and change.

    A hold'em starting hand contains two of 52 cards. There are 52 × 51 / 2 = 1,326 unordered combinations. The familiar 13-by-13 matrix groups them into 169 labels, but the labels do not have equal numbers of combinations. A pair such as QQ has six combinations: choose two of four queens. A suited unpaired label such as KQs has four, one per suit. Its offsuit counterpart KQo has twelve. Across the full deck, that is 78 pair combinations, 312 suited combinations and 936 offsuit combinations . Their total is 1,326. Counting selected matrix squares therefore does not give a range's percentage of dealt hands. Ten pair labels and ten suited labels cover different numbers of physical combinations. Once the board and your hand are known, count again rather than carrying the preflop totals forward unchanged.

    You hold ace of spades and queen of clubs . The river board is ace of hearts, seven of diamonds, two of clubs, nine of spades and three of hearts . Your hand is a pair of aces with a queen kicker. Seven specific cards are known, so an opponent's two cards must come from the remaining 45, giving 45 × 44 / 2 = 990 possible combinations before considering their actions. Combinations remaining after removing those seven known cards Hand label Before any removal In this river example AA 6 1 AK, all suits 16 8 AKs only 4 2 AKo only 12 6 KQs only 4 3 Only the ace of clubs and ace of diamonds remain, so AA has one combination. Each remaining ace can pair with four kings, giving eight AK combinations. Two are suited. The queen of clubs removes the clubs version of KQs, leaving three suited versions. These are availability counts. They do not prove that all eight AK combinations would have played the hand this way or that any KQs combination would bluff. The board also does not reveal a folded opponent's cards. Remove only genuinely known cards, not a convenient guess about what someone probably folded.

    For a deliberately narrow river model, suppose the opponent's only value bets are the one AA and eight AK combinations. Suppose the only candidate bluffs are the three remaining KQs combinations. Your hand loses to every value combination and beats every bluff, with no ties. If all twelve combinations arrive and bet with equal weight, three out of twelve are bluffs: 25% . Facing a half-pot river bet, the call would be exactly break-even in the simple chip model because its threshold is also 25%. Change one assumption, not the cards. Now keep the nine value combinations at full weight but suppose each KQs combination takes this betting line only half as often. The effective bluff weight is 3 × 0.5 = 1.5. Its share of the betting range is 1.5 / (9 + 1.5) = 14.3% , not 25%. It is the same list of possible hands and the same board. The conclusion changes because the action frequencies changed. A fractional combination is a probability weight, not half of a physical hand. More generally, assign a weight to each surviving combination and normalize by the total weight. The weight must represent how likely that combination is to reach the decision and take the observed action. If it already includes the earlier action history, do not multiply that history in again.

    Your ace removes value combinations. Your queen also removes one candidate KQs bluff. Calling a card “a blocker” says that it changes availability; it does not, by itself, say that the net change favors a call or a bluff. Check the hands it removes from both sides of the proposed range. Then ask whether those hands actually take the relevant line. A card that removes three hypothetical bluffs matters little if those hands never bluff in the first place. Equally, an attractive narrative about blocking the nuts does not establish the opponent's remaining frequencies. Three versions are more informative than one confident version. Keep a conservative, central and more bluff-heavy version of the same clearly defined model. “Conservative” should describe an assumption, not be mistaken for a statistically proven bound. Record which hands or frequencies changed and whether your conclusion survived. If a call is profitable only when every candidate missed draw bets, that dependence belongs in the review. If the conclusion survives several reasonable constructions, explain the common mechanism rather than displaying an artificially precise single estimate.

    Write the known cards, value candidates, bluff candidates and the reasons each could reach this street. Cross out physically impossible combinations. Give the remaining candidates explicit frequencies, including uncertainty. Only then compare the weighted range with the call price . A useful narration might say: “I can name three suited combinations that miss, but the important question is whether they actually bet. With half-weight bluffs, my simplified model is not close to the required frequency.” That is more honest and more interesting than announcing that an opponent “always has bluffs.”

    GTO Wizard: poker combinatorics explains starting-hand counts and card removal. The river fixture, weighting example and calculations here are independently constructed. Prepared with AI assistance. No actual opponent frequencies or hand-range accuracy are claimed.

    On this site · Results and review

    Results deserve context.

    Separate tournament ROI, trip costs, sample uncertainty and decision evidence with worked accounting and probability examples.

    Read matching section

    Searchable article text, without exercise answers

    Workshop / Results After-play study. All money amounts and probabilities are fictional examples, not Nolan's results or estimates of any player's ability.

    A cash is a real outcome. A losing trip is a real cost. Neither should be erased by a story about variance, and neither is a complete assessment of how well someone played. A useful record separates the financial outcome, the decisions available for review and the uncertainty about long-run ability. The practical objective is a record you can continue keeping after an ordinary session, not a dashboard that turns every upswing into proof and every downswing into a crisis. The same separation also makes a vlog's results segment clearer.

    One tournament event can involve several paid entries. Record the event and each entry or re-entry, its full cost including the fee, any add-on, refunds and all returns. Keep bounties separate from finishing prizes while still including both in a clearly defined total. Do not describe a trip as “three tournaments” in a way that hides six paid attempts. Choose a consistent cashing-rate denominator and label it. “Events with a finishing prize divided by events played” is not the same measure as cashes per entry. Report the counts as well as the percentage. Bounty-only returns and multi-flight formats may need their own labels rather than being forced into an ambiguous cash/no-cash field. Keep receipts or source notes privately when available. A public summary does not need reservation details, opponents' identities, account information or precise travel movements. The result log is a record of your activity, not a reason to publish other people's data.

    A fictional twelve-entry sample Twelve entries cost $200 each, including fees: total entry cost $2,400 . Total tournament returns are $3,100 . Net tournament result is $3,100 − $2,400 = +$700 . Tournament ROI, using total entry cost as the denominator, is $700 / $2,400 = 29.2% , rounded. If the trip also costs $500 in travel and lodging, the trip surplus is +$200 before other uncounted expenses or taxes. The $700 poker result, 29.2% tournament ROI and $200 trip surplus are not interchangeable. State what is included before comparing two trips. If entry sizes vary, add all returns and all costs before calculating aggregate ROI. An unweighted average of entry-level percentage returns gives a small entry the same influence as a large one and generally answers a different question. Do not silently mix the two methods. Show concentration without rewriting history. Suppose $2,000 of the fictional $3,100 came from one finish. That is 64.5% of all returns. The largest result matters a great deal to this sample. A sensitivity illustration that removes its payout leaves $1,100 in returns against $2,400 in costs, or −$1,300. That last calculation is not an alternative actual ROI and not an estimate of “what normally happens.” The finish really belongs in the sample. Its purpose is to show how concentrated the result is, not to delete success or manufacture a losing record.

    For a deliberately simplified exercise, assume each event independently has exactly a 10% chance of a specified kind of cash. Under those assumptions, the chance of no cash in ten events is 0.9 to the tenth power, or 34.9% . In twenty events it is 0.9 to the twentieth power, or 12.2% . Those probabilities do not describe this site's author or your next trip. Real fields, formats, entry decisions and player performance vary. Independence and a constant cash probability are assumptions used to demonstrate a calculation. A cash probability also says nothing by itself about profitability without the distribution of payout amounts and entry costs. Another player could have the same cashing rate but a different expected return because their deep finishes pay more. Larger samples can reduce some uncertainty, but there is no universal count of live tournaments that certifies a win rate. A short, highly concentrated sample deserves more context, not more decimal places. “All-in adjusted” is not “luck removed.” Even where a tool calculates an adjustment for recorded all-in runouts, that adjustment addresses only the events and model it includes. It does not undo which starting hands were dealt, which opponents were seated nearby, earlier runouts, prize effects or omitted hands. Do not turn a partial adjustment into a statement that the entire sample now measures skill alone.

    Alongside the financial ledger, keep a short review queue: one decision, the information available then, the uncertainty and the next check. A small pot with a clearly reconstructable error can teach more than a spectacular elimination with missing sizes and stacks. Choose some review hands before deciding whether their outcomes are emotionally interesting. Include an ordinary win, an ordinary fold and an unresolved decision over time. This is a practical selection habit, not a promise that a small curated queue represents every hand played. Track what the review actually established: corrected pot arithmetic, a chart-input mismatch, a range assumption tested or an unanswered question. Do not award yourself a “good decision” merely for writing a plausible explanation after winning. The hand-review guide keeps the record and later interpretation separate.

    Choose spending, re-entry and time limits before starting a session or trip. Keep essential living money separate from money allocated to playing. A loss is not a reason to enlarge the budget, and a successful vlog is not a reason to play a hand or buy another entry solely to manufacture drama. This page does not prescribe a bankroll size or an investment strategy. Variance calculations cannot make an unaffordable loss affordable. A useful session can end with a complete record and a break rather than another tournament or another hour of analysis. Download the results-review sheet

    GTO Wizard: variance and bankroll management is background reading on dispersion and risk. The ledger definitions, figures and constant-probability exercises here are independently stated and calculated. Prepared with AI assistance. No confidence interval, true ROI, personal cash probability or profitability claim is inferred from these examples. For a deeper mathematical treatment, Poker under uncertainty explains sample precision, test power and model assumptions. Its examples use hypothetical noise levels, not measurements of my performance.

    On this site · Make a vlog

    From hand notes to a poker vlog.

    An editing workbench for honest hand reconstruction, clear graphics, useful narration and poker episode companion pages.

    Read matching section

    Searchable article text, without exercise answers

    Creator workbench / Story After-play creator work. A proposed editing workflow with one actual public-page editing case. Hand examples and suggested narration are fictional, not accounts of a released episode. Recording permission and tournament rules must be checked separately.

    “I had ace-queen” supplies cards. “Which worse hands would bet?” supplies a question. Establish what the player is deciding before explaining the answer. The cards then have a purpose in the story. Separate footage, notes, recollection, and later study. A useful sequence does not require a dramatic result. The actual editing case below shows a small presentation change without claiming a new poker insight.

    For each candidate hand, ask whether it has a clear situation, a decision that can be explained, enough reliable detail to reconstruct and a reason for a viewer to care. Mark each as ready, needs verification or leave out. This is an editorial screen, not a numerical quality score. A smaller, well-recorded hand may be more useful than a dramatic incomplete one. A recollection should not acquire exact graphics simply because the edit needs them. Keep one primary question. Supporting hands should develop it rather than become a collection of unrelated all-ins.

    Write positions, blinds and ante, relevant starting stacks, known cards and street-by-street actions. Record whether each amount is a bet, a raise to a total or an additional call. Reconcile the pot after each street and account for uncalled refunds and side pots. Privately label each detail: visible in footage, noted at the time, remembered later, or unknown. Surface uncertainty that affects the explanation. A precise graphic does not make a remembered amount exact. A useful uncertainty label A fictional note says “about one-third pot.” Keep that approximation if trustworthy; do not invent “2,400.” If the missing amount could change the conclusion, keep that limitation beside the analysis. Keep filenames and timecodes private. Use neutral participant labels such as button or big blind. Remove identifying documents, messages, and unrelated personal details.

    Suggested narration labels for a reconstructed hand Voice What belongs there What happened Recorded action and clearly marked recollection. “The button raised to 2.5 BB.” What I thought then Your actual remembered reasoning, without importing cards or analysis learned afterward. What I think now Later calculations, alternative ranges and corrections, with their assumptions visible. Suggested fictional narration: “At the table I thought a missed draw was possible. During review I realized I had not estimated how often it would actually bet.” That distinguishes the original assumption from its later review. An edit can compress time without inventing causation. Label a reaction recorded later when it would otherwise appear to be the immediate reaction to a hand. Do not splice an unrelated player's expression into a decision sequence as evidence of a tell or motive.

    Reveal the board one street at a time. Keep the focal player's cards, positions, pot and current bet legible before adding extra statistics. Avoid showing an opponent's eventual cards or a known-card equity graphic before the story reaches the point when they became known, unless the sequence is explicitly framed as a later reconstruction. For “30% equity,” identify the information set: a revealed hand, assumed range, or particular model. Without a defensible calculation, omit the number. For a hand with an uncertain pot, use a visibly approximate label. For a side pot, explain which pot the focal player can win. Check the incremental call before animating a raise-to amount as fresh money. Review the sequence on a phone-sized screen with sound off. Can the reader identify the decision? Then listen without looking. Does the narration explain the stakes without requiring constant visual decoding? These are practical editorial checks, not formal accessibility certification. Captions should be reviewed for card ranks, suit names and poker terms rather than trusted blindly. Behind the edit / Actual website example

    This case documents an edit to this site's published hand-review guide . The page edit is real; the hand is fictional. It is not a recovered tournament note, a vlog screenshot, or evidence of a player's result. The guide already recorded the button holding king-queen of spades on a queen-eight-three flop, 30 big blinds effective at the start, and the action in order. Its arithmetic was already consistent. The editorial question was narrower: could someone arriving at the decision find the acting player, current pot, and extra call without first reading the whole explanation? Before: inside the action ledger The earlier published paragraph read: The pot is now 14.5 BB: 5.5 + 2 + 7. The button faces 5 BB more to call, not 7 BB. The information was present. Finding the decision required reading it within the chronological account. After: a decision snapshot Acting player Button Pot before the response 14.5 BB Additional amount to call 5 BB The snapshot now sits before the cards and full ledger. It gives the reader an entry point, not a replacement for the recorded action. What changed, and what stayed put The edit promotes three existing facts into labeled fields and adds a direct link to them. The full pot ledger stays below: 5.5 BB before the flop bet, 2 BB from the button, and a raise to 7 BB from the big blind. The extra call remains 7 minus the button's 2, or 5 BB. No cards, bets, opponent range, or result were added to make the presentation feel complete. “Pot before the response” identifies the moment the number describes. “Additional amount to call” distinguishes the missing chips from the opponent's total wager. The 30 BB effective stack remains labeled as a starting stack, rather than being relabeled as chips remaining. Those labels explain what a number means, not just how large to draw it. What this edit does not establish This was a presentation change, not the discovery of a miscounted pot or a strategic mistake. The example still supplies no opponent hand or eventual result. A clearer price does not settle whether calling, folding, or reraising is best. The earlier and revised explanations stop at the same unanswered decision. The fields are ordinary page text, so readers can select, enlarge, and print them rather than relying on text inside a picture. Whether the change actually helps new viewers remains a question for willing readers; no audience test or improvement in comprehension is claimed here. Inspect the revised decision and its ledger

    Opening: establish the question and enough context to care, without requiring a spoiler. Orientation: explain the tournament format and relevant stakes. Development: use a small number of hands or moments that change the situation. Review: revisit one assumption. Close: state the result honestly and name what remains unresolved. This is a starting structure, not a mandatory duration or platform-performance claim. Use travel footage for atmosphere or progression, not padding. Start with one coherent question, one documented hand, accurate graphics, reviewed captions, and a truthful ending. Add complexity only when it helps.

    Choose one addition the video does not already provide: a checked pot ledger, a precise guide reference, a useful chapter index, or a later correction. Publish one companion for the episode and a separate hand review only when it adds distinct analysis. One package, one source record Keep the verified facts, unknowns, actual remembered thinking, approved public image, and final video details together in a private packet. Give the owner one consolidated approval pass. Raw footage, draft narration, and completed worksheets stay outside the public repository. No finished video? An approved written story can stand alone. Do not label it an episode, invent a runtime, or use planned timestamps. No complete hand? Narrow the observation or choose a better-documented example. Keep outcomes in the existing spoiler disclosures when appropriate. A closed disclosure is a reading choice, not privacy. Do not duplicate the whole voiceover. Before publication, verify that any linked video is public and approved; chapter times match the released edit; graphics agree with the hand record; fictional examples are labeled; and any venue, music, footage and participant permissions are resolved. Remove license plates, private correspondence, account details and precise overnight locations from public material. The site's contact form is not a place to collect raw private footage. Use Behind the edit for a process case and After the session for later review. Link to the review method or graphic key only where useful. Updated October 7, 2026 : added an actual before-and-after page-editing case, shortened general guidance, and retained the single-packet workflow and publication fallbacks. Download the episode planning sheet

    Poker TDA's published rules address recording, electronic devices and outside assistance. They do not establish permission to film at a particular venue; consult the event's own rules and staff. The editing sequence is an original proposed workflow, not a proven audience-growth formula. Prepared with AI assistance. No footage, actual hand, private trip detail or published episode is implied by this guide.

    On this site · Try a decision

    Twelve checks. One useful repair.

    Twelve answer-reveal exercises on pot odds, ranges, short stacks, ICM, results and honest poker storytelling.

    Read matching section

    Searchable article text, without exercise answers

    Practice / Twelve checks After-play practice only. These are fictional exercises with explicitly limited models, not live-hand recommendations or an assessment of poker ability.

    Choose three questions rather than racing through all twelve. On paper or in a private note, write your answer and the assumption it needs. Open the explanation, mark the specific error if there is one and retry that kind of question in a later session. Correct arithmetic with the wrong model is still a useful mistake to catch. The answers use native disclosure panels. They do not require an account or extra JavaScript, and your answers are not entered on this website. Ordinary sitewide pageview analytics is described in the privacy notice . Nothing here uploads your notes or assigns you a skill score.

    01 / The pot was eighteen. A heads-up river pot contains 18 BB before your opponent bets 6 BB. You may call or fold. There are no deductions, side pots or tournament adjustments. What equity makes calling break even? 02 / Raised to eleven, not by eleven. The street starts with 12 BB. You bet 3 BB and the opponent raises to 11 BB. No one else is involved. How much must you add, and what is the final pot if you call? 03 / A flush draw and a promised river. A fictional flop model has nine target cards among 47 unseen cards. A call would need 25% equity in a no-future-betting model. A friend says, “The draw hits about 35% by the river, so calling is definitely profitable.” What information is missing? 04 / Risk five to win eight. You make a zero-equity river bluff of 5 BB into 8 BB. The only responses are fold or call, and you always lose when called. How often must the opponent fold? Is that the same as their calling-equity threshold?

    05 / Two aces are already visible. You hold the ace of spades and queen of clubs. The board is ace of hearts, seven of diamonds, two of clubs, nine of spades and three of hearts. How many AA, AK and KQs combinations can the opponent physically hold? 06 / Six possible bluffs, but only half bet. A constructed river range contains eighteen full-weight value combinations and six possible bluff combinations. Each bluff candidate bets at half frequency. Your hand beats every bluff and loses to every value hand. What share of this betting range do you beat?

    07 / A familiar-looking chart. Your recorded spot is five-handed, 4.5 BB at the start before posting, with a 1 BB big-blind ante and a prize jump approaching. The reference is six-max, 5 BB, no ante and chip value only. Is this an exact match? 08 / Where did two blinds go? A big blind starts with 8,000 chips at 500/1,000 with a 1,000 big-blind ante and posts both in full. How much remains behind? Which posted amount counts toward a live call?

    09 / A profitable chip gamble. Use the workshop's three equal 10-unit stacks and $50/$30/$20 prizes. In its no-blinds, no-ties transfer gamble, keeping the state is worth $33.33, winning is worth $43.33 and losing pays $20. Is a 55% win probability enough under standard ICM?

    10 / One trip, two results. Six entries cost $300 each including fees. Tournament returns total $2,100. Travel and lodging cost another $450. Calculate tournament profit, tournament ROI using entry costs, and trip surplus before other costs or taxes. 11 / The edit needs a comeback. A player reaches a precommitted entry limit. The footage has no triumphant ending, and the player considers another entry to recover the loss and improve the episode. What should the editing plan change?

    12 / The polished graphic knows too much. A hand note says the turn bet was “around half pot.” The draft overlay says exactly 3,200, shows an opponent's cards before showdown and labels a made-up percentage as equity. What should change before release?

    Classify the most useful miss: pot bookkeeping, probability, range weighting, mismatched inputs, prize model or storytelling. Choose one workshop and write one new example of your own. Retrying an already memorized answer is not the same as explaining a changed situation. Download the five-session study cycle

    The linked workshops provide the derivations and external background. All twelve exercises are original fictional teaching cases. Prepared with AI assistance. The answers test the stated calculations and distinctions, not whether you are a winning player. Use away from the table and follow the event's rules.

    On this site · Try a decision

    One river. Two different stories.

    A visual, fictional river exercise: price a call, test the assumed range and reveal two endings without confusing the result with the decision.

    Read matching section

    Searchable article text, without exercise answers

    Decision Lab / 01 After-play study. This is a fictional river exercise, not footage of an actual hand or a solved tournament recommendation. Work the question before revealing the explanations.

    You have a pair of aces. The opponent bets. A call could become the satisfying bluff-catch at the center of an episode, or the moment you wish you could take back. Before either story exists, what do you actually know? This lab uses the same physical cards as the range-combinations workshop , but turns the review into a sequence. You will separate an exact price from an assumed range, then watch two possible showdowns compete to rewrite the explanation. The snapshot / Before your decision Aces, a queen kicker, and a question. Your hand A Q River board A 7 2 9 3 The pot was 20 BB. Your opponent bets 10 BB. You are deciding whether to call or fold. Before the bet 20 BB Opponent adds 10 BB Still owed to call 10 BB The model: heads-up on the river; each player had 30 BB behind at the start of this street. No rake, side pots or further betting after a call. We compare calling with folding using chip value only. Raising is outside this exercise, not declared a bad action. Earlier action and tournament payouts are deliberately unspecified, so they cannot justify a range or an actual tournament verdict. 01 / Before the answer

    Write down the pot now, the final pot if you call, and the break-even equity. Do not supply an opponent's hand yet. This part does not require one. 02 / The assumption that matters

    Build a deliberately narrow teaching range: AA and AK for value, and KQs as the only bluff candidate. On this board, your hand loses to the value hands and beats the bluffs. There are no ties. We are supplying these range assumptions, not claiming that a real opponent would arrive here this way. After known-card removal there is one AA combination, eight AK combinations and three KQs combinations. Compare two constructions: every combination has equal weight, or every value hand has weight one while each bluff has weight one-half. 03 / The reveal

    Suppose the player calls. Both endings below are physically possible within the supplied range. They are alternative fictional outcomes, not consecutive hands. Open one, write the first verdict that comes to mind, and then open the other. Ending A Ending B A showdown adds one piece of evidence. It does not retroactively give the decision-maker access to hidden cards. You can celebrate or dislike an outcome while keeping the evaluation tied to what was knowable at the decision. 04 / Make the story better

    Try three sentences: one for the recorded action, one for what the fictional player thought, and one for the later review. The review should still make sense after either ending. The more interesting story is not necessarily “hero call” or “bad call.” It may be the gap between identifying one possible bluff and estimating the entire betting range. That question survives both endings and gives the next study session a concrete purpose.

    The call-price relationship is explained in PokerStars Learn's pot-odds lesson . Card-removal background is in GTO Wizard's combinatorics guide . This site's range workshop derives the specific combination counts. The scene, outcomes and narration are independently constructed teaching examples. Prepared with AI assistance. The calculation ignores tournament-prize effects and does not establish an optimal unrestricted strategy. No live assistance, personal result or validated solver output is provided. Use away from play.

    On this site · Try a decision

    The flush arrives. What can still change?

    Follow a fictional flush through the turn and river, count all remaining cards, and distinguish improving from winning.

    Read matching section

    Searchable article text, without exercise answers

    Decision Lab / 02 After-play study. A face-up replay about runouts. Opponent cards are shown for explanation, not treated as information available during ordinary betting. All cards and action are fictional, not a personal hand or a solver recommendation.

    A completed draw is an obvious turning point in a poker video. It can also hide the next question: what can still change? Follow the hand one street at a time, then count every possible river from the turn snapshot. The cast / Both hands shown Player A A J Player B 9 9 Start on the flop. Do not reveal the turn until you can describe both hands.

    9 7 2 B has three nines. A has four hearts across the hole cards and board, not a completed flush. B is ahead now. That is different from being guaranteed to win. Before revealing: name a kind of turn card that could put A ahead. Keep a description of the current hand separate from a probability of eventually winning.

    Continue after opening the turn. Both hands are exposed and one river remains. Which exact ranks could let B beat the flush? Count physical cards, not just rank names.

    Before opening the river, say what the best hand is now and what type of hand could overtake it. Neither statement needs the eventual result.

    Return to the turn with the four of hearts on the board. Keep A's cards fixed, but change B's hand to the nine of clubs and seven of clubs . How many rivers now beat A's flush?

    A useful fictional voiceover is: “The heart moved A ahead. With both hands exposed, ten of the forty-four possible rivers would still beat the flush. This river was one of them.” It explains the changing situation without calling the result inevitable or impossible. For your own review, save three items: cards known at the decision, cards that change the winner, and whether another bet must be paid before seeing them. A correct runout count does not by itself establish whether an earlier bet or call was good. Draws and future payments explains that last distinction. The board-reading guide gives a broader vocabulary for what can change.

    PokerStars: full houses explains why a full house beats a flush in standard hold’em. The displayed river counts are checked against all 44 remaining physical cards, not copied from a draw shortcut. The scene and arithmetic are independently constructed. Prepared with AI assistance. No real hand, personal result or optimal strategy is claimed.

    On this site · Try a decision

    Three all-ins. Two pots.

    Separate a fictional three-way all-in into a main pot, side pot and refund, then check the winners and final stacks.

    Read matching section

    Searchable article text, without exercise answers

    Decision Lab / 03 After-play study. A three-handed, no-ante hold’em example about contribution levels, pot eligibility and refunds. All cards and action are fictional, not a personal hand or a solver recommendation.

    Three players announce all-in. One player has the best hand, another wins the side pot, and the deepest stack gets uncalled chips back. To follow the result, the viewer needs more than a single pot total. This case is about settlement, not whether the shoves were strategically good. There are no deductions, bounties, additional players or earlier pots outside the contributions described here. Starting stacks / Before posting A / Button 6 BB A A B / Small blind 14 BB K K C / Big blind 25 BB Q Q The cards are shown for this fictional replay. The board is revealed later.

    The blinds are 0.5 / 1 BB. A shoves to six. B goes all-in to fourteen. C moves the full twenty-five forward. A and B have no more chips to match anything above fourteen. The totals 6, 14 and 25 BB already include the blinds where applicable. B adds 13.5 beyond the small blind; C moves 24 beyond the big blind. Do not add those blinds again. Before revealing: separate the 45 BB moved forward into money all three can win, money only two can win, and money that was never matched.

    Once the pots are separated, name the eligible players before comparing cards. A can win only the main pot. B and C contest both pots. The refund already belongs to C regardless of the board.

    How many chips does each player finish with? Can a player lose to the strongest hand and still gain chips? Does the deepest player actually bust?

    Use the same order of hand strengths, but suppose A moves four blinds, B ten and C sixteen. There are still no other chips or deductions. Rebuild the two pots and refund before opening the answer.

    Use separate on-screen labels for the main pot, side pot and refund. Keep the eligibility beside the amount: “Main 18 BB: A/B/C” and “Side 16 BB: B/C.” Do not animate returned chips as a showdown win. A short narration can say: “A wins the main pot with three aces. B beats C for the side pot, so B still gains two blinds. C keeps the eleven blinds nobody called.” That gives the audience the complete result without an elaborate explanation of every chip. The same layers matter in a study calculation. A short stack's call price must be compared with pots the player is eligible to win, not someone else's side pot. The bets and side-pots guide covers the underlying bookkeeping, and the graphics workbench explains how to keep it readable.

    PokerStars rules explains table stakes and side-pot eligibility. The displayed amounts are a fictional no-ante, no-deduction example; consult the event’s rules for actual procedures. The scene and arithmetic are independently constructed. Prepared with AI assistance. No real hand, personal result or optimal strategy is claimed.

    On this site · Live tournament preparation

    Your first live tournament, without the guesswork.

    Prepare for registration, finding your seat, asking procedural questions, and leaving with one useful observation.

    Read matching section

    Searchable article text, without exercise answers

    The unfamiliar part of a first tournament may not be the cards. It may be finding the registration desk, knowing when to sit down, or asking what a dealer's announcement means. Prepare for those moments before trying to learn every strategic detail. For the whole beginner route, use the first-session and first-month guide . It connects rules rehearsal, cost and stopping boundaries with the short foundation lessons.

    Choose an event whose game, total entry cost and possible duration you understand. Check whether it can continue on another day. Decide what you are comfortable spending for the whole outing, including transport and food, without relying on a payout. Choosing to watch, or deciding not to enter, is also a complete plan. For a venue-specific example, read the first-timer’s Thunder Valley guide . It connects current official information with registration questions to resolve before traveling. Put a number on the whole outing with the local, overnight and weekend budget examples , then copy the blank trip worksheet before committing. Read the structure-sheet guide before comparing events. A large starting chip count is not enough to judge the pace. Save the official event page and the organizer's contact information, then confirm anything that would change your decision to go.

    Ask the organizer what identification, membership card, payment method and eligibility checks apply. Confirm the event number and starting flight, not just its headline name. Ask whether advance payment still requires an in-person verification step. As a concrete example, the WSOP registration page describes identification and Caesars Rewards checks. It is an example of one organizer's process, not instructions for every room. Allow space in your plan for finding the desk and resolving an issue. Keep your ticket and receipt private. A photograph that includes a barcode, membership number or payment detail is not a suitable public trip update.

    Before taking a seat, check the table and seat assignment with staff. Tell the dealer that this is your first live tournament. Ask which denominations you have, what the current blinds and ante are, and where the button is. These are procedural questions, not requests for advice about which hand to play. Under TDA rules , players are responsible for following the action, acting in turn and making intentions clear. Rather than copying a chip motion you saw in a video, ask staff to explain an unfamiliar procedure before using it. A useful question is specific. “Is the total bet 2,000, and is it my turn?” asks for clarification. “Should I call with this hand?” asks someone else to make part of your decision. Save strategic discussion for a completed-hand review away from play.

    Before acting, ask the dealer to clarify the action or amount. For a disputed procedure, ask for the floor and describe what happened calmly. Do not reach into another player's stack, announce an opponent's cards, or try to settle a disagreement with a louder argument. The floor can explain the event's applicable procedure. The table-context guide explains common moments such as oversized chips and floor calls. Reading it beforehand is useful; opening a strategy aid at the table is not the purpose of this site.

    Pick one process goal: understand the announcements, keep track of your position, or preserve one hand accurately afterward. Avoid making “prove that I belong” the day's assignment. A first outing does not have to establish your ability or fund the next one. If one of those questions concerns playing 10–20 BB, review the short-stack lesson after the event . Start with its stack and ante record before comparing actions. When play is over, record what was unfamiliar and one question worth following up. Keep the result separate. The tournament-day guide covers breaks, moves and the end of a day; the printable planning sheets give you a small place to start.

    On this site · Live tournament preparation

    Read the structure before choosing the tournament.

    Compare total cost, starting big blinds, blind progression and time commitments using two fictional event structures.

    Read matching section

    Searchable article text, without exercise answers

    “Deep stack” and “big guarantee” are headlines. The structure sheet tells you what you are considering. Read it as a description of the time, cost and format, not as a forecast of how well you will do.

    Find the game and format, the full amount payable, the starting stack and blinds, the level schedule, and the event's stopping or continuation conditions. Read the rules about late registration, re-entry and multiple starting flights. Confirm which document applies to the exact date and event number. The format guide explains freezeouts, bounties and satellites. These are not interchangeable prize structures. A ticket event is not simply a normal tournament with a different name.

    Fictional comparison: Event A starts with 30,000 chips at blinds of 100/200. Event B starts with 50,000 chips at 200/500. Their starting depths are 30,000 / 200 = 150 BB and 50,000 / 500 = 100 BB . The smaller chip count is the deeper starting stack. Two fictional schedules, with no breaks during the first hour Scheduled play time Event A: big blind Event B: big blind Start 200 500 15 minutes 200 600 30 minutes 300 800 45 minutes 300 1,000 60 minutes 400 1,200 If the stacks were held constant solely for this comparison, an hour later A would represent 75 BB , while B would represent about 41.7 BB . Actual stacks will change through play and forced bets. These figures compare units and schedules; they do not predict survival, hands played or strategic advantage. Also check when antes begin and how they are posted. Dividing by the big blind does not capture every forced cost. Longer levels do not by themselves tell you how many hands will be dealt.

    Suppose a fictional event lists $250 toward prizes plus a $50 fee. The total entry price is $300 . The fee is 16.7% of the total payment , but 20% of the prize contribution . Both percentages can be arithmetically correct; comparing them as though they use the same denominator would be misleading. For travel and lodging beyond the entry, use three worked tournament trip budgets . They separate planned spending, optional reserves and the result after every actual cost. Read the actual breakdown instead of assuming every dollar goes into the regular prize pool. Ask about any mandatory charges not included in the headline. A lower fee alone does not establish that an event is profitable or appropriate for you.

    Find the start, registration cutoff, scheduled breaks, day-ending condition and any restart. Put these beside your own commitments. A late-registration cutoff is not a finishing time, and a published starting stack is not necessarily the depth you would receive after several blind increases. Read what the prize actually is and how it is allocated. For a satellite, confirm ticket restrictions; for a bounty event, confirm when bounties become eligible and how the advertised payment is split. The organizer's terms are more useful here than a screenshot shared without a date.

    Complete this sentence: “This event fits my time and spending limits; I understand its format; these details still need confirmation.” Mark missing information instead of replacing it with an assumption. Use the event planner to compare a small number of options. The Thunder Valley examples show how two completed events at the same venue differed in eligibility, re-entry, level length and later-day commitments.

    On this site · Live tournament preparation

    Registration, re-entry and the cost of another attempt.

    Separate advance registration, starting flights, re-entry and rebuys, then account for each payment without treating previous losses as a reason to continue.

    Read matching section

    Searchable article text, without exercise answers

    A registration window tells you when entry may be possible. It does not tell you whether another attempt fits your plan. Separate the event's permissions from your own limits before the first entry.

    Late registration allows a first entry after play begins, within the stated window. Re-entry allows a new entry after elimination, subject to the event's conditions. A rebuy is a purchase of additional chips under a rebuy event's eligibility rules. An add-on is a separate offered chip purchase at a specified stage. Do not assume one is available because another is. PokerStars' format definitions illustrate these distinctions for its tournaments. For a live event, the applicable structure sheet decides the actual limits, timing and eligibility.

    Confirm the event number, starting flight, full payment and registration deadline. Ask whether a deadline refers to payment, completion of verification or being seated. Check how alternates are handled and whether advance registration guarantees an immediate seat. Do not assume an online receipt completes every on-site step. For a particular room, use the Thunder Valley registration question list . It leaves payment methods and current desk arrangements as matters to confirm with that organizer. The WSOP registration page , for example, describes an in-person verification process for initial online registration. Use your organizer's current instructions rather than carrying that particular process over to another event. For multiple flights, ask whether qualifying more than once is possible and what happens to multiple qualifying stacks. Do not assume they combine, or that an existing qualifying stack can be abandoned. For entry through a ticket or satellite, check the restrictions attached to that ticket.

    Before play, decide a maximum total entry spend and a latest time at which you would even consider a new entry. Those are ceilings, not targets. Being permitted to spend more is different from having a reason to do so. Leaving after the first attempt remains an option even if your original plan allowed another. After elimination, step away before making a new purchase. Ask whether you still want the new experience at its current starting depth and time commitment. The earlier entry has already been spent. A desire to get it back does not reduce the next entry's price or improve its prospects.

    Fictional costs, not a suggested budget Two entries at $300 each cost $600 . With $90 of transport and food, the outing has cost $690 before any return. A $500 payout would leave a $100 tournament loss and a $190 loss including those trip costs . Counting only the last entry would conceal part of the cost. The overnight tournament budget extends this ledger to a room, travel and defined reserves. An unused re-entry reserve is available money, not a payment or loss. Keep the entry ledger and broader trip costs in separate columns so both remain visible. Record amounts actually paid, including additional chip purchases when relevant. Keep receipts and completed records private. For the distinction between cashes and overall results, read variance and honest results .

    Time, fatigue, a changed mood or simply not wanting another attempt are sufficient reasons to stop. Watching a video or reviewing a completed hand later does not require paying another entry. When gambling is becoming difficult to control, changing the study plan is not the only response available. The National Council on Problem Gambling provides a current route to support. That resource is separate from coaching or performance advice.
