    On this site · Cash-game study

    Your first live cash-game session.

    Prepare for a live cash table: questions for the desk, buying chips, taking a seat, leaving and recording the session without double-counting costs.

    Read matching section

    Searchable article text, without exercise answers

    Before taking a seat, know the game, the permitted buy-in, the charges and your own stopping point. You do not need a tournament entry or a software subscription to understand a cash-game session. You can also decide not to play. For the whole beginner route, use the first-session and first-month guide . It connects rules rehearsal, cost and stopping boundaries with the short foundation lessons. This guide is for: someone who knows basic hold'em but has not joined a live cash table. New to the betting sequence? Start with one complete hand . The preparation steps below are a suggested checklist, not a room's official rules.

    Set a total gambling-spend limit and a leaving time before you enter the room. Keep transport, food and essential expenses outside that amount. A posted minimum buy-in is an entry condition, not advice about what you can afford. When the available game exceeds your limit, skip it rather than increasing the limit to fit the game. Use the room's official information to check its hours, entry requirements and game listings. Ask what identification and membership procedures apply. A listing on a third-party directory is a research lead, not proof that a seat exists or that you are eligible to play. The player-protection guide explains how to distinguish operator claims from the applicable authority.

    A useful opening question is: “I am new to this room. What hold'em cash games are running, what is the buy-in range, and how are the games charged?” Confirm the betting structure, number of seats, any ante or straddle, and whether the displayed range includes a match-the-stack option. Do not assume another room's conventions apply here. Visiting Lincoln, California? The Thunder Valley guide separates a cash-game waitlist from tournament registration and lists the details to confirm with the room. Ask how the waiting list works, how your seat will be called and where to obtain chips. Get the assigned table and seat from staff rather than occupying an apparently empty chair. Before buying in, read the cash-game cost guide : a percentage, a cap, a fixed collection and a time charge are different inputs. A fictional desk conversation The board says “1/3 NLH.” You learn that this invented room allows 100 to 300 in chips and takes a charge from qualifying pots. That tells you more than “1/3,” but you still need the charge amount and trigger. A possible straddle also changes the betting context. None of these invented amounts are a recommendation or a quote for a real room.

    Confirm your buy-in, check the chip denominations and ask when you may receive a hand. Posting requirements, waiting for the big blind, missed blinds and table changes depend on house rules. Do not move chips or take cards based on a rule remembered from a tournament. One published example is PokerStars Live's cash-game rules . Its table-stakes rule ordinarily limits a pot to money in play at the start, with specified house-approved exceptions. It also sets its own buy-in, entry, seat-change and return-to-game procedures. These illustrate what to ask about, not a universal rulebook for your room.

    Wait for your turn and make your intended action clear. Before an unclear action, ask the dealer to clarify the amount facing you or the house procedure for announcing a raise. Leave chips countable, protect your cards, and let the dealer finish settling a pot before moving anything. For a disputed rule or an uncomfortable interaction, ask staff to assist instead of arguing with other players. Keep other players' live hands and your strategic questions out of table discussion. PokerStars Live's published rules, for example, prohibit outside consultation during a hand. A phone policy is not permission to use an equity calculator or ask someone else how to act. Use this site away from play; the table-procedure guide offers more context.

    Finish any hand you are involved in, then tell the dealer you are leaving and ask where to cash out. Do not remove part of a stack while continuing unless the house expressly permits the particular transaction. Rejoining or changing tables may carry buy-in obligations, so ask rather than treating a brief departure as a way to reset a stack. You do not owe the table another orbit or a chance to win your losses back. Treat reaching your planned limit, being tired or feeling pressure as reasons to stop. Ask staff for help with a safe departure when needed. Gambling-support resources are available without completing this learning path.

    After leaving, record each buy-in, each top-up and the final cash-out. A fictional buy-in of 200 plus a top-up of 100 followed by a cash-out of 260 produces 260 - 200 - 100 = -40 , not a 60 profit. Charges or tips already paid from the stack are already reflected in that difference; separately paid costs need their own line. Then choose one completed hand worth understanding. Use positions instead of identifying other players, label uncertain amounts and record only what you actually know. The five-session study route can use a fictional hand instead of requiring another gambling session. Source boundary: the linked PokerStars Live rules were read for this guide on October 8, 2026. They describe that operator's procedures, not rules for every live room. The desk questions and planning sequence are original suggestions. Published October 8, 2026 . Prepared with AI assistance. Examples are fictional, not Nolan's hands or results. Study before or after play, not as live assistance.

    On this site · Cash-game study

    Understand the cost of a cash game.

    Compare rake, caps, fixed collections, extra drops and time charges with fictional schedules and a reconciled session ledger.

    Read matching section

    Searchable article text, without exercise answers

    The amount printed next to the blinds is not the full cost of a cash game. First identify what gets charged, when it gets charged and whether the amount you are reviewing already includes it. This is a bookkeeping guide with invented schedules, not a ranking of rooms or a prediction of profitability. Obtain the schedule for the exact game from its operator. PokerStars' own rake page , for example, distinguishes game types, stakes and the number of players dealt into a hand. It does not supply a live room's charges.

    Percentage rake with a cap A fraction of a qualifying pot, limited by a stated maximum. Record the percentage, cap, rounding and qualifying condition. Fixed collection A stated amount charged according to the house's trigger, rather than a percentage of every pot. Ask whether the collection changes with game size or player count. Promotional or jackpot drop A separate deduction under its own conditions. Do not assume it is included in a quoted rake cap, or treat a possible future prize as a guaranteed offset. Time charge A charge per player or seat for a stated interval. Confirm how partial intervals and breaks are handled. Do not divide it by a single pot as though it were that pot's rake. “No flop, no drop” should be checked against the exact schedule, not assumed from the phrase cash game. PokerStars describes its own first-betting-round exception in the source above. A different provider or a separate promotional charge may have different conditions.

    Fictional schedules: Game A takes 5% of the final pot, capped at 6, plus a separate 1 drop. Game B takes a fixed 5. Every pot below qualifies for both schedules, no charge has already been removed, and there are no other fees, refunds or side pots. These are deliberately simplified whole-number examples, not observed room prices. Same pot, different deductions Final pot before charges A: rake + drop A: awarded B: charge B: awarded 20 1 + 1 = 2 18 5 15 80 4 + 1 = 5 75 5 75 200 6 + 1 = 7 193 5 195 The cheaper deduction changes with the pot. Comparing only the percentage or only the cap would miss that. This table does not choose a game for you: different rules, actual pot distributions, personal limits and the rest of the playing conditions are not modeled.

    Suppose an invented game charges 7 per half-hour per player . Six complete charged intervals cost one player 42 . With eight continuously charged players, the table pays 112 per hour in aggregate. Neither number is a charge that one winner should subtract from one pot. Track the intervals actually billed. Sitting out, arriving halfway through an interval or leaving early does not automatically establish a refund or pro-rata charge. Ask the room. Do not use an assumed hands-per-hour figure to claim an exact personal rake comparison.

    The existing cash-game river example shows a charge changing a marginal call calculation. It assumes no further betting, a specified pot and a deduction from the final award. Read those assumptions before using its percentage. An already paid time charge is normally part of the session record, not a new cost created by one later call. Conversely, a deduction that changes when a pot grows belongs in the modeled branch where it changes. A pot already displayed after rake must not have that same rake removed again. The study calculators state their no-rake assumptions; they do not silently account for a room's fee schedule.

    Fictional session record Buy-in: 200. Top-up: 100. Cash-out: 260. Stack balance: -40 . Suppose 8 in tips were paid from those chips and pot deductions also came from the chips. Those costs are already reflected in the -40. A further 28 time charge was paid separately from a wallet, not from the chips. Including that makes the gambling-session cash flow -68 . A separate 12 transport expense makes the overall trip cash flow -80 . These are bookkeeping views, not tax categories or long-run win-rate estimates.

    Write the exact game and official source; the charging method and trigger; the cap and any extra drop; whether your pot is before or after deductions; and which costs were paid outside the chips. Mark an unconfirmed item as unknown. A precise-looking percentage is not a substitute for a missing fee rule. Use the blank cash-game study sheet to keep this record privately. Then review a completed hand, not whether a single session happened to finish ahead. Read results in context before interpreting a short sample. Source boundary: the operator rake page was read October 8, 2026 for how to identify a schedule, not to quote current live-room prices. The compared schedules, charges and ledger above are original fictional examples. Published October 8, 2026 . Prepared with AI assistance. Examples are fictional, not Nolan's hands or results. Study before or after play, not as live assistance.

    On this site · Cash-game study

    A practical cash-game study route.

    Five self-paced study sessions, free source shortlists and a private worksheet: describe the game, price a call, inspect ranges and finish one review.

    Read matching section

    Searchable article text, without exercise answers

    A useful cash-game study session ends with something you can explain: a game description, a checked pot, a range assumption or a question to investigate. This five-session route starts with free reading and does not require playing for money. New to live rooms? Start with your first cash-game session . Already have a completed hand? Begin at the first step that reveals something missing from your record. These are self-paced study tasks, not a required course or a promise to improve your results.

    Read: the cash-game assumptions and the cost guide . Outside source: an example of an official rake schedule , used to see what needs recording rather than to copy a live room's prices. Produce: five lines naming the game and stakes, positions, relevant stacks, the charging rule, and who can still act. An invented 1/3 game with stacks of 300 and 180 is 60 BB effective between those two players before any chips are committed. A third player requires another comparison; there is no single effective stack for every possible pot. Stop when: you can explain why “100 BB cash” is not a complete description. Keep unknowns visible rather than filling them from a convenient chart.

    Read: the pot-odds workshop . Outside source: a step-by-step call-price explanation . Use the source for the accounting, then check whether later action or charges invalidate a simple threshold. Produce: a three-line ledger. In a fictional heads-up river pot of 60 before a 30 bet, the current pot is 90 and the extra call is 30. With no charges or further betting, the final pot is 120 and the threshold is 30 / 120 = 25% . This is not an estimate of the hand's equity. Stop when: you can distinguish the current pot from the final pot and name an assumption needed to turn the price into a decision.

    Read: the combination workshop . Outside source: the beginner combinatorics article . List specific combinations before assigning any weights. Produce: two explicitly hypothetical opponent ranges for a completed or fictional hand. Explain why changing one assumption might change the conclusion. These ranges remain hypotheses. A shown hand is one observation, not verification of an entire range. As a small card-removal check, holding A♠ K♦ leaves three available aces, so only 3 pocket-ace combinations remain, rather than six. An equity calculator is optional, not required. Before using one, write the hands, board and range assumptions on paper. An equity percentage alone does not model every future bet. The equity-realization explanation addresses that gap.

    Read: the multiway workshop and its linked side-pot case . Outside source: the multiway discussion , especially the distinction between shared defense and a personal heads-up quota. Use the fictional four-way cash hand for this session, then copy its blank review sheet and change one range assumption. Produce: an action-order note and a pot-eligibility sketch. Name every player who can still raise and every pot your hand can win. Do not include an uncalled amount in a contested pot. You can complete this with the site's fictional cases instead of collecting a new hand. Stop when: you can explain why a cheaper-looking call is not necessarily better when another player remains to act. Use the exercise's answer panel only after writing your own explanation.

    Read: how to review a hand without starting from its result . Outside source: the expected-value introduction for the distinction between an outcome and an average over specified possibilities. Produce: a short conclusion that names the facts, the assumed range, the cost model and the remaining uncertainty. Change the ending from a win to a loss: which parts of your explanation should remain the same? A one-session result cannot verify a strategy or a long-run win rate. Select further material only after naming what is unresolved. Use the task-based tool shortlists for range analysis or model setup. Reading public documentation can be enough; buying access is not the required final step.

    These are editorial starting choices, not performance rankings. Each offers a different kind of help. Expanded fit notes and current catalogue context remain attached to the listing.

    Download a blank Markdown copy for a notes app or text editor. No answers are submitted to this site. Use positions and fictional examples instead of identifying other players. Download the cash-game study sheet Source boundary: outside links lead to reviewed directory listings and their publishers. Selection notes explain intended tasks; they do not certify software or endorse every conclusion in an article. The study sequence and examples here are original suggestions.     On this site · Learn the basics

    Your first poker decisions.

    Learn to read starting hands, choose legal actions, count calls and compare the best five cards through twelve beginner poker exercises with explained answers.

    Read matching section

    Searchable article text, without exercise answers

    Stage 1 of 6: Name your legal actions, count an additional call and build the best five cards. Work through this short lesson, then pause or continue. The full explanation and other practice are available below. 1. Learn one idea Your cards, your turn and your payment are different questions. Your two private cards belong to you. The board is shared by everyone still in the hand: three cards on the flop, a fourth on the turn and a fifth on the river. On the flop, those five available cards make your current hand. On the turn and river, choose the best five again. At showdown, when all five shared cards are out, you may use zero, one or two private cards. A check keeps your hand without paying when you owe nothing. A call matches a wager; a raise increases it. Folding gives up your claim to the pot. On your turn facing a bet, with enough chips and raising permitted, you may fold, call or raise. You cannot check past the bet. Count a call using this betting round only: the current total wager minus what you already paid on this round. Payments on an earlier round stay in the pot. The amount owed says what a call costs, not whether it is a good decision. 2. Follow a worked example It is your turn on the flop. The opponent bets 4. You have paid nothing on this round and have ample counters. Both short-lesson examples exclude antes, fees and all-ins. Your private cards Shared flop Your best five are Q-Q-J-8-3: a pair of queens. Calling adds 4 - 0 = 4 counters. You can fold, call 4 or make a legal raise; checking is unavailable. Having a pair does not choose an action for you. 3. Explain a changed situation A different hand reaches this flop. You paid 6 preflop. The opponent now bets 7; you have paid nothing on this new round. It is your turn, with ample counters and raising permitted. Your private cards Shared flop Your task: Name your best five. How many additional counters would a call add? Explain whether checking is available and whether the earlier 6 reduces the call. Say your explanation or write it on paper before opening the answer. Before you move on: Explain why paying on the previous round does not cover a new bet. If that is still difficult, use the repair link or pause and return. Your explanation stays with you. Updated October 15, 2026: Added a short course lesson with a worked example, a changed situation to explain and a direct next lesson; the full reference remains below. Prepared with AI assistance. All scenes are fictional teaching examples. This is a self-check, not a skill score or betting recommendation.

    Knowing the hand rankings is a start. The next step is looking at a table and understanding what you can do, what it costs, and what your cards actually make. Work through one small decision at a time. For complete beginners to standard 52-card no-limit Texas hold'em. Every scene below is fictional. Use a deck, counters or paper; no wager, account or purchase is needed. These are explanations of mechanics and questions to ask, not a starting-hand chart or a promise of profitable play. Start from zero Read the short explanation, say your answer, then open the answer panel. Repeat a lesson when its words still feel unfamiliar. Begin with your two cards Know the rules already? Try the checkpoints without looking at the explanations first. Each answer names the mistake it is designed to catch. Try a complete practice hand Need a quick reference? Keep the full rules and rankings nearby. You do not need to memorize a glossary before starting. Follow the rules walkthrough

    Each player receives two private cards, called hole cards. The shared cards form the board: the first three are the flop, the fourth is the turn, and the fifth is the river. A card has a rank , such as an ace or a seven, and a suit : spades, hearts, diamonds or clubs. Aces can be high, or low in an A-2-3-4-5 straight. A pocket pair means your two private cards have the same rank. Suited means they share a suit; offsuit means they do not. Those labels describe useful features, not a decision by themselves. A pair begins with a made pair. Two nearby ranks can work together in straights. Suited cards can work together in flushes. None of that means every pair, connector or suited hand should be played in every situation. Three different starting shapes A pocket pair: two eights. Suited connectors: a jack and ten of hearts. An ace with a lower, offsuit companion. If you see AKs , the final “s” means suited; AKo means offsuit. These are groups of hands, not particular suits. In a full card code such as As , however, “s” means spades. This guide shows the suit symbols and gives each displayed card an accessible full name.

    An ace is not a guarantee of a strong hand after the flop. When two players pair the same high card, their other cards can decide the winner. A hand is often called dominated when an opponent shares its higher rank and has a better accompanying card. The weaker hand can improve and still be behind. A pair of aces is not the whole comparison Your cards: Other player's cards: Final board: Before committing chips, identify your position, the price, the effective stack and the action before you. Position tells you who acts before and after you; acting later gives you their actions to consider. In a two-player contest, the effective stack is the smaller relevant stack: with 60 and 100 chips, those players can each contest at most 60 from that point. An unopened pot and a raise followed by a caller are different situations, even when your two cards are identical. Folding is an ordinary option, not a failure to participate. Avoid a rule such as “any ace” or “any two suited cards.” Learn the situation before using a chart. A chart must match the game, stack depth, position and action it describes. The chart-reading guide explains those inputs when you are ready; this lesson does not prescribe a fixed range or bet size.

    Your choices depend on the current wager, not just your cards. On a new postflop betting round with no bet yet, you can check or bet . Facing a wager, the usual choices are fold , call or raise , when a raise is permitted and your stack allows it. Short all-ins can create exceptions; ask the dealer when the action is unclear. Three distinctions to say out loud Action What it does Check versus fold Checking keeps your hand in without adding chips when nothing is owed. Folding gives up your claim to the pot. Call versus raise Calling matches the current wager, subject to your stack. Raising increases the wager that others must respond to. Bet versus raise A bet opens wagering on a street. A raise increases an existing wager. The big blind is already a live preflop wager.

    The button is a marker identifying the dealer position, even when a staff member deals. The small blind and big blind are forced wagers posted before the cards. The cutoff is the seat immediately before the button in preflop action order. At a table with three or more players, preflop action begins clockwise after the big blind. After the flop, action begins with the first remaining player clockwise after the dealer button. Skip folded players and players who are all-in with no chips left to bet. Do not act simply because the player beside you moved: follow the actual order. The big blind has already paid a live wager. If other players only call it, the big blind still gets an option to check or raise. The small blind usually has more to add to complete a call. An ante is a separate contribution and does not reduce the amount owed to a bet. An unraised six-player pot Blinds are 1/2, with no ante or fees. The first two players fold. The cutoff calls 2, the button folds, and the small blind adds 1 to the 1 already posted. The big blind has already posted 2. All players have ample chips. Two-player exception: when the entire table is heads-up, the button is the small blind and acts first preflop, last after the flop. This does not change the positions midway through a hand just because everyone else folded. The position guide develops the difference between a seat and acting after an opponent.

    Keep two separate numbers: the current total wager on this street , and what you have already contributed on this street. Their difference is the additional call, unless your remaining stack is smaller. Previous-street contributions are already in the pot and do not pay for a new bet. At a live table, wait until it is your turn and the amount is clear. State your action clearly before moving chips. Do not experiment with silent chip motions: one oversized chip facing a bet is normally a call under TDA procedures, not automatically a raise. The house or tournament rules govern the actual ruling.

    A betting round is not finished merely because every player has acted once. A later bet or raise can send the action back around. Players who have not folded and are not all-in must respond to the current wager; everyone entitled to act must have had that opportunity. When all but one player have folded, the hand ends without a showdown. A player who is all-in still has a claim to eligible pots and has not folded. Three players on the flop A checks, B bets 4, C calls 4, and A raises to 12. All three began the street with enough chips to continue. The action goes back to B.

    In hold'em, use the best five cards from your two private cards and the five shared cards. You may use two, one or zero private cards. There is no sixth-card tiebreaker, and suits do not break equal hands. This differs from Omaha, which requires exactly two private cards. One private card plays Your cards: Board: The board plays Your cards: Other player's cards: Board: For more comparisons, open four worked showdowns . A useful habit is to say the category first, then list the five cards. “I have an ace” is not a complete description of your final hand.

    Use this scene before looking at any answer. It is a mechanics exercise, not a recommended betting line. Four players use counters with blinds 1/2, no ante and no fees. Everyone starts with 100. The first player folds, the button raises to 6, the small blind folds its posted 1, and the big blind calls. Preflop: Say the additional cost of the big blind's call, then total the pot. Flop, K♠ 8♣ 3♦: The big blind checks, the button bets 4, and the big blind calls. Update the pot. Turn, 7♥: Both check. Does the pot change? River, 2♠: Both check. The button shows K♥ J♦ and the big blind shows K♣ T♦. Compare the best five.

    The order felt confusing: replay one hand from the deal to showdown . The amount owed was unclear: work through bets, raises and side pots . The winner surprised you: use kickers and ties . The mechanics now make sense: continue to your starting hand in context , stage 2 of the free course. You are considering a first visit: read first cash-game preparation or first tournament preparation , including costs and room procedures. Being able to answer these questions is a learning checkpoint, not evidence of a profitable strategy or readiness to risk money. You can keep learning with a deck and counters. If you choose to play for money, follow local eligibility rules, use only an amount you can afford to lose and do not treat losses as something you must win back. Support and safer-play resources remain available without an account.

    Stage 2 of 6: Describe position and earlier action before judging two private cards. Work through this short lesson, then pause or continue. The full explanation and other practice are available below. 1. Learn one idea Read the action before deciding what two cards mean. The button marks the dealer position. At a table of three or more players, preflop action starts after the big blind and proceeds clockwise. In a six-player game, the initial order is first seat, next seat, cutoff, button, small blind, big blind. The cutoff is the seat immediately before the button. After the flop, the first remaining player clockwise after the button acts first. The button therefore acts after a blind on the flop, but the blinds still have initial turns after the button preflop. A later raise can give earlier players another decision. Describe your seat, earlier action, price and relevant stacks before using a hand label or chart. Suited means your two cards share a suit; it does not establish that playing them is best. These examples use six players who began with 100 counters each, blinds 1/2 and no ante or fees. 2. Follow a worked example The first seat, next seat and cutoff fold. You are on the button with queen-jack of spades. The small blind has posted 1 and the big blind 2. Neither blind has taken its initial turn. Find your seat before reading your cards. Six seats, numbered clockwise for this hand. Seat 1 starts preflop; the button moves for the next hand. Payments are counters on this round. Seat 1 First seat Folded Paid 0 Seat 2 Next seat Folded Paid 0 Seat 3 Cutoff Folded Paid 0 Seat 4 Button Dealer button You: your turn Paid 0 Seat 5 Small blind Not acted yet Paid 1 Seat 6 Big blind Not acted yet Paid 2 Your private cards You face an unraised big blind. A call would add 2 because you have paid zero. Both blinds still have decisions after your initial action; either may raise. Being on the button does not finish preflop. This description does not prescribe a call or a raise. Next initial turns before the flop Small blind Big blind First turns on the flop, if every live seat continues Small blind Big blind Button (you) Skip folded seats. These are initial turns, not a complete betting round: a later bet or raise can give an earlier player another decision. The maps describe six players, not the special two-player blind rules. 3. Explain a changed situation You now sit in the small blind with the same private cards. The first two seats fold, the cutoff raises to 6, and the button calls 6. Your posted small blind is 1. The big blind has not yet acted. Find your seat before reading your cards. Six seats, numbered clockwise for this hand. Seat 1 starts preflop; the button moves for the next hand. Payments are counters on this round. Seat 1 First seat Folded Paid 0 Seat 2 Next seat Folded Paid 0 Seat 3 Cutoff Already acted Paid 6 Seat 4 Button Dealer button Already acted Paid 6 Seat 5 Small blind You: your turn Paid 1 Seat 6 Big blind Not acted yet Paid 2 Your private cards Your task: How much more would your call add? Who still has an initial decision after you? Explain two ways this situation differs from the worked example, despite the same private cards. Say your explanation or write it on paper before opening the answer. Before you move on: Name the players still to act and the earlier action before describing your private cards. If that is still difficult, use the repair link or pause and return. Your explanation stays with you. Updated October 16, 2026: Added six-seat table maps and action-order comparisons to the short lesson, showing why the button and blinds act in different orders before and after the flop. Prepared with AI assistance. All scenes are fictional teaching examples. This is a self-check, not a skill score or betting recommendation.

    “Should I play these cards?” becomes a much better question when you can describe the table around them. Learn how position, earlier action, the price and stack depth change what a starting hand can do. Then use eight small exercises to practice seeing those differences. A beginner lesson for standard 52-card no-limit Texas hold'em. Every scene is fictional and uses chips or counters, not Nolan's recorded hands. No wager, playing account or purchase is needed. If calling, raising or the order of a hand is unfamiliar, begin with your first poker decisions . Learn one difference Read a section, answer its question aloud, then open the explanation. The goal is to notice what changed between the two scenes. Start with the cards Put it together Already know position and big blinds? Reconstruct a complete preflop decision without guessing the opponents' cards. Try the final exercise Keep a useful note Copy a short record onto your own paper. Separate what happened from what you assumed. Use the study template

    Preflop means before the first three shared cards appear. Your two private cards have possibilities, not a guaranteed finishing hand. A range is a collection of hands someone could hold or choose to play. Comparing your hand with one imagined opponent hand is different from comparing it with an appropriate range. Hand features to recognize, not a list of automatic plays Feature What to notice A high pair, such as two kings Already a pair, with strength against many unpaired hands. Shared cards and opponents' holdings can still produce a better hand. Two high cards, such as ace-queen Can make high pairs. When an opponent shares your paired rank, kickers can matter. Connected cards, such as jack-ten Can work together in straights. A straight possibility does not guarantee a useful flop or a winning straight. Suited cards Can work together in a flush. A low flush can lose to a higher one. A small pair, such as two fives Already a pair, but higher shared cards can complicate later decisions. A hoped-for third five is not a plan by itself. Several features can combine: jack-ten of hearts is both suited and connected. Features can also come with a weakness: ace-seven offsuit can pair the ace yet lose to a better kicker. Use the worked domination example if that comparison is new. A helpful beginner habit is to describe both an advantage and a vulnerability before declaring a hand “good.” Do not let a suited label excuse every price, or let one memorable win turn a weak situation into a rule.

    At a six-player table, the initial preflop order is first to act, the next seat, cutoff, button, small blind and big blind. The cutoff is the seat immediately before the button. Some seat labels vary between teaching materials; the number of players and actual action order are the useful facts. For the two scenes below, everyone starts with 100 big blinds before posting, the blinds are 1/2, and there is no ante. Your cards are jack-ten of hearts in both scenes. Nothing about the cards changed. Scene A: You are first to act. All five other players still have their initial decision. Scene B: You are on the button. The first three players folded. Only the two blinds remain to take their initial decision. Being later in the order gives you other players' actions to consider. It does not reveal their private cards. The big blind acts last in the initial preflop order but usually acts before the button after the flop. “Last preflop” and “in position after the flop” are different descriptions. Heads-up has a special order: the button posts the small blind and acts first preflop, then last postflop. See position and stacks for the longer explanation.

    An unopened pot has no voluntary call or raise yet: earlier players have folded, or you are first to act. Posting a blind does not count as a voluntary opening raise. A limp is a preflop call of the big blind. An open-raise enters an unopened pot with a raise. Raising after someone has limped is a different situation. A three-bet preflop is a re-raise after that first raise; it does not mean three times the previous amount. For a concrete sequence with blinds 1/2: someone raises to 6, and another player raises to 18. That second raise is a three-bet. A later raise would be a four-bet. “To 18” means a total contribution of 18 on that street, not 18 added on top of an earlier contribution. Same king-queen, different action At a six-player table with blinds 1/2 and no ante, you are the cutoff with king-queen of spades. In scene A, the two earlier players fold. In scene B, the first player raises to 6 and the next calls 6. The button and both blinds are still behind you in either scene. All players began with 200 chips. Always read the action heading of a reference. “Cutoff, unopened” is not the same question as “cutoff, facing a raise and a call.” Also distinguish opening a pot from defending a blind. A chart cell has meaning inside its stated situation, not everywhere those two ranks appear.

    The cost of calling is what you must add now to match the current wager, subject to your remaining stack. It is not the total pot, not the opponent's whole stack and not a ticket to see every remaining shared card. Future betting can create new decisions even when your call ends the current round. In these separate six-player scenes, blinds are 1/2 with no ante or fees. The cutoff raises to 6 and the button folds. The earlier players have folded, and everyone has chips left after matching 6. Same raise, different blind decisions You are Already posted Add to call Still to act Small blind 1 5 Big blind Big blind, after the small blind folds 2 4 A call completes this preflop round In that big-blind scene the pot is 9 before your call and 13 after it. The fraction 4/13 is about 30.8%, but it is not a sufficient preflop calling rule : later betting and how the hand reaches showdown matter. The clean river examples in the pot-odds workshop first remove those complications. A small-looking price and a large-looking pot are prompts to calculate, not reasons to stop thinking.

    A stack's chip count becomes more informative when compared with the big blind. For these examples, a starting stack is measured immediately before posting this hand's blind or ante. State that convention in your notes so you do not mix starting chips with chips remaining after bets. Starting stack in BB = starting chips / big blind. The small blind is not the denominator, and a separate ante does not change which number is the big blind. If an ante exists, record it separately because it affects the pot and the situation. Shallower stacks leave less room for later bets relative to the blinds. Deeper stacks create more possible future exposure, not an obligation to commit it. Neither depth guarantees safety or profit. Tournament payouts and remaining players can also affect decisions; a cash-game chart should not silently stand in for a tournament decision near a payout boundary.

    Between two players, the smaller starting stack limits how many starting chips each can contest against the other in this hand. That is their effective starting stack . When several players remain, record the separate comparisons. A single number can hide an important deeper opponent. “I cover them” means you have at least as many relevant chips, not that those chips are already yours. If you instead report stacks remaining at a later decision, label the street and contributions already made. Do not compare your remaining stack with an opponent's starting stack as though the numbers describe the same moment.

    A small pair may improve to three of a kind, and suited cards may improve to a flush. The possibility of receiving later bets is often discussed as implied odds . The missing word is “if”: if you improve, if your hand is best, and if an opponent contributes more. A deep stack makes more chips available; it does not promise to pay them. Two ceilings on a possible payout You are the button with two fives and 200 chips before posting. The cutoff raises to 6 at blinds 1/2 with no ante. Compare two separate scenes: the cutoff began with 14 and now has 8 behind, or began with 200 and now has 194 behind. Both blinds still have a turn. Later costs can move the other way, too. You might make a pair or a low flush, continue paying and lose to a better hand. This is why “I will win a big pot when I hit” needs more than a hopeful ending. Do not substitute a fixed stack multiplier for a full decision without understanding the assumptions behind that shortcut.

    Use this final fictional scene. Six players are in a fictional no-limit hold'em cash game with blinds 1/2, no ante and no fees. You are the button with ace-jack of spades. Starting stacks before posting: you 150, cutoff 60, small blind 200, big blind 400. The first two players fold. The cutoff raises to 6. It is your turn. Before opening the answer, write the current pot, your additional call, the players behind, your starting stack in BB and your effective starting stack against each remaining opponent. Then name what you still do not know. You are reconstructing a study problem; the example has no prescribed best action. The progress is being able to explain why this is a particular decision, instead of asking whether ace-jack is always a good hand. To study choices next, use how to read a preflop chart . To understand what earlier action can and cannot tell you, continue with ranges and reasons for betting .

    Copy these prompts onto paper or into your own private notes. Use invented player labels, and record only information you are entitled to use. This page has no form and stores no answers. Setting: game, cash or tournament, number of players, blinds, ante and known fees. Cards and seat: exact private cards or hand class, your position and players still behind. Action so far: folds, calls and raises in order. Label raise totals clearly. Price and depth: pot now, amount already contributed, additional call and relevant starting stacks in BB. Evidence: what you observed, what you assumed and what is unknown. Study question: one decision, a reference matching the setup, and any mismatch that limits its answer. A useful completion check: explain the last scene without reading its answer, then change just one input and describe what needs reconsidering. Do not grade yourself by a later pot won or lost. You can keep practicing without money; learning these concepts is not proof of a winning strategy. Safer-play and support resources are available without an account.

    Stage 3 of 6: Name a made hand and a draw separately, then read the action. Work through this short lesson, then pause or continue. The full explanation and other practice are available below. 1. Learn one idea Name the hand you have and the draw you still need. A made hand describes what your cards make now. A draw describes cards that could improve it. You can have both. A pair needs two cards of one rank; a flush needs five of one suit. Four cards of one suit are not a completed flush. Count distinct cards, including your private cards and the shared flop. Then describe the action separately. A check does not reveal a weak hand, and a possible improvement does not guarantee the winning hand. These scenes assume it is your turn, ample counters, no all-ins and raising permitted. 2. Follow a worked example You are on the button. Only you and the big blind reached the flop. The big blind checks to you; nobody has bet on this round. Your private cards Shared flop Your best five are T-T-A-7-2: a pair of tens with an ace kicker. There are four hearts, so you also have a heart-flush draw. You may check or bet because nothing is owed. The opponent's check does not tell you which private cards they hold. 3. Explain a changed situation In another heads-up flop, the opponent bets 5. You have paid nothing on this round. Your private cards Shared flop Your task: Name your best five and your draw separately. Is checking available? Does another spade guarantee that you win? Say your explanation or write it on paper before opening the answer. Before you move on: Say what your cards make now before naming a card you hope to receive. If that is still difficult, use the repair link or pause and return. Your explanation stays with you. Updated October 15, 2026: Added a short course lesson with a worked example, a changed situation to explain and a direct next lesson; the full reference remains below. Prepared with AI assistance. All scenes are fictional teaching examples. This is a self-check, not a skill score or betting recommendation.

    The flop gives you three new cards and a new decision. Start by naming what you have, what could change, whose turn it is and what continuing would cost. These eight lessons turn those questions into a repeatable way to study a hand. For beginners to standard 52-card no-limit Texas hold'em. Every scene is fictional, not Nolan's recorded play. Practice with paper or a deck; no wager, account or purchase is needed. Begin with the basic actions and starting-hand context if those are still unfamiliar. Build the habit Name the hand and the draw separately. Then ask what the other player could have and what the action actually tells you. Read your first flop Watch the hand change A card can improve both players. Compare the best five again instead of carrying the flop's verdict to the river. Try the changing-winner examples Put it together Reconstruct a complete decision after a raise, with a current price and clearly named unknowns. Try the final exercise

    A made hand describes what the available cards make now. A draw describes a possible improvement that still needs another card or cards. These labels can both apply. You do not have to choose one box and ignore the other. When your flop has several opponents, continue with limped and multiway pots . The action order and each opponent’s range become part of the decision. One hand, two useful descriptions Your cards: Flop: “Top pair” compares your pair with the board's ranks. It does not mean the best possible hand. An opponent could already have two pair or three of a kind. See the hand-ranking reference when the categories are unfamiliar.

    In a heads-up pot between the big blind and the button, the big blind acts first after the flop. Imagine you are on the button, you raised before the flop, and the big blind now checks. There is no wager to match on this street. Checking is an active choice. It may preserve a hand's chance to win at showdown while avoiding a new bet, but it also lets another shared card arrive. Whether that tradeoff is useful depends on the situation. A bet can be raised, and a check by the first player does not necessarily end the round when other players still have a turn. Before studying strategy, say the available actions correctly. Facing a bet, checking is no longer an option; your choices are fold, call or make a permitted raise. Rules for short all-ins can complicate raising rights. The betting guide handles those mechanics.

    A value-betting explanation asks which worse hands might call. A bluffing explanation asks which better hands might fold. Before the river, a bet can also make a hand with chances to improve give up those chances. These purposes can overlap. They are questions to investigate, not proof that any chosen size works. Return to ace-ten of hearts on T♠ 7♥ 2♥. Consider two hypothetical opponent holdings separately: T♣ 9♦ and 7♠ 7♦. These are possible comparisons, not a measured range or a claim that the opponent is equally likely to have each one. A draw can be used as a semi-bluff : it may win immediately if opponents fold, or improve if called. That label is not a license to bet every draw. An opponent can continue or raise, the draw can miss, and improvement can still lose. The ranges and betting guide develops these ideas after the basic hand reading feels comfortable.

    Instead of saying “I am close to a straight,” point to the missing ranks. In these separate scenes, you hold eight-seven and only your two cards plus the three flop cards are known. Treat the remaining card locations as unknown. Scene A: either end can fill Your cards: Flop: Your 5-6-7-8 sequence can become 4-5-6-7-8 or 5-6-7-8-9. This is an open-ended straight draw. Scene B: the missing rank is inside Keep the same private cards, but replace the six of clubs with the four of clubs. The flop is Now 4-5-7-8 needs a six to become 4-5-6-7-8. This is a gutshot, or inside straight draw. The draws and overlap examples show how to combine straight and flush possibilities. Do not assume that two hands described as “draws” have the same chances or should face the same price.

    For this comparison, turn both private hands face up. You hold queen-jack of hearts; the other player holds two eights. This is an open-card teaching scene. In an ordinary hand, you do not get to see the opponent's private cards while deciding. The heart that also pairs the board Your cards: Opponent's cards: Flop: Turn: Notice that the three of hearts is a single shared card doing two jobs. It supplies your fifth heart and pairs the board for both players. Looking only at its suit would miss half the information. This example compares current hands after the turn; it does not calculate river equity or prescribe a call.

    Your private pairings do not reserve places in the final five. Shared cards can create a higher pair for everyone and replace a lower pair you were relying on. Players call this kind of loss of usefulness counterfeiting . Two pair before and after, but a different comparison Your cards: Opponent's cards: Flop: Turn and river: A paired board does not automatically mean you have lost. This result follows from the two shown holdings. With hidden cards, you would need a plausible account of the opponent's range and actions. A possible stronger hand is not proof that the opponent has it.

    Use this separate fictional heads-up cash-game snapshot, with no fees. There are 18 chips in the pot and each player has 50 behind at the start of the flop. The opponent bets 6. You call 6. The pot becomes 30, and both players have 44 remaining. The turn arrives. The opponent bets 15. Earlier contributions are already in the pot; they do not count as credit toward this new street's wager. A probability of improving by the river assumes access to both remaining cards. It cannot quietly replace a next-card probability when another payment may be needed on the turn. Completing a draw also differs from winning the pot. Use the card-probability table for that distinction and the pot-odds workshop for the conditional calculations. Earlier chips are already committed. Review the new price and your current information. Do not continue simply to make a previous call feel worthwhile, and do not treat a lost hand as money that must be recovered in the next one.

    Return to ace-ten of hearts on T♠ 7♥ 2♥. You are on the button against the big blind in a fictional cash-game hand with no fees. The pot is 13 before flop action, and each player has 94 behind. The big blind checks, you bet 4, and the big blind raises to 12 . It is your turn. Before revealing the answer, record: your made hand and draw; the current pot; the extra amount a call costs; whether checking is available; the pot and remaining stacks after calling; and what the raise does not tell you. A useful study note ends with a question you can investigate: “Which hands might raise here, how would they respond if I raise again, and how can later cards change this decision?” Keep observed facts separate from guessed frequencies. If a later showdown reveals a bluff or a strong hand, it adds evidence about that one hand; it does not retroactively make the hidden cards knowable.

    The hand comparison was difficult: revisit worked showdowns and reading the board . The betting purpose was unclear: use ranges and reasons for betting . The extra payment was confusing: reconstruct a call after a raise . You want a deeper open-card example: study the flush and redraw lab . Try the questions again with the answers closed. Explain the current hand before predicting the ending. You can keep practicing without money, and completing this lesson does not establish a profitable strategy.     Stage 4 of 6: Rebuild the best five after each new card and distinguish a call price from a reason to call. Work through this short lesson, then pause or continue. The full explanation and other practice are available below. 1. Learn one idea Rebuild the hand, then price the call without inventing its chances. The turn is the fourth shared card; the river is the fifth and last. Rebuild your best five when a card arrives. A missed draw can leave a pair, but no later community card can complete a draw once the river is out. For a heads-up river call that ends betting, the break-even pot share in chips is the additional call divided by the pot after your call. This is a price. Your expected share against possible opposing hands, including ties, is a different question. Both scenes assume a fictional cash game, ample chips, no fees, no side pots and no tournament payout effects. A fold or legal raise may also be available; pricing a call does not compare every action. 2. Follow a worked example The opponent bets 12 into a river pot of 24. You have paid nothing on this round. Your private cards Shared river board Your best five are J-J-T-8-5. The heart draw missed; you still have a pair of jacks. The bet makes the current pot 36. Calling adds 12 and makes 48, so 12 / 48 = 25% is the break-even share. It is not a measured chance that your hand wins. 3. Explain a changed situation A different river pot contains 36 before the opponent bets 12. You have paid nothing on the river; a call ends betting under the same assumptions. Your private cards Shared river board Your task: List the best five. Did the spade draw arrive? Give the current pot, the pot after calling and the break-even share. What is still missing before recommending a call? Say your explanation or write it on paper before opening the answer. Before you move on: Explain the difference between a call's break-even share and evidence that your hand meets it. If that is still difficult, use the repair link or pause and return. Your explanation stays with you.     The turn leaves one card to come. The river leaves none. That small change transforms the questions worth asking: what can still improve, what already wins at showdown, and what a bet or call could actually accomplish. For beginners to standard 52-card no-limit Texas hold'em. Every scene is fictional, not Nolan's recorded play. Practice with a deck or a private note; no wager, account or purchase is needed. This lesson follows your first decisions after the flop . It teaches interpretation, not a recommended betting strategy. Track what changed Follow one pair and one draw through the last two community cards. Rebuild the hand before judging the result. Start with the turn Understand the final decision Separate checking, betting and calling. A river call cannot buy another card or make the bettor fold. Understand a river call Remember shared pots A hand can receive chips without winning outright. Work through the final split-pot exercise. Try the shared straight

    The turn is the fourth community card. There is one more shared card to come if the hand continues. Before thinking about another bet, separate three observations: your best hand now, the improvement you are still drawing to, and the hands the new board makes possible for someone else. The king changes the description Your cards: Flop: Turn: On the flop you had a pair of jacks with a queen kicker, plus a heart-flush draw. Jack was the highest board rank, so the pair was top pair. Now say what is different without guessing the opponent's cards. An overcard here means a card ranked above the jacks you paired. Your pair's category did not disappear when its position on the board changed. Conversely, retaining a pair does not guarantee you remain ahead. Naming the actual five cards helps avoid both mistakes.

    Continue the same runout River: The complete board is J♠ 7♥ 2♥ K♣ 8♦. Keep your Q♥ J♥. The river is the fifth and final community card. Your heart draw did not arrive. There is no sixth shared card waiting after the next call. Start the river description with the hand you actually have, rather than only the draw you wanted. Even on the river, the outcome may be unknown to you because the opponent's private cards are hidden. That uncertainty is about the existing hands, not a chance of being dealt a helpful sixth card. More betting can still happen; more community cards cannot in this ordinary single-board hand.

    Use the same final board and your pair of jacks. You are on the button, only the big blind remains against you, both have chips, and the big blind checks on the river. You act last. You can check behind or bet. On an earlier street, checking behind can allow the next shared card to arrive without another payment on that street. On the river, no later shared card remains. The reason “I must bet to stop the flush draw getting there” no longer fits. A value-betting explanation would name worse hands that might call, such as a weaker pair, and justify why enough of them continue. A bluffing explanation would name better hands that might fold. The card comparison alone establishes neither response. You do not have to turn every hand with uncertain strength into a bet. Order matters: if you check first with another eligible player still to act, your check does not close the river. That player can bet, bringing the decision back to you. “Checking reaches showdown” is true only when the required action is complete. Follow the dealer's procedures for showing cards; these examples do not replace house rules.

    Start a separate open-card comparison. The final board is already dealt, and both players check the river. The two private hands are exposed only to explain the showdown. They are not information either player possessed while choosing an action. Two missed heart draws, different high cards Your cards: Opponent's cards: Final board: “I missed, so I have to bluff” skips the comparison with checking. A bet could make a better hand fold, but a hand that could win by checking may also get called only by stronger hands. Naming a possible bluff is not evidence that bluffing this size against this opponent would improve your result. On the river, the draw cannot improve after a call. A bet intended to make better hands fold is a bluff, not a semi-bluff that may later hit its draw. A hand can still have some showdown value while being used as a bluff. The label describes the bet's intended effect; it does not certify the decision.

    Return to Q♥ J♥ on J♠ 7♥ 2♥ K♣ 8♦. Change the river action: in this fictional heads-up cash-game snapshot there are 24 chips in the pot, and each player has 60 behind before river betting. The big blind bets 12. You are on the button and must respond. The current pot is 36. A call adds 12, making a final pot of 48. Each player would have 48 left behind. A call closes this heads-up river action. There are no fees, side pots or tournament-prize effects in this example. You may fold, call or make a legal raise with the stated stacks. The arithmetic above compares calling with folding only; it does not show that raising is bad. A raise creates a new wager and asks the opponent to respond, which a call does not. Checking is unavailable when facing this bet. A complete study answer names the price and the missing evidence: “Calling costs 12; I need a credible account of which hands bet and how often.” Do not replace that evidence with “they could be bluffing.” Finding one possible bluff proves possibility, not frequency. The river Decision Lab develops that distinction with explicit range weights.

    Use a final, separate heads-up river example. Your cards are two of clubs and three of diamonds. The board has the highest possible straight, with no suit appearing more than twice. Both players are still eligible for the same pot. The board supplies all five cards Your cards: Final board: There are 24 chips before the opponent bets 12. Both players had 60 behind at the start of the river. Suppose your call closes the action. No fees are taken, and there are no other players or side pots. Compare calling with folding using chips only. For a heads-up river model with wins, losses and equal splits, equity is the chance of winning outright plus half the chance of tying. On this board the first term is zero and the second is half of 100%. Other pot structures require their own accounting. The pot-odds workshop explains the general comparison.

    Close the answers and explain the difference between these three sentences: “my draw missed,” “my hand cannot win at showdown,” and “betting is better than checking.” None automatically proves the next. Then say what a call can accomplish that a bluff tries to accomplish differently. Track the cards: revisit board reading if rebuilding the best five was difficult. Track the action: return to the first decisions if checking, calling and raising became mixed together. Track the assumption: try the river Decision Lab when you can explain the price without inventing an opponent's range. Track the share: use worked showdowns if the tied-hand exercise was surprising. Keep one private note: what you observed, what you assumed, and which question remains. This page has no answer form and stores no practice responses. Being able to explain the examples is not evidence of profitable play. You can continue learning without money; safer-play and support resources are available without an account.

    Close the explanation and try this from memory: A river pot is 20 before a bet of 10. A call adds 10 and makes 40. Explain what 10 / 40 = 25% does and does not establish. Compare your reason with a fresh practice situation . If a part is unclear, use its repair link and return later.

    Your first poker range.

    Learn poker ranges through six explained exercises: remove impossible cards, compare four hands, and see why a possible bluff is not a measured frequency.

    Stage 5 of 6: Separate known cards, possible opposing hands and assumptions about their frequency. Work through this short lesson, then pause or continue. The full explanation and other practice are available below. 1. Learn one idea A possible hand is different from a likely hand. A range is a model of the hands an opponent could hold in a situation. First remove exact cards you already know. A card cannot be in your private hand, on the board and in an opponent's hand at the same time. Then separate possibility from frequency. A legal holding may be possible without being common. A check is an observed action; the cards and frequencies behind it remain uncertain. Listing three candidates does not give each a one-third chance, and these candidate lists are not complete ranges. 2. Follow a worked example The opponent checks to you on the river. Consider the three exact candidate holdings below. Your private cards Shared river board Candidate A Candidate B Candidate C A is impossible: it reuses your ace of hearts. B is physically possible, but its frequency is unknown. C is also possible and makes three tens, which beat your pair. Checking therefore does not prove the opponent holds a weaker hand. None of these observations supplies probabilities. 3. Explain a changed situation In another river hand, the opponent checks. Consider these different exact candidates. Your private cards Shared river board Candidate A Candidate B Candidate C Your task: Which candidate is impossible? Can a legal candidate beat your queens? Does a candidate being legal, or appearing once at showdown, establish how often it checks? Say your explanation or write it on paper before opening the answer. Before you move on: Name one observed fact, one physically possible hand and one frequency you do not know. If that is still difficult, use the repair link or pause and return. Your explanation stays with you.     “They might have aces” names one possibility. It does not explain what else the opponent could hold, which hands your cards beat, or how often each hand takes this action. A range is a way to make those missing parts visible. For beginners to standard 52-card no-limit Texas hold'em. Every scene is fictional, not Nolan's recorded play. Use cards, counters or paper; no wager, account or purchase is needed. This lesson follows turn and river decisions . It teaches how to describe uncertainty, not a recommended range or betting strategy. Separate fact from possibility Begin with the cards you actually know. Cross out impossible holdings without inventing the opponent's hand. Start with the information Compare several hands Use four exact two-card holdings. Learn what each makes before asking how likely it is. Read the four possibilities Change one assumption Keep the cards and call price fixed, then see why a different betting frequency changes the model. Try the optional frequency step

    A range describes a collection of possible private hands. In a useful decision model it also describes their relative likelihoods. You can begin with a short list in words; you do not need a colored chart or software before you understand the idea. Keep three layers separate. Known cards are your private cards and the shared board, plus any other genuinely exposed cards. Possible holdings are hands that do not reuse those cards. A proposed betting range is a model of which possible holdings reach this decision and choose this action. That last layer needs assumptions or evidence. One river snapshot for the lesson Your cards: Final board: Only one opponent remains. Your best five are K-K-Q-9-5: a pair of kings with a queen kicker. No further community card will arrive. Imagine the opponent checks. That action is something you observed. “The opponent has a weak hand” is an interpretation. A player can legally check a strong hand, a medium hand or a hand that is unlikely to win. The rules do not turn a check into an exposed card. A range is not a special ability to see hidden cards. It is a model you can examine and revise. Even a carefully reasoned range can be incomplete or wrong. Naming the assumption makes an explanation more useful than presenting a confident guess as a fact.

    Return to your king of hearts and queen of diamonds on K♠ 9♣ 5♥ 3♦ 2♣. The king of spades is already on the board, and the king of hearts is in your hand. The opponent cannot hold either card. Those are physical exclusions, independent of how that opponent tends to play. Consider four candidate holdings separately: K♠ A♠, K♥ J♦, A♣ A♦ and Q♥ J♥. A card code names an exact rank and suit: K♠ is the king of spades, not any king. In written study notes, the same card might be written Ks. Your known cards are often called blockers because they remove combinations from other players' possibilities. The label does not automatically favor your decision: a card can remove a strong opposing hand or remove a hand you hoped the opponent was bluffing with. First state what is removed; investigate the strategic consequence separately.

    Now use only the four holdings below as a deliberately small teaching model. Each row names one exact two-card combination. These are alternatives for the same opponent, not eight cards that opponent holds at once. Cards may appear in more than one alternative in a general range, but no individual holding may duplicate a known card. A: one exact pair of aces B: one exact ace-king C: one exact pair of nines D: one exact queen-jack Keep your K♥ Q♦ and the same complete board beside the four rows. Write the best five cards for each alternative before opening the answer. Saying “I have top pair” is not enough to compare it with all four. Do not confuse these four exact holdings with the labels AA, AK, 99 and QJ. A label can represent several physical combinations. Before any cards are removed, a pocket-pair label contains six combinations; an unpaired label containing both suited and offsuit versions contains sixteen. This exercise intentionally starts smaller. The combination workshop teaches group counts after the distinction feels comfortable.

    Change the action to a bet. In a fictional heads-up cash-game river decision there are 40 chips before the opponent bets 20. Both players began the river with 100 behind. You face 20 with enough chips to call. A call closes betting. Assume no fees, side pots or tournament-prize effects. The current pot is 60. Calling adds 20 and makes 80; both players then have 80 remaining. The simple break-even share is 20 / 80 = 25% . This prices calling relative to folding now. It does not estimate your hand's equity or compare calling with a legal raise. For this calculation only, suppose our opponent has exactly A, B, C or D at this betting decision, each with the same chance. No other holding is included. The equal likelihood applies after the observed action; we are not measuring how a real player arrives here. In this model your hand loses to A, B and C and wins against D. Here the three stronger alternatives can be treated as the model's value candidates, and D as its bluff candidate. Those labels describe this restricted betting model. A weaker made hand could bet in another model, and a real opponent can have hands we left out. Your kings are not automatically a pure bluff catcher against every possible betting range.

    This optional step introduces a weight : a relative amount of probability assigned to a hand. Keep the same cards, same bet and same price. Assign weight 1 to each of A, B and C, but weight 0.5 to D. Those values describe the relative likelihood of the four alternatives at this betting decision, including the action history. The weights total 3.5: 1 + 1 + 1 + 0.5. The share belonging to D is therefore 0.5 / 3.5 = 1 / 7, about 14.3% . A half-weight hand is not half of a physical card. It is a way to say that this alternative appears half as often as each full-weight alternative in the constructed model. Do not quietly turn “could be a bluff” into “is as common as every value hand.” Conversely, removing every bluff without evidence is also an assumption. When you cannot justify frequencies, preserve that limitation. A precise calculation conditional on uncertain inputs remains uncertain as a description of the real decision.

    Imagine the opponent eventually shows D, queen-jack of hearts. That reveals what happened in this one fictional hand. It does not reveal all the hands the opponent could have arrived with, how often they bet them, or which alternative model best described your earlier information.

    Close the answers. Explain, in order: the known cards; the holdings those cards exclude; which remaining hands beat or lose to yours; the price of continuing; and the assumptions about how often each alternative appears. You can use the four exact holdings again without pretending they are a realistic complete range. Keep a private study note with two columns, “Observed” and “Assumed.” Put the board, bet and amount to call in the first. Put the candidate range and frequencies in the second. Add one sentence about what would change your conclusion. There is no answer form here and no practice response is stored. If the five-card comparison was difficult, revisit kickers and ties . If the 20-chip call was unclear, revisit river calls . If exact holdings and labels became mixed together, use the combination workshop . If the model now makes sense, try the river Decision Lab before opening its answers. These checks develop a way to describe a hand, not evidence of a profitable strategy or readiness to risk money. You can keep learning with fictional cards and counters. Safer-play and support resources are available without completing a lesson or opening an account.

    Stage 6 of 6: Say which worse hands might call or better hands might fold, and compare betting with checking. Work through this short lesson, then pause or continue. The full explanation and other practice are available below. 1. Learn one idea Explain the response a bet needs, then compare checking. A value-bet explanation needs worse hands that will call. A bluff explanation needs better hands that will fold. A hand's label or one winning result is not a complete reason to bet. Different opposing hands may respond differently. When the opponent checks to you last to act on the river, checking takes the hand to showdown without a new wager. Compare that option with betting. The frequency of each opposing hand and its response matter, including possible raises. Both examples use fictional heads-up river hands, ample counters, no fees or side pots and the supplied response assumptions. They teach questions to ask; the site has not measured any player's actual responses. 2. Follow a worked example The opponent checks to you. Suppose, for this restricted example, a worse pair of nines always folds to your proposed bet and a better hand of three eights always calls. These are two illustrative candidates, not an estimated range. Your private cards Shared river board Worse: pair of nines Better: three eights Your pair of tens beats the nines and loses to three eights. Under these supplied responses, neither candidate supports the proposed value-bet argument: the worse hand does not call, and the better hand does. The better hand does not fold to support a bluff either. Checking already wins against the nines without a new wager. This conclusion is about this restricted model. 3. Explain a changed situation In a different hand, the opponent checks to you last to act. For a proposed bet of 4, suppose the worse eights call and the better jacks also call. No frequency or complete range has been supplied. Your private cards Shared river board Candidate: pair of eights Candidate: pair of jacks Your task: Which candidate could pay a value bet, and which beats you? What changed from the worked example? What is still missing before saying betting is better than checking? Say your explanation or write it on paper before opening the answer. Before you move on: Name a worse caller or a better folder, then say what checking would achieve. If that is still difficult, use the repair link or pause and return. Your explanation stays with you.
