    On this site · Learn the basics

    Get started with no-limit Texas Hold’em

    A beginner’s guide to a first poker session: formats, full costs, rules rehearsal, time and money boundaries, and a practical first month of study.

    Read matching section

    Searchable article text, without exercise answers

    Start with a small, concrete goal: follow a hand accurately, understand what a game costs, and finish a practice session with better questions. Real-money play is optional. This guide takes an adult beginner from choosing a format through a first session and a first month of practice. For a connected explanation of the whole game, use the complete Hold’em guide . For shorter lessons, begin with your first decisions . You do not need to read either guide in one sitting. Prefer a visual introduction? Read the first Hold’em comic and its rules notes , then rehearse the action here.

    Use this guide for the task in front of you Your task Start here I have never played Choose a practice setting , then follow the cards and action I am considering a first game Read the listing and full cost , then set time and money boundaries I want to rehearse Follow a counted hand and explain the practice questions before revealing their answers I have just played Record one uncertain hand , then choose a learning stage Scope: standard 52-card no-limit Texas Hold’em with no wild cards. All worked hands, prices and practice situations are fictional. Dollar examples are arithmetic, not offers from a venue. Cash examples assume table stakes and exclude fees unless stated. TDA procedures below apply to tournaments using those rules; cash rooms, home games and online platforms can differ. Ask the actual venue about its rules.

    A beginner’s first major choice is not which starting hands to play. It is what kind of poker environment to enter. Cash games and tournaments use the same hand rankings and core Hold’em mechanics, but they place very different meanings on chips, time, and elimination. Live and online poker differ again in pace, interface, social procedure, and accessibility. There is no format that is universally “best for beginners.” The better question is which environment creates the lowest practical and financial pressure while teaching the skills you most need. In a cash game , chips ordinarily represent money at the table. The blinds generally remain fixed for the session, and a player can normally leave between hands and cash out remaining chips whenever house procedure allows. A listing such as “$1/$2 NLHE, $100 to $300 buy-in” commonly means the small blind is $1, the big blind is $2, and a new player may initially buy a stack within that stated range. A $200 stack in that game equals 100 big blinds. Cash rooms differ on minimum and maximum buy-ins, top-ups, straddles, missed-blind rules, and rake, so the game listing is the beginning of the inquiry, not the whole answer. Operator descriptions of cash games likewise emphasize stable blinds and cash-valued chips, but venue rules determine the details. ( cash and tournament structures ; operator rake schedule ) In a tournament , the entry fee purchases tournament chips that are accounting units rather than redeemable dollars. Blinds and often antes increase on a schedule. Players who lose all their chips are eliminated unless the event permits a rebuy or re-entry and the player chooses to use it. Prizes are paid according to the event’s payout structure rather than by cashing tournament chips at face value. Some events allow one re-entry; some permit many during a registration period; some are single-entry. The total price can include both money that goes to the prize pool and a fee retained by the organizer. PokerStars, for example, currently displays a combined tournament price in some interfaces while making the prize-pool contribution and fee breakdown available in the tournament lobby. That operator example illustrates why a beginner should inspect the structure rather than assume the title tells the whole cost. ( tournament price disclosure ; cash and tournament structures ) Tournament chips therefore should not be treated as cash-game dollars. Losing 10,000 tournament chips does not mean losing $10,000, and doubling a tournament stack does not generally double the monetary value of the entry. Payouts are nonlinear: surviving from one stack size to another can change a player’s chance of reaching paid places or higher prizes in ways that depend on the remaining field and payout ladder. The Independent Chip Model, or ICM, is one framework for translating tournament stacks into estimated prize equity, but a new player does not need to calculate ICM at the table. The beginner-level lesson is simply that a tournament decision can be influenced by elimination risk and payout structure in ways that have no direct cash-game equivalent. (see the site’s tournament equity guide ) Cash games and tournaments are game formats. Live and online are settings that can host either format. These rows are not mutually exclusive choices. On a narrow screen, scroll the comparison sideways to see all columns. Choose a format Format or setting What the chips mean Blinds When play ends Main cost questions Beginner tradeoff Cash game Usually direct cash value Usually fixed Player may leave between hands under house rules Buy-in, possible reloads, rake, travel Flexible duration, but every chip has immediate money value Tournament Tournament units, not cash redemption value Increase by level Elimination or tournament completion Entry fee, re-entry rules, travel, time Fixed initial entry can be simple, but duration and re-entry temptation can be substantial Live poker Physical chips and dealer procedure Depends on format Depends on format Venue costs plus game costs Slower pace and staff assistance, but more procedural and social demands Online poker Digital balances and automated dealing Depends on format Depends on format Entry/stakes, rake/fees, deposit limits Convenient and fast, but interface errors and rapid volume can magnify mistakes Home or play-money practice Whatever the group defines Flexible Flexible Often little or no financial exposure Excellent for rules practice, less realistic incentives and procedure Live versus online. Live poker gives a beginner more time between hands and puts a dealer in charge of cards, pot movement, and much of the procedure. It also requires the player to track action, protect physical cards, recognize chip denominations, speak clearly, and wait for the correct turn. Online software automatically posts blinds, deals cards, tracks the pot, and constrains many illegal actions, but the pace is much faster. Buttons, bet sliders, auto-action checkboxes, multi-tabling options, disconnection policies, and time banks create a different set of failure modes. An accidental click can be binding, just as an ambiguous chip movement can be binding live. A home game can be a gentle way to practice if the group is genuinely low pressure and everyone agrees on rules before play. It can also teach bad habits if house customs are unclear, side games are added impulsively, or players use informal procedures that do not transfer to a casino. Play-money online games are useful for learning interface mechanics and board reading, but because the chips lack meaningful financial value, opponents may make decisions that would be rare in a real-money game. Treat these environments as procedural laboratories, not proof that a strategy will work for money.

    Learn four quantities before you sit down: blinds, buy-in, table size, and effective stack. “$1/$2 NLHE, 9-handed, $100-$300” tells you the forced blinds and the allowed initial buy-in range, but not how deep the opponents are, how large the rake is, whether straddles are common, or how aggressively the table is playing. “$100 tournament, 20,000 starting stack, 100/200 blinds” tells you that the initial stack is 100 BB before accounting for antes, but you still need the blind schedule, fee breakdown, re-entry rules, and expected duration to understand the event. For a tournament away from home, use the full trip budget : three local, overnight and weekend examples plus an editable worksheet. An advertised entry price is only one line. Hypothetical example E: effective stack in dollars and big blinds You sit in a $1/$2 cash game with $240. The opponent most likely to contest the next pot with you has $150. Between the two of you, the effective stack is $150 because neither can win more than the other has available. Since the big blind is $2, the effective stack is $150 ÷ $2 = 75 BB. Your visible stack is 120 BB, but the hand is effectively 75 BB deep against that opponent. If another opponent has only $60, the effective stack between you and that player is $60, or 30 BB. Stack depth is therefore a relationship between players, not simply the number in front of you. That concept matters because the same starting hand can behave differently at 30 BB and 150 BB. With deep stacks, later betting rounds can put much more money at risk, and hands capable of making strong disguised combinations can gain relevance. With short stacks, preflop and flop decisions can consume a much larger fraction of the effective stack. A beginner does not need a library of stack-depth charts to appreciate the principle: before committing significant chips, ask not only “How good are my cards?” but “How much can actually be won or lost between these stacks?” Understand the full likely cost. A blind level is not a price tag. In a cash game, your maximum direct loss during a session depends on how much you bring into play, including any planned reloads, while rake reduces the value of pots over time. Rake is commonly a percentage of qualifying cash-game pots subject to a cap, though exact methods differ by venue and stake. PokerStars’ published USD no-limit and pot-limit schedule, for example, currently varies both percentage and cap by stake and player count. That is evidence of variation, not a benchmark every room follows. ( operator rake schedule ) In tournaments, the relevant figure is not only the nominal first entry. Check whether the displayed amount includes an organizer fee, whether add-ons or re-entries exist, and how many you are willing to purchase. Re-entry availability is an option, not an obligation. Hypothetical example F: fees and total session exposure A tournament is displayed at a total price of $110. Its structure states that $100 goes to the prize pool and $10 is the entry fee. One re-entry is permitted during the first six levels. If you decide before arriving that you will buy only one entry, your maximum tournament entry expense is $110. If instead you authorize yourself one re-entry, your maximum tournament entry expense is $220, even though the event is casually described as a “$110 tournament.” Suppose you also budget $15 for parking and $10 for food. Your maximum planned outing expenditure becomes $245, of which $220 is gambling entry expense and $25 is ordinary trip spending. The example is hypothetical, but the distinction between total tournament price and its prize-pool/fee breakdown is real and is disclosed in operator tournament information. ( tournament price disclosure ; cash and tournament structures ) For a cash-session comparison, suppose you plan one $200 buy-in and allow one $200 reload. Your maximum amount deliberately exposed to poker losses is $400, not $200. Rake is not an additional lump-sum loss automatically charged on top of that $400; it is generally removed from pots according to the room’s schedule and therefore affects your results within the money already circulating at the table. Travel, food, tips, parking and any separate time or collection charges also belong in the outing budget. Check the room’s schedule; a charge paid separately is not covered by a pot-rake example. See the site’s cash-game costs guide for the different charging methods. The point is to write down the full exposure before play rather than mentally treating each additional purchase as a new decision. Legality and legitimacy. In the United States there is no responsible one-sentence answer to “Is online poker legal?” or “How old must I be?” that covers every jurisdiction and venue. State law, tribal gaming rules, operator licensing, geolocation, and age requirements can differ. Verify the current rules with the relevant state or tribal regulator and the venue itself. Do not treat an app’s availability, a social-media advertisement, or the ability to create an account as proof that real-money play is authorized where you are physically located. Michigan’s Gaming Control Board, for example, warned as recently as October 8, 2026 that unlicensed offshore sites were operating outside Michigan safeguards, including self-exclusion and regulator recourse, and directs residents to its authorized-operator list. ( Michigan regulator example ) Try it: which stack matters? At $1/$2, you have $180 and one opponent has $126 at the start of the hand. How deep is your heads-up contest in big blinds? Try it: what is the whole outing cost? A fictional tournament costs $55 per entry, including its fee. You allow one re-entry. Travel costs $12 and food costs $8. What is the maximum planned entry expense, and what is the maximum outing expenditure?

    A beginner should distinguish an entertainment budget from a poker bankroll . An entertainment budget is money already designated as discretionary spending and fully affordable to lose without affecting rent, debt payments, food, savings goals, medical needs, or other obligations. A bankroll is a separate pool that experienced players may use to absorb normal swings across repeated play. The absolute beginner should start with the first concept, not the second. There is no need to “build a bankroll” merely because poker literature talks about bankroll management. Rules of thumb such as “keep X buy-ins” can be useful in specialized contexts, but no universal number guarantees safety or prevents loss. Appropriate reserves depend on format, game variance, the player’s true edge or lack of one, financial circumstances, risk tolerance, and whether poker is being treated as entertainment or as an attempted income activity. A beginner whose underlying advantage is unknown should not interpret a large bankroll as permission to play higher or longer. The stronger first rule is to decide a fixed amount that can be lost without practical harm and not replenish it impulsively. NCPG’s current responsible-play guidance similarly recommends limiting gambling funds to money that can be lost without affecting necessities or savings. ( NCPG guidance ) Money limits and time limits control exposure and behavior. They do not change the cards, improve pot odds, or create a mathematical advantage. Decide before play how much money can enter the game, whether any re-entry or reload is allowed, and when the session ends. NCPG advises establishing both time and financial limits before gambling and stopping at those limits. ( NCPG guidance ) A stop time is especially useful because fatigue erodes attention. In a 28-day observational study of 23 regular online poker players, Hamel and colleagues found higher emotional and behavioral tilt, more hands played, and worse financial results in sleep-deprived sessions; alcohol consumption was also associated with higher emotional and behavioral tilt. The study was small, observational, and not generalizable to every poker player, but it supports the practical case for avoiding poker when sleep-deprived or impaired. ( Hamel and colleagues ) “Chasing” means continuing or increasing gambling primarily to recover prior losses. It is dangerous reasoning because the next hand does not owe you compensation for the previous one. Re-entering a tournament can be a strategically legitimate option for a prepared player, but a beginner should decide the maximum number of entries before the first entry, not in the emotional minutes after busting. Borrowing to play, gambling with money needed for obligations, hiding losses, repeatedly breaking self-imposed limits, or treating poker as a solution to debt are strong reasons to stop and reassess rather than study more strategy. NCPG’s guidance emphasizes not chasing losses and keeping funds needed for necessities or savings out of gambling. ( NCPG guidance ) The same is true of tilt , a poker term for emotionally disrupted decision-making. Anger after a bad beat is not evidence that the next hand deserves more action. A useful stop condition is behavioral rather than financial: if you notice yourself clicking faster, calling “to see it,” making unusually large bets to get even, arguing, or no longer tracking pot and action, end the session. Stopping while behind is not an admission of defeat. The money already lost is a sunk cost. Winning it back before leaving is not a requirement. Warning signs deserve attention before they become a crisis. Patterns worth taking seriously include increasing preoccupation, betting more money more frequently, chasing losses, difficulty stopping, and continued gambling despite negative consequences to personal, family, or vocational life. Those are not labels a poker guide should diagnose, but they are reasons to step away and use qualified support. ( NCPG guidance ) For U.S. gambling-related support, NCPG's National Problem Gambling Helpline offers call, text and chat services 24/7, connecting people with local resources. The number is 1-800-MY-RESET . Check the official page for current information. This is a support and referral service, not an emergency hotline. The site's access and protection guide explains other protections and where to look for local help.

    At the beginning of an ordinary Hold’em hand, a dealer button marks the nominal dealer position. The player immediately to the button’s left posts the small blind and the next player posts the big blind, forced wagers that seed the pot and help create action. Some games also use antes, forced contributions that may come from every player or, in many tournaments, from the big blind as a single “big blind ante.” Each player then receives two private hole cards. After the first betting round, the dealer exposes three community cards together, the flop. A second betting round follows. One community card, the turn, is dealt, followed by another betting round. The fifth and final community card, the river, is then dealt, followed by the last betting round. If two or more players remain, the hand can reach showdown. ( Hold’em rules ; TDA tournament rules ) Post blinds and any antes; deal two private cards each. Bet preflop. Deal the three-card flop, then bet. Deal the turn, then bet. Deal the river, then bet. Compare hands at showdown if at least two players remain. The hand ends earlier if every opponent folds. Once all remaining players are all-in and betting is complete, deal the remaining board with no further wagers. A pot can be won in two different ways. The first is uncontested: everyone except one player folds, so the remaining player wins without having to prove a particular hand. The second is at showdown: among the remaining live hands, the best five-card poker hand wins, with ties splitting the pot subject to house procedures for indivisible odd chips. Hold’em does not require you to use both hole cards. You may use both, one, or none, because the task is simply to construct the best five cards available from your two hole cards and the five-card board. In tournament play, the TDA’s “cards speak” rule means the cards themselves determine the hand value even if a player verbally misidentifies the hand. ( Hold’em rules ; TDA tournament rules ) For a ranking chart, keep the site's hand rankings guide open during practice. From strongest to weakest: straight flush, four of a kind, full house, flush, straight, three of a kind, two pair, one pair, high card. A royal flush is simply the highest possible straight flush, A-K-Q-J-10 of one suit, not a separate mathematical category. In ordinary Hold’em an ace can be high in A-K-Q-J-10 or low in A-2-3-4-5, but it does not “wrap” around in combinations such as Q-K-A-2-3. Within the same category, ranks and then kickers break ties. A kicker is a side card used to distinguish otherwise equal hands. With two pair, for example, compare the higher pair, then the lower pair, then the fifth card. With one pair, compare the pair and then the remaining kickers from highest downward. If the best five cards are identical, the pot is tied. Suits do not break an ordinary Hold’em showdown tie. These mechanics are reflected in mainstream operator rules; specific showdown presentation procedures can vary by venue. ( Hold’em rules ; TDA tournament rules ) Hypothetical example A: reading the board, a kicker, and playing the board The board is A♠ J♦ 8♣ 4♥ 2♠. Riley holds A♦ 9♦ and Morgan holds A♥ 7♥. Riley’s best five are A♠ A♦ J♦ 9♦ 8♣. Morgan’s best five are A♠ A♥ J♦ 8♣ 7♥. Compare their kickers in order: J-9-8 against J-8-7. The first kicker, the jack, ties. The next comparison is nine against eight, so Riley wins. You stop at the first difference; you do not compare nine against seven. Now consider a separate board of K♠ K♦ Q♣ Q♥ A♣. Riley holds 8♠ 7♠ and Morgan holds 6♣ 5♣. Neither player can improve on the five board cards, so both play K-K-Q-Q-A and tie. In a TDA tournament, a player claiming a share while “playing the board” must properly table both hole cards at showdown, a procedural requirement that illustrates why hand construction and showdown procedure are distinct ideas. ( TDA tournament rules ) The legal actions are easier to understand if you separate “putting money in” from “responding to somebody else’s money.” Fold means surrender the hand and any claim to the pot. Check means remain in the hand without betting, but it is available only when no wager is currently facing you. Bet means make the first voluntary wager on a betting round. Call means match the current wager, up to your remaining stack. Raise means increase the current wager. All-in means commit all remaining chips. An all-in can be a call, a bet, or a raise depending on the action before it. Clear verbal declarations such as “call,” “raise,” and “all-in” are recognized in TDA tournament play, and many live rooms use similar language conventions, but beginners should still ask the house about its specific procedures. ( TDA tournament rules ) Betting order. Before the flop in an ordinary multi-player hand, action begins with the first active player to the left of the big blind and continues clockwise. The blinds act later if they still have live hands. On the flop, turn, and river, action begins with the first active player to the left of the button. Heads-up is the important exception: the button is the small blind, receives the last card on the initial deal, acts first preflop, and acts last on each postflop betting round. The TDA codifies that heads-up procedure for tournaments, and mainstream operator rules use the same basic structure. ( TDA tournament rules ) “No-limit” is often misunderstood. It does not mean every bet can be any arbitrary amount. There is ordinarily a minimum opening bet, and raises must meet minimum-raise rules unless a player is all-in for less. It means there is no fixed upper betting limit below the player’s stack. If the big blind is $2, a player with $180 in play can, where action permits, wager up to $180. A player with $40 cannot call a $100 wager by reaching into a wallet for another $60 during the hand. The short player can call only for the $40 available, becoming all-in; any amount contested only among deeper-stacked players belongs in one or more side pots. Operator rules describe no-limit betting as allowing a player to bet up to the chips available, while exact table-stakes and add-on procedures remain house matters. ( Hold’em rules ; cash and tournament structures ) Try it: compare the kickers in order The board is Q♦ Q♥ 9♠ 5♣ 2♦. Riley holds K♠ J♣; Morgan holds A♦ 8♥. Write each best five-card hand before opening the explanation.

    The minimum raise is based on the size of the largest prior full bet or raise increment in the current betting round, not merely on “doubling whatever number you see.” Under the 2026 TDA rule, a raise must be at least equal to the largest prior full bet or raise of that round. The distinction matters after a raise that is larger than the opening bet. ( TDA tournament rules ) Hypothetical example B: a legal minimum raise On the flop, Avery bets $20. Blake raises to $55 total. Blake has raised by $35, because $55 minus the prior $20 bet equals $35. If Casey wants to make a full raise, Casey must add at least another $35 to the $55 current wager, so the minimum total is $90. A raise to $75 would not be a legal full raise. If Casey makes it $90, the latest full raise increment is still $35, so the next player’s minimum full raise would be to $125. This example follows the TDA tournament rule; a cash room may express the same principle in house language, and its floor staff controls the ruling. ( TDA tournament rules ) A short all-in can increase the price without constituting a full raise. Suppose Avery bets $20, Blake calls $20, and Casey is all-in for $35 total. Casey has raised only $15, short of the $20 minimum full raise. Under TDA no-limit tournament rules, that short all-in does not by itself reopen raising to Avery or Blake if they have already acted and are not facing at least a full raise when action returns. They can call or fold, but cannot use Casey’s short increment as a fresh opportunity to re-raise. Multiple short all-ins can cumulatively reopen action when the total increase a player faces reaches a full raise. This is one of the places where asking the dealer or floor is far safer than trying to improvise a rule from memory. ( TDA tournament rules ) All-ins, main pots, side pots, and uncalled chips. A player can win only the portion of a pot that the player has matched through wagers. When several players have unequal stacks and one or more go all-in, the dealer conceptually separates contributions into layers. Every eligible player contributes the same amount to the main pot up to the shortest all-in. Extra matched amounts among deeper players form side pots. A chip amount that no opponent matches is not at risk and must be returned as an uncalled wager. TDA tournament procedure also requires all live hands to be tabled once at least one player is all-in and all further betting has finished. ( TDA tournament rules ; Hold’em rules ) Hypothetical example C: unequal all-ins and side-pot construction Three players remain. The following amounts are their total contributions for the whole hand, with no earlier pot or folded money to add. Alex can contribute at most $40, Blair can contribute $100, and Cameron can contribute $150. After the betting is complete, all three have attempted to commit those full amounts. The main pot is $40 from each player, or $120. Blair and Cameron can each match another $60 above Alex’s $40, creating a $120 side pot. Cameron’s final $50 has no opponent contribution to match it, so that $50 is returned to Cameron as uncalled. The total contested amount is therefore $240, not $290. Alex is eligible only for the $120 main pot. Blair and Cameron are eligible for the main pot and the $120 side pot. If Alex has the strongest hand overall and Blair’s hand beats Cameron’s, Alex wins the main pot, Blair wins the side pot, and Cameron still retains the returned $50. No player can win a side pot to which that player did not contribute. This example excludes rake or fees. ( Hold’em rules ; TDA tournament rules )

    A complete hand helpsconnect the vocabulary to actual action. Hypothetical example D: one complete annotated hand Six players are in a $0.50/$1 no-limit cash game. Everyone begins the hand with $100. The small blind posts $0.50 and the big blind posts $1. The player under the gun folds. The next player folds. In the cutoff, Jordan holds A♠ K♠ and raises to $3. The button folds. The small blind calls the additional $2.50. The big blind folds. The pot is now $7: Jordan’s $3, the small blind’s $3 total, and the big blind’s forfeited $1. The flop is K♦ 8♣ 3♥. The small blind acts first after the flop and checks. Jordan bets $4. The small blind calls $4. The pot becomes $15. The turn is 6♠. The small blind checks. Jordan bets $10. The small blind calls. The pot becomes $35. The river is 2♦. The small blind checks. Jordan checks behind. The small blind shows K♣ Q♣. Jordan shows A♠ K♠ and wins with a pair of kings and an ace kicker against a pair of kings with a queen kicker. Jordan invested $17 in the hand: $3 preflop, $4 on the flop, and $10 on the turn. The small blind also invested $17 in total, and the big blind’s $1 completed the $35 pot. Before any rake, Jordan’s $100 starting stack would finish at $118, a net gain of $18. No card is duplicated in the deal. This is a procedure and accounting example, not a claim that each strategic choice is uniquely correct. In a real cash room, rake could reduce the amount pushed to the winner. ( Hold’em rules ; operator rake schedule ) Several common beginner mistakes disappear once “best five cards” becomes automatic. Two hole cards that look attractive do not constitute a poker hand until they are evaluated with the board. A flush draw is not yet a flush. Three hearts on the board do not mean every player “has a flush”; a player still needs five hearts among the seven available cards. A pocket pair does not automatically beat an overcard-heavy board. And if the board itself contains the strongest five-card combination available to everyone, weak private cards may be irrelevant because all remaining players can play the board.

    Once the rules are comfortable, strategy begins with position , meaning where you sit relative to the button and therefore when you act. Acting later is valuable because you have observed more opponents before choosing. A player on the button usually has the last action after the flop; a player in early position must make decisions with many opponents still able to act. That informational difference is why a hand that is reasonable to enter on the button may be a fold from early position. This is a strategic principle, not an iron rule that every table or stack depth turns into the same chart. For a beginner, a useful simplification is to enter fewer pots with marginal holdings, especially from early position, and to prefer starting hands that can make strong top pairs, overpairs, straights, or flushes without depending on unusually favorable boards. High pairs and high connected cards are easier to navigate than weak, disconnected hands. Later position allows somewhat more flexibility because fewer players remain behind and more information is available. The action before you matters too. A hand that may be suitable to open when everyone has folded can become an easy fold after a raise and a re-raise. Effective stack depth, table size, opponent tendencies, rake, and tournament conditions all change the details. A static starting-hand chart can therefore be a training aid, but never a universal law. A useful beginner distinction is between value betting and bluffing . A value bet is made because worse hands are expected to call often enough to make betting profitable. A bluff is made because better hands may fold often enough to make betting profitable. Many beginner mistakes come from using aggressive-looking bets without knowing which of those jobs the bet is supposed to do. Before betting, ask: “What worse hands can call?” and “What better hands can fold?” If the honest answer to both is “almost none,” checking may deserve serious consideration. Aggression is valuable when it has a purpose, but “always be aggressive” is poor instruction. Raising can win a pot immediately, build a pot with a strong hand, deny opponents a free card, or clarify the price they must pay. It can also put more money at risk with a second-best hand. Calling can be correct when the price and hand strength justify continuing, but habitual calling allows opponents to realize equity cheaply and leaves you with difficult later decisions. Folding is not a failure. Because poker is a repeated game, preserving chips in a bad situation is part of rational play. Think in ranges, not one magical guess. An opponent who raises from early position can hold many possible combinations. As the hand develops, some become more plausible and others less plausible based on cards exposed and actions taken. Range thinking means considering a set of reasonable holdings rather than announcing “they have aces” from one gesture or bet. Beginners do not need solver-generated frequencies to start doing this. A simple range question is enough: “What strong hands, medium hands, draws, and bluffs could reasonably take this line?” Hand strength is always relative. Top pair can be a very strong hand on a dry heads-up flop and a vulnerable hand in a multiway pot on a coordinated board. A small flush can be strong in absolute ranking yet dangerous when four cards of that suit are visible. The number of opponents matters because more players create more possible combinations that can beat you. Betting history matters because a large river raise represents a different information set from a check. Stack depth matters because a decision for ten big blinds cannot simply be copied at 200 big blinds. Bet sizing should therefore follow a reason, not a superstition. Larger bets generally offer opponents a worse immediate price to call and put more money at risk; smaller bets offer a better price but can be appropriate when a range advantage or value target supports them. There is no single correct fraction of the pot for every board. A beginner is better served by choosing a small set of clear sizes and asking what each size accomplishes than by memorizing an unexplained rule such as “always bet two-thirds pot.” For a next lesson on what a bet is trying to accomplish, use Betting with a purpose .

    The minimum mathematics startswith the price of a call. Pot odds compare the amount you must call with the final pot you can win after making that call. The clean break-even equity formula, when there will be no future betting and ignoring rake, is: required equity = call amount ÷ final pot after calling Hypothetical example G: pot odds with the correct denominator There is $60 in the pot. An opponent bets $20, making the pot $80 before your decision. You must call $20. If you call, the final pot will be $100. Your break-even equity is therefore $20 ÷ $100 = 20%. A common mistake is to divide the $20 call by the $80 currently visible and conclude 25%. That compares the wrong quantities. The $20 you call becomes part of the pot you receive when you win, so the final-pot denominator is $100. If your true chance of winning were 25% and there were no future betting, ties, or rake, the call’s expected value relative to folding would be 0.25 × $100 - $20 = +$5 . In real poker, estimating that 25% is often the difficult part. Equity is your expected share of the pot under stated assumptions. A hand with 30% equity is not promised to win three of the next ten trials, and its equity can change sharply with the next card or with a different opponent range. Expected value , or EV, asks whether an action is worth more or less on average across repeated comparable situations. Positive EV does not mean “wins this time.” Negative EV does not mean “loses this time.” The distinction is essential because short-term outcomes contain substantial card variance. Schoenberg emphasizes that even formal equity calculations can mislead when future betting and folding are ignored. ( Schoenberg ) An out is an unseen card that, under your assumptions, improves your hand to one you expect to be winning often enough to matter. Counting outs is not the same as counting every card that makes a prettier hand. Some outs are “dirty”: they complete your draw but also make a stronger hand possible for an opponent. Others may be duplicated in effect. You usually do not know opponents’ exact cards, so outs are estimates conditioned on a range. Hypothetical example H: a drawing probability, with limitations You hold A♣ Q♣ on a flop of J♣ 7♣ 2♦. Four clubs are known, so nine clubs remain among the unseen cards. This model uses only your two hole cards and the three flop cards as known information, so 47 cards are unseen. Treat those cards as equally possible; an opponent’s known cards or information in their actions could change the conditional calculation. The probability that the turn is a club is therefore 9/47, about 19.1%. If you will see both turn and river and want the probability of making a flush by at least one of those cards, the clean calculation is the complement of missing twice: 1 - (38/47 × 37/46) ≈ 35.0% The familiar “rule of four” would estimate about 36% on the flop by multiplying nine outs by four, reasonably close here. On the turn, the “rule of two” would estimate roughly 18% for nine outs, compared with the exact 9/46, about 19.6%, after a non-club turn. But “35% to complete a flush by the river” is not “35% to win the hand.” An opponent might already have a set and later make a full house if the board pairs. Your opponent may fold before you realize the draw, or future betting may make continuing too expensive. Conversely, you may sometimes win without making the flush. The rule of two and four is only a quick approximation, and its error grows with larger out counts or unusual conditions. Exact drawing probability is useful only when the definition of an “out” and the future-action assumptions are also reasonable. Pot odds also have limits. A call that appears profitable from the current pot may be unattractive if a later street is likely to demand another large payment. A call that appears slightly unprofitable on immediate odds might become reasonable if winning creates credible additional value from future bets, though beginners should be cautious about optimistic “implied odds.” Rake raises the hurdle in cash games because not all contested money is ultimately returned to players. Multiway pots complicate equity. Uncertain opponent ranges complicate it further. The arithmetic is a decision aid, not a machine that removes uncertainty. Try it: price a different call On the river, a pot of $48 faces a $12 bet. Calling costs $12. With no future betting, rake or ties, what is the break-even percentage? If your assumed win chance were 20%, what would the call average relative to folding?

    Ask the poker-room desk what game is running, the minimum and maximum buy-in, how the waiting list works, where chips are purchased, whether there are house-specific betting-line or straddle rules, how rake is taken, and whom to call if a rule question arises. When seated, identify chip denominations before the first hand, keep large-denomination chips visible, and tell the dealer you are new if doing so makes you more comfortable. There is no strategic advantage in pretending to understand a procedure you do not understand. Arrive with the game and maximum expenditure already chosen. Check in at the poker-room desk, join the waiting list if necessary, and ask where to buy chips. When seated, confirm the blinds and any house-specific procedures. Stack chips so denominations are easy to see. Keep your hole cards on the table surface and protected, but do not conceal them. Watch the dealer button so you know your relative position and follow every action even after folding. TDA tournament rules explicitly place responsibility on players to protect their hands, follow action, act in turn, keep cards visible, and keep chips countable. Cash-room details may differ, but these are sound habits. ( TDA tournament rules ) When action reaches you, make the decision before moving chips. Clear speech prevents expensive ambiguity. Ask a neutral question before committing, such as “How much is the wager?” Once you have decided, state your action clearly before moving chips. Under TDA rule 3, even an action word used in a question can be interpreted as a binding declaration, so avoid an ambiguous question such as “Did he raise?” Under TDA tournament rules, pushing a single oversized chip forward while facing a bet is a call unless “raise” is declared first. Thus, facing a $15 bet, silently putting out one $100 chip can be ruled a call, not a $100 raise. TDA rule 44 requires the full raise in one motion or the full amount declared before chips are pushed. Saying only “raise” is not permission to add chips in successive motions. Say “raise to fifty” if fifty is your intended total, then move the chips. House procedures control the actual ruling. Many live rooms follow similar conventions, but house rules control. ( TDA tournament rules ) Premature action creates another avoidable problem. Do not fold, check, call, or raise before the players ahead of you have completed their turns. In TDA tournaments, action in turn is binding, and out-of-turn action can itself become binding depending on whether intervening action changes. For a beginner the operational lesson is simpler: pause, identify whose turn it is, then act. If you cannot tell how much a wager is, ask the dealer for clarification before declaring a call. ( TDA tournament rules ) Protect your cards from accidental mucking, especially in live cash games where physical cards can be swept into discarded cards. Keep them visible and under control. Do not expose a live hand casually. At showdown, table the cards properly if you want the dealer to read them and award a contested pot. Tournament rules emphasize that cards speak and that a properly tabled hand must be readable; the exact showdown order and mucking rights can be venue-specific. ( TDA tournament rules ) Poker is one player to a hand. Do not ask a friend, neighbor, phone, chart, artificial-intelligence system, or coach what to do while a live decision is pending. The 2026 TDA rules bar betting apps, charts, and other strategy tools at the table and prohibit receiving strategy data from another source. Major online operators likewise prohibit forms of real-time assistance and automated play. Study tools belong away from active play unless the applicable rules expressly permit them. ( TDA tournament rules ; operator assistance policies ) When a procedural dispute occurs, stop moving chips and ask the dealer. If the issue is not resolved, request the floor supervisor or tournament director. Another player can be sincere and still be wrong, or can have an interest in the outcome. Staff rulings and applicable house rules govern. Do not argue strategy while the ruling is being made; explain observable facts such as the prior wager, what you said, and which chips moved. Respect is part of competent procedure. Do not criticize another player’s play, celebrate an opponent’s loss, delay unnecessarily, or pressure someone to show folded cards. The 2026 TDA rules explicitly address disruptive and abusive behavior in tournament settings. A calm table also makes it easier for a beginner to concentrate. ( TDA tournament rules ) Leave when your planned time arrives, when your authorized gambling amount is exhausted, or when your decision quality deteriorates. None of those conditions depends on whether you are ahead or behind. A session is complete when the boundary says it is complete, not when the scoreboard gives emotional permission. Try it: say the action before moving chips In a TDA tournament you face a 12-chip bet. You silently push forward one 100-chip token. Have you raised to 100?

    Use a unique password and the operator’s available account-security features, verify that you are in the intended cash stake or tournament, and examine how the interface expresses bet amounts. Learn whether the displayed number means “raise to” a total amount or “raise by” an increment. Turn off optional automatic re-entry or rebuy features until you have decided deliberately whether you want them. Begin with one table and a pace at which you can read every action. Also read the operator’s rules on prohibited software and assistance. Major operators prohibit real-time decision assistance, bots, and forms of external advice during play, but exact policies vary, so the applicable operator policy controls. ( operator assistance policies ) A first online session needs the same deliberate pace in a different form. Open one table. Confirm whether the game is cash or tournament and verify the blind level. Check your displayed stack before every significant action. Type bet amounts carefully and review the number before clicking. Avoid keyboard shortcuts until they are familiar. Disable auto-rebuy or re-entry features unless they match your predetermined plan. Close unrelated strategy tools and communications that could violate the site’s assistance policy. If the connection becomes unreliable or you are repeatedly misclicking, stop rather than trying to compensate by playing faster.

    Think of the first month as four learning stages. A stage may take longer than a week. The aim is to explain fresh situations in your own words and identify what needs more work, rather than to finish by a deadline. The suggested exercises are an editorial practice plan, not validated standards of readiness or profitability. 1. Read the cards and name the actions Practise: Memorize hand rankings; practise fold, check, bet, call and raise. Deal mock boards and identify the best five cards. Explain a fresh situation: Name both players’ best five cards; compare tied categories in order; explain a board-only tie. Practise the first decisions 2. Follow the action and the stacks Practise: Follow betting order, learn position names, track simple pots, convert stacks to BB and identify effective stacks. Explain a fresh situation: Pause a mock hand and identify the next actor, amount to call and relevant effective stack. Put starting hands in context 3. Price a call and describe a draw Practise: Calculate pot odds, count basic outs, distinguish draw completion from equity and begin thinking in ranges. Explain a fresh situation: Price a new call using the final pot; state whether another payment may be required; explain a dirty out. Work through call prices 4. Practise, stop and review Practise: Use a low-pressure home or play-money setting. A real-money session is optional and requires its own predetermined entertainment limit. Explain a fresh situation: Follow a practice session, record one unclear decision honestly, and end at the planned time. Review one completed hand During the first week, speed is irrelevant. Use a deck of cards and deliberately construct pairs, two pair, straights, flushes, full houses, and ties. Practice the “best five” rule until you stop trying to use both hole cards automatically. Then deal random seven-card Hold’em situations and identify the winner. Board reading is the grammar of the game; strategic discussion is premature if the grammar is unstable. During the second stage, watch complete hands even after folding. Track the button, blinds, and action. Estimate the pot at the end of each street, then verify it if the platform or dealer information makes verification possible. Convert stacks into big blinds: at $1/$2, $100 is 50 BB; at 100/200 tournament blinds, a 6,000 stack is 30 BB. Ask which two players have the relevant effective stack before considering a large bet. These exercises turn apparently abstract strategy into quantities you can actually observe. During the third stage, work pot odds on paper. Write five lines every time: pot before the wager, opponent’s wager, pot now, amount to call, final pot after your call. Then calculate the break-even percentage. Separately work draw probabilities, always stating what cards you are treating as outs. This separation prevents the classic error of saying, “I have nine outs, therefore I should call,” without comparing the draw to the price or considering whether those outs actually win. During the fourth stage, practice making decisions under normal time pressure. Real-money play remains optional. The purpose is not to prove courage or profitability but to find procedural weaknesses that quiet study does not reveal. Did you miss action? Forget a stack size? Confuse the pot before and after a bet? Click the wrong amount? Feel compelled to recover a loss? Those observations are more educational than the session’s dollar result. “Suited cards are automatically strong.” Suitedness adds flush possibilities, but 9♣ 3♣ is still a weak, disconnected starting hand in many contexts. Attractive appearance is not the same as strategic value. “Aggressive players are skilled players.” Aggression is a tool. Betting large without a plausible value target or fold target can simply magnify errors. “I have a flush draw, so I have a flush.” A draw describes a possible future hand. Until the needed card arrives, evaluate the hand you actually hold and the probability and price of improving. “I have lost several times, so I am due.” Independent future cards do not compensate a player for a prior losing sequence. Session results do not create a debt the deck must repay. “Live poker is mainly about tells.” Physical behavior can sometimes add information, but beginners have far more reliable work to do first: position, stack size, legal action, board texture, bet size, and the sequence of prior decisions. Overconfidence in theatrical “tells” can distract from information that is openly available. “I won my first few sessions, so I am good enough to move up.” Short-run winning is compatible with both good and poor underlying decision-making. The empirical literature finds skill effects over repeated play, but also substantial noise from chance. Move your learning standards, not your stakes, when a short sample goes well. ( Levitt and Miles ; Potter van Loon and colleagues ; Schoenberg )

    A useful hand history distinguishes facts from reconstruction. Record the format and stakes, number of players, positions, approximate starting stacks, your exact hole cards, the board, and the wager sequence street by street. Record showdown cards only if actually seen. Then list the decision you want to review. If you cannot remember whether the river bet was $30 or $40, write “river bet approximately $30 to $40, uncertain” rather than silently choosing a number. False precision can turn a hand review into analysis of an event that never happened. Keep reviews selective. One carefully reconstructed hand in which you misunderstood the minimum raise is more valuable than fifty screenshots with no question attached. Label the type of uncertainty: rule, arithmetic, range, bet size, emotional decision, or missing fact. Rule questions should be resolved from the applicable official or house rules. Strategic questions can then be examined under explicit assumptions. Use the hand-review guide or the hand-review sheet . For an unfamiliar situation, the beginner checkpoint offers explanations and routes back to the relevant lessons. A useful learning record: “I thought I could check because I had posted a blind. I missed that the wager had increased. I will practise the amount to call.” This identifies something to repair. “I lost, so I played badly” does not identify a decision or its cause. If a passage left you unsure, you can send feedback . Include the page and section, what you thought it meant, and the point where you got stuck. A fictional example is enough; leave other players’ private details out. Reader feedback helps reveal problems that editorial and browser checks cannot measure.

    Copy these prompts to paper or download the first-session and practice sheet . The sheet stays with you; this page does not collect answers. I can identify both players’ best five cards and explain an ordinary tie. I can tell whose turn it is and distinguish checking, calling and raising. I know the format, blinds, buy-in range, fees and any re-entry rules. I know how to convert the relevant stack into BB. I have chosen the total discretionary gambling amount, including any reloads, and a stop time. Zero is a valid money limit. I have checked current age, location, licensing and venue requirements if money is involved. I am rested, unimpaired, and using no borrowed money or funds needed for obligations. I know to ask the dealer or floor about procedure before committing chips. Online, I have checked the stakes, account security, bet controls and assistance policy. I have one learning question to review afterward. Finishing this checklist is preparation, not evidence that a game is affordable for someone else or that you have a profitable strategy. You can decide to observe, practise without money, or leave.

    Poker contains skill-sensitive decisions and substantial chance. Levitt and Miles compared groups identified before the 2010 WSOP; the stronger group performed better in that sample. Potter van Loon and colleagues found persistent performance in historical online cash games. Their 1,500-hand result came from study-specific simulations, not a universal threshold for measuring one person’s skill. Schoenberg explains why the share attributed to luck or skill depends on definitions and assumptions. None of these studies tells a beginner how soon they can earn money. The first-month sequence and practical strategy suggestions here are an editorial synthesis. They have not been validated as a teaching curriculum with actual beginners. Use the exercises to expose confusion, then return to the relevant lesson. A correct calculation is not the same as an accurate opponent model; following procedure is not the same as beating a game after fees. Source check: October 14, 2026. The TDA reference was rechecked October 16, 2026; the official page displayed 2026 Rules, Version 1.1, September 21, 2026 . Rules, policies, laws, fees and support contacts can change. Commercial sources describe their own services. Local rules and current operator policies control actual play. Poker Tournament Directors Association. 2026 Rules, Version 1.1, September 21, 2026 . Tournament procedure, including rules 2, 3, 5, 14, 17, 20, 34, 44–46 and 49. It does not govern every cash or home game. PokerStars Learn. Texas Hold’em rules . Core mechanics from a commercial operator. The side-pot amounts above are independently worked fictional examples. PokerStars. Poker tournament types . Operator examples of structures, entry fees and rebuy formats. Actual events vary. PokerStars Help. Simplified buy-in display . Explains the combined price and where the prize-pool contribution and fee are disclosed. PokerStars. Poker rake . An operator schedule showing variation by stake and player count. No rate here is assumed to apply at another venue. PokerStars and GGPoker. Assistance policies . PokerStars separates permitted, prohibited and client-open restrictions. GGPoker has its own stricter chart and external-assistance rules. Also read GGPoker’s Security & Ecology Policy . Michigan Gaming Control Board. October 8, 2026 consumer-protection release . Michigan-specific illustration of licensing and self-exclusion protections, not a nationwide legality determination. National Council on Problem Gambling. Responsible-gambling guidance, February 5, 2026 . Time and money limits, affordable discretionary funds, avoiding impairment, no chasing, and the option not to bet. National Council on Problem Gambling. About the National Problem Gambling Helpline . Current U.S. gambling-related support and referral information. Steven D. Levitt and Thomas J. Miles. The Role of Skill Versus Luck in Poker, NBER Working Paper 17023 (2011) . Observational comparison using the 2010 WSOP. A group comparison does not estimate a new player’s profitability. Rogier J. D. Potter van Loon, Martijn J. van den Assem and Dennie van Dolder. Beyond Chance? The Persistence of Performance in Online Poker, PLOS ONE 10(3), e0115479 (2015) . Historical player-hand observations and study-specific simulations; the time horizon is not universal. Frederic Paik Schoenberg. Is poker a game of luck or skill?, Significance 15(6), 30–33 (2018) . Statistical definitions and worked examples, with simplifying assumptions. Alexandre Hamel, Célyne Bastien, Christian Jacques, Axelle Moreau and Isabelle Giroux. Sleep or Play Online Poker?, Frontiers in Psychiatry 11, 600092 (2021) . 23 regular online players followed for 28 days. Associations with sleep deprivation and tilt do not establish causation or a universal effect. Prepared with AI assistance. Adapted and edited from a research draft supplied for this website. Published October 14, 2026 . Revisions checked card comparisons and arithmetic, clarified live declarations and source scope, and connected practical exercises to the existing lessons. No learner study or learning outcome is claimed. Use study tools away from active play.

    On this site · Tournament study

    What does a $400 poker tournament really cost?

    Plan a poker tournament trip budget: three worked $400 WSOP Circuit examples separate entry fees, travel, hotels, meals, re-entry reserves, time and actual profit.

    Read matching section

    Searchable article text, without exercise answers

    The entry buys a seat. The trip also buys travel, meals, a place to sleep and time away. Three transparent budgets show how a $400 tournament becomes a $451.50 local outing, a $734.25 overnight trip or a $1,417.50 two-event weekend. Illustrative budgets, not price quotes or accounts of Nolan’s trips. Event information checked October 15, 2026. The October 2026 WSOP Circuit at Turning Stone is a dated worked example; use the method with your own event and current booking totals. All amounts are US dollars. Before reading every line, choose the closest plan: local, one entry ; one entry and a hotel ; or two events over a weekend . Then copy the worksheet . If you are still comparing events, start with the structure-sheet guide .

    A useful tournament budget answers three questions. What do I intend to spend? What extra money have I set aside for defined possibilities? What did I actually spend when I got home? Three modeled budgets: spending and accessible funds Model Planned spending Reserves Funds available Local, one entry $451.50 $50.00 $501.50 Overnight, one initial entry $734.25 $649.75 $1,384.00 Weekend, two planned entries $1,417.50 $649.75 $2,067.25 On a narrow screen, scroll the comparison sideways. Each model below gives the full breakdown. The reserves in the last two rows consist of $400 for at most one optional re-entry plus $249.75 for an extra night, meals and incidentals. The local reserve is $50 for a possible return visit and food. Unspent reserves are not expenses or losses. The funds column excludes any hotel authorization hold and costs outside the stated scenarios. These figures describe three invented travelers. They are not an average price, a recommendation to spend this amount or a forecast of winnings. The model works only if a zero-payout trip fits the traveler’s discretionary budget. Necessary household money and the means to get home remain protected. Planned spending = planned entries + planned direct trip expenses. Funds available = planned spending + optional-entry reserve + defined contingencies. Actual spending = entries and trip expenses actually paid, including reserves used. Money held temporarily on a card is a separate liquidity issue. It can reduce spending capacity before checkout without becoming a final charge. Time and foregone income also deserve their own record; they are not hidden additions to these cash totals.

    The official October 2026 Turning Stone structure packet lists the Mini Main, Event #2, as a $400 total entry: $330 toward the prize pool and $70 administrative fee . Its fee includes staffing/dealer fees and rake. Events #12 and #14 show the same breakdown. [1] The fee is inside this $400 entry Part of this entry Amount Prize-pool contribution $330.00 Included administrative fee $70.00 Total payment for one entry $400.00 The disclosed fee is 17.5% of the total payment: $70 ÷ $400. The prize-pool component is 82.5%. Do not add $70 again and call this a $470 entry. These percentages describe these particular events, not every $400 tournament. A separate payment-method charge, if applicable, would need its own line. A voluntary tip is not assumed to be mandatory. A re-entry is another paid attempt after elimination during the permitted window. Here that means another $400 , not another $70. A starting flight is a scheduled starting session of the same tournament. A separately numbered event is a different tournament. Read registration and re-entry for the distinctions. Check: how much for two entries? The entry is listed as $330 + $70. You use one initial entry and one permitted re-entry. Is the entry bill $470, $730 or $800?

    The official schedule places the series in Verona, New York, October 15–26, 2026. The examples use these events. Times are local to the venue. [2] Mini Main, Event #2: five starting flights, October 15–17. The overnight model chooses Flight D, Saturday, October 17 at 10 a.m. Survivors return Sunday, October 18 at noon. The listed $600,000 guarantee concerns the event’s prize pool, not any individual entrant’s return. Event #12: $400 No-Limit Hold’em, Friday, October 23 at 4 p.m. The local and weekend models use it. Event #14: $400 Turbo No-Limit Hold’em Double Stack, Saturday, October 24 at 6 p.m. The weekend model also plans for it. The matching structure sheets allow re-entry until the beginning of level 9. They permit an additional day if needed. For the Mini Main’s chosen morning flight, Day 1 is scheduled for 22 thirty-minute levels or the stated field threshold, whichever comes first, plus breaks. A start time is not a promised finish time. [1] The venue directs players to its WSOP app registration link; WSOP’s schedule points to WSOP LIVE for tournament details. Confirm the current instructions, payment methods, identification requirements and availability for the exact event. A Las Vegas summer-series payment policy is not evidence of what a New York Circuit desk accepts. [3] This guide is a budget example rather than a booking or registration service. Recheck the organizer’s schedule and matching structure sheet before paying, particularly when planning flights, multiple entries or a return on another day.

    Profile: the player lives 30 road miles away and attends Event #12. One $400 entry is the entire poker allocation. No hotel or re-entry is planned. The driving inputs are assumptions: 60 miles round trip, 28 miles per gallon and $3.50 per gallon. Fuel is 60 ÷ 28 × $3.50 = $7.50 . The model assumes a route without tolls and uses the venue’s advertised free self-parking. Meals and incidentals are personal spending caps, including applicable taxes and tips, not claims about menu prices. [4] Local plan with one entry and no hotel Local plan Amount One entry $400.00 Fuel $7.50 Self-parking and modeled tolls $0.00 Meals cap $32.00 Incidentals cap $12.00 Direct trip expenses $51.50 Planned spending: $400 + $51.50 $451.50 Optional-entry reserve $0.00 Return-trip/food contingency $50.00 Funds available: $451.50 + $50 $501.50 The $50 gives a possible added tournament day somewhere to live in the plan. The published one-day format can be extended. It is a modest modeled buffer, not a guarantee that every disruption fits. [1] If the player receives no payout, spends the base plan and never touches the buffer, the pre-tax trip result is −$451.50 . It is not −$501.50. The $50 remains theirs. The entry is about 88.6% of planned spending. Buying another $400 stack would change this outing much more than a small snack purchase. This player’s precommitted limit is one entry even though the event permits more. Protect the afternoon, evening and a possible later day. Include registration and a safe journey home after a late finish. The budget cannot predict when the player will be eliminated.

    Profile: the player drives 150 miles each way to the Saturday morning Mini Main flight and books Saturday night. If they advance, Sunday’s noon restart does not require a late 150-mile drive followed by an immediate return. The base plan has one entry; one additional entry is optional. Driving assumptions are 300 miles round trip, 28 mpg and $3.50 per gallon, producing $37.50 of fuel. The $12 toll allowance is an assumption , not a quoted Thruway fare. Use the official calculator for the actual route, vehicle and payment account. New York’s Thruway uses cashless tolling; payment method affects the amount. [5] Room assumption: a nearby taxable offsite hotel costs $180 before tax for one person for one night, with no separate mandatory fee in this model. Neither that rate nor availability has been quoted for the event dates. The illustrative tax load is 13.75%, using an 8.75% sales-tax component and 5% county occupancy-tax component. State and county references support those components; they do not establish the checkout total at a particular property or the tax treatment of every resort room. [6] [7] Modeled room: $180 × (1 + 0.0875 + 0.05) = $204.75. Replace the whole line with the selected booking’s verified total, including every applicable mandatory charge. Do not add tax a second time to an already tax-inclusive quote. Overnight plan with separate optional reserves Overnight plan Amount One initial entry $400.00 Fuel $37.50 Toll allowance $12.00 Venue self-parking; hotel parking assumed included $0.00 One modeled room night, including tax $204.75 Meals cap for the two-day window $65.00 Incidentals cap $15.00 Direct trip expenses $334.25 Planned spending: $400 + $334.25 $734.25 Optional reserve: at most one re-entry $400.00 Extra night, meals and incidentals $249.75 Funds available: $734.25 + $400 + $249.75 $1,384.00 The extra-night reserve is $204.75 room + $35 meals + $10 incidentals = $249.75 . It assumes another room is available at the same modeled price. A real extension may cost more, so establish a workable backup before entering. Sunday play can end late or extend to another day. Advancing does not make lodging free, and the trip should work before a payout is known. If the player busts Saturday, uses the already-booked room and returns Sunday, the unused $649.75 reserve is not a loss. If they use the optional entry, spending becomes $1,134.25 before an extra night. If they use both defined reserves, spending reaches $1,384.00 under these assumptions. A vehicle problem or a higher last-minute room price can exceed that modeled amount. The room is about 27.9% of the base plan. It is now a substantial part of the decision. Check cancellation terms as well as the nightly rate: an early exit does not necessarily make a booked night refundable. Check: was the unused reserve lost? You made $1,384 available, used one entry and the base trip, received no payout, and left the reserves untouched. What did the outing cost?

    Profile: the player drives 240 miles each way, books Friday and Saturday nights, and plans to enter Event #12 on Friday and Event #14 on Saturday. There is one optional re-entry across the whole weekend , not one per event. The second event is conditional on being free to play it. If the first tournament extends and conflicts with the second, the player skips the second. Planning for two entries does not require paying both in advance or abandoning a surviving stack. Check the day’s transitions and continuation arrangements before committing. Driving assumptions produce 480 ÷ 28 × $3.50 = $60 in fuel, plus an assumed $18 in tolls. Two nights at the same modeled all-in room price cost 2 × $204.75 = $409.50 . Two-event weekend with a solo room Solo weekend plan Amount Two planned entries $800.00 Fuel $60.00 Toll allowance $18.00 Venue self-parking; hotel parking assumed included $0.00 Two modeled room nights, including tax $409.50 Meals cap for three days $105.00 Incidentals cap $25.00 Direct trip expenses $617.50 Planned spending: $800 + $617.50 $1,417.50 Optional reserve: one re-entry total $400.00 Extra night, meals and incidentals $249.75 Funds available: $1,417.50 + $400 + $249.75 $2,067.25 Entries account for about 56.4% of the base plan and lodging for about 28.9%. The advertised $400 entry is real; it is simply a small description of a much larger purchase. Sharing the room changes only the costs actually shared. If the same $409.50 room total covers two people without an extra charge, each pays $204.75 toward lodging. Holding every other input fixed, each person’s base plan falls by $204.75 to $1,212.75 . This comparison deliberately leaves the driving cost unchanged. If they also share a car, allocate the actual vehicle bill separately rather than halving everything. Each person still pays for their own entries. After an early bust, there is no requirement to replace the event with another tournament or cash game. Rest, a non-poker activity or going home when reservations permit can all fit the plan. A reserve is a ceiling, not an assignment to fill every free hour with play.

    Small adjustments are easier to judge when the baseline is visible. Changes to a plan with every other input held fixed Change Effect under these assumptions Use the overnight plan’s one optional entry Add $400; total $1,134.25 before an extra night Add one room night only Add $204.75 Add a room night, $35 meals and $10 incidentals Add $249.75; overnight total $984 without re-entry Split the weekend room equally with one person Subtract $204.75 per person; base $1,212.75 Skip the second planned weekend event Subtract $400 if not paid or fully refundable; base $1,017.50 None of these is a recommendation to enter. The point is to change an input and recalculate, rather than stretch the spending limit after a loss. Flying is a replacement transport plan. Suppose airfare is an assumed $300 return and checked bags an assumed $70 total. Turning Stone advertises private Syracuse airport transportation at $125 each way, including tax and gratuity, subject to availability and requested at least 48 hours ahead. Confirm that the service is available for your chosen hotel and dates; an offsite stay may require additional transport. [8] If those transfers fit the itinerary, the illustrative package is $300 + $70 + $250 = $620 . Replacing the weekend’s $78 fuel-and-toll line increases the base by $542 , to $1,959.50 . This is not a fare quote or a general comparison of flying and driving. It assumes a free drop-off at the origin airport, no airport parking bill and no other ground transfers. Replace those assumptions for an actual itinerary. Do not leave both complete drive and flight packages in the same total unless both really occur. The drive models count fuel and toll cash expenses, not depreciation or maintenance. You may track vehicle wear separately. A tax mileage allowance is not literal gasoline spending.

    For this guide, the accounting is: Pre-tax trip result = gross tournament payouts − actual entry spending − actual direct trip spending. “Gross payouts” means the tournament prizes before personal tax consequences. It does not mean profit. Count every entry and all direct trip spending once, including any reserve actually used. Exclude reserves left untouched. Keep another event’s cash-game result separate if you want to understand this tournament trip. Consider a hypothetical $600 gross payout on the overnight base plan: $600 − $400 entry − $334.25 trip expenses = −$134.25 pre-tax. The player cashed and still spent more than they received. Pre-tax break-even gross payouts are $451.50 for the local base, $734.25 for the overnight base and $1,417.50 for the solo weekend base. Using the overnight re-entry raises that threshold to $1,134.25, assuming all other spending stays fixed. These are accounting thresholds, not estimates of the chance of reaching them. The examples supply no expected return, cashing probability or evidence of an edge. A prize-pool guarantee does not establish any of those things. The results guide explains why an individual cash and a record of profitability answer different questions. Personal income-tax treatment is outside these models and depends on the applicable rules and the player’s situation. The arithmetic here is consistently pre-tax. This trip limit also does not prescribe the size of an overall poker bankroll. Check: what if the player re-entered? The overnight traveler receives the same hypothetical $600 payout but paid for two $400 entries and $334.25 of trip expenses. What is the pre-tax result?

    Protect a calendar window for travel, registration, play, rest and a possible continuation. For these profiles that means a local day with possible return, a Saturday–Sunday overnight trip with a possible extension, and a Friday–Sunday weekend with a possible extension. They are planning windows, not predictions of playing time or elimination. Then ask what the time displaces. If eight hours away genuinely cost $200 of wages, record $200 in foregone income , separately from receipts. Paid vacation does not automatically mean losing a day’s salary. It uses limited time that you may value differently. A leisure valuation is also possible, but label it as a personal judgment rather than a cash payment. Avoid counting the same hours twice as both lost wages and another full hourly opportunity cost. Likewise, a cash budget can count the full casino meal bill while a separate incremental-cost comparison subtracts spending genuinely avoided at home. Use a documented baseline; do not invent a food offset to make the trip look cheaper. The useful leisure question is: If payouts are zero, is this experience worth the money and time I have chosen? Enjoying the experience and demonstrating a profitable poker edge are separate judgments.

    Start with the organizer’s complete entry price and the booking checkout total. Replace every assumption above. When a cost is unknown, leave it marked unknown until you have a workable answer. For the venue questions behind a trip plan, the Thunder Valley first-visit guide covers official information, registration, waitlists and a private checklist. Its historical event examples are separate from the Turning Stone budgets here. Download the blank tournament trip budget or copy the same sheet below. It is plain text for your own notes; completed amounts stay with you. Use the event and day planner beside this budget for seat, schedule and procedural questions. A money worksheet does not replace reading the event rules. Before leaving, resolve these points: Entry cap: the total number and price of planned and optional entries, and when a new entry would no longer fit the day. Booking and return plan: checkout total, cancellation terms, card holds, safe transport home and a possible later day. Available funds: the base plus defined reserves, without depending on a payout. This does not require carrying the whole amount in physical cash; verify the accepted payment methods. Stop rule: losses do not authorize more entries. An unused reserve can stay unused.

    How much money should I bring? Enough accessible funds for your plan and chosen reserves, plus any separately disclosed authorization hold. The three examples require $501.50, $1,384 or $2,067.25 under their stated assumptions. They are not universal amounts to carry in cash. Check payment instructions and protect return transport independently of poker winnings. What happens if I reach another day? The event continues according to its rules. Reaching it can trigger another room, more food, changed transport or displaced commitments. Here an extra night plus meals and incidentals is modeled at $249.75. Verify actual availability and price rather than assuming the sample reserve guarantees a room. Do not count a future payout as the funding source. Can I budget for no re-entry? Yes. The local plan does exactly that. A permitted re-entry is an option under event rules, not an obligation. Leaving after one attempt can be a complete plan. What if the trip only works if I cash? The budget is relying on an uncertain return. Reduce the outing, stay local, remove optional entries, wait or skip it. A cash game after elimination is not a dependable way to recover the hotel bill. For gambling that is becoming difficult to control, NCPG’s help and treatment resources are separate from poker coaching. The site’s player-protection guide explains how to find official support routes. The advertised buy-in tells you the price of one entry. A complete budget lets you decide whether the whole outing fits before the first hand.

    WSOP / Turning Stone: October 2026 structure packet . PDF pages 2, 12 and 14, labeled Events #2, #12 and #14, support the $330 + $70 split, included staffing/dealer fees and rake, re-entry windows and continuation conditions. Page 2 supplies the selected Mini Main flight and Sunday restart. Read the matching event sheet; other pages are not interchangeable. WSOP: Turning Stone series schedule . October 15–26, 2026; Mini Main flights and guarantee; Events #12 and #14 dates, times and prices. Schedule and guarantees can change. Turning Stone: World Series of Poker Circuit . Series information and app registration direction. WSOP’s schedule also points to WSOP LIVE. The reviewed pages did not establish a complete payment-method list for these entries; confirm it with the organizer. Turning Stone: guest-services FAQ . New York State Department of Taxation and Finance: Publication 718 . The reviewed combined sales-tax table lists 8.75% for Oneida County. It does not give a hotel’s complete bill. Oneida city, in Madison County, is a different listed jurisdiction. Oneida County: hotel/motel occupancy tax . Lists a 5% room occupancy tax.     Thunder Valley’s poker page advertises an online waiting list. That listing alone does not establish a tournament entry, a paid seat or a guarantee that your game will run. Confirm which list you are joining and how the desk expects you to check in. Check: does joining a list buy a Circuit entry?

    These two completed fall 2026 events show why a price and start time are not a day plan. The official packet supports the comparison below. The Seniors event was for players 50 or older , an additional restriction beyond the casino’s general gaming age.     The resort FAQ describes a 3,700-space parking structure connected to the casino and hotel. It does not establish a reliable walking time to a particular tournament desk. At the desk, a useful opening is: “This is my first visit. I’m here for [event and flight]. Where do I complete registration, and what must I do before taking a seat?” For cash, name the game you are asking about instead. Get a table and seat assignment rather than occupying an apparently empty chair. Before play, locate the restrooms and a practical food route. Ask staff about access needs, luggage arrangements or other assistance that would affect your day.     Use the actual break schedule when making a meal plan. Check the venue’s dining outlets and the specific restaurant’s current hours. A list of restaurants does not establish that ordering, eating and returning will fit a short break. This guide has not timed a food route or verified a tableside-service promise. [7] Set an outing budget that includes entries, transport, lodging when needed, food and defined contingencies.
