If you bust while registration is open, the event’s permission to re-enter does not require another purchase. A cash game is also a separate decision, not a reliable way to recover the day’s bill. If you advance, confirm the restart and the costs it could trigger. Keep the means to get home and necessary household money outside the poker allocation. Arrange a return plan that also works after a late finish, without assuming a tournament payout will fund it.

    The reviewed public pages did not establish a poker-room-specific filming policy. The hand-to-vlog guide explains how to build an account around an actual record and authorized material. Check: does the concert camera rule answer the poker question?

    Download the blank Thunder Valley visit checklist , or copy the same text below. Keep completed notes, staff confirmations and receipts private. Use the event and day planner for a fuller schedule and the trip-budget worksheet for money. You do not need to complete every poker lesson before asking a desk a procedural question.

    Write down what actually happened: the date and event, where you checked in, what remained unclear, and what you would change next time. Separate those observations from official policies. “This queue took me 20 minutes on this date” would be a personal observation, not a normal waiting-time estimate for everyone.     Limped and multiway pots: how to think through live poker

    Play against limpers in low-stakes live poker: isolation raises, position, stacks, ranges, a counted cash hand, tournament pressure and solver limits.

    Read matching section

    Searchable article text, without exercise answers

    Two players limp. You raise. Three people call. The flop arrives, and a hand that looked straightforward on a preflop chart has become a decision against several ranges. Start by rebuilding the situation: action order, relevant stacks, likely hands and what your next bet needs to accomplish. For study away from play. This guide separates cash games from tournaments and model results from opponent assumptions. Worked hands are fictional, not Nolan’s sessions. Product documentation and linked research were checked October 15, 2026. For a quick route, read the questions to ask , the cash-game hand , then copy the review sheet . The companion multiway pot workshop covers call prices, side pots and shared defense in more detail. If ranges are new to you, start with ranges for beginners .

    An open-limp is entering an unopened pot by calling the big blind rather than raising. Overlimping means calling after someone else has limped. A limp-call is limping and then calling a raise; a limp-reraise is limping and then raising after another player raises. A multiway pot has at least three players still contesting it. It need not be limped: an ordinary open and two calls also produce a three-way flop. A limped pot can become heads-up. Name both the preflop route and the current number of opponents. An isolation raise aims to play against a selected opponent with fewer other players involved. If the whole table routinely calls, you have raised over limpers without achieving isolation. That can still be a good value raise. It changes the reason for choosing your hand and size.

    Who acts before and after me? Write the actual order, including players who checked but can still respond to a bet. Being on the button helps, but a call closes the action only when nobody else can act again on that street. How much can I win or lose against each opponent? Use pairwise effective stacks and any existing all-ins. The largest stack on the table is not the effective stack against everyone. How did each range arrive here? A limp-call, cold-call and blind defense are different actions. Earlier calls can also change the incentives of players behind. What does my hand make, and what beats it? Separate current hand strength, improvement to the best hand, redraws and domination risk. What would a bet accomplish? Name plausible worse calls, better folds or useful equity denial. “I raised preflop” does not answer this question. Which inputs are observations, and which are guesses? “Called two raises with weak suited hands at showdown” is evidence. “Limpers always call anything” is an unsupported generalization. Effective stacks are pairwise. Suppose the stacks still behind are $500 for you, $110 for one opponent and $650 for another. You can contest another $110 with the short stack and $500 with the deeper player. At $1/$3, those are about 37 and 167 big blinds. Existing contributions and pot eligibility still matter. A short all-in can create a main-pot problem alongside a deeper side-pot problem; use the side-pot lab for the accounting. Position is also relational. Facing a bet with two players behind is different from facing the same bet after those players fold. A cheaper-looking call can expose you to a raise, an overcall or a difficult later street. Record the sequence rather than only your seat name. The older GTO Wizard multiway overview is useful on these positional and shared-defense ideas; use the newer documentation below for software capabilities. 1

    The practical question is not “How do I punish limping?” It is “Which action performs well against these players, at this price, with these stacks?” A raise may get heads-up, collect value from several worse hands, deny cheap entry to the blinds or create an expensive pot with a hand that struggles when called. Upswing’s isolation framework explicitly varies with the limper’s tendencies, players behind and stack depth. Its wider case relies on a weak opponent, low limp-reraise risk and relatively unthreatening players behind. It also distinguishes limping first from limping behind. Those are conditional coaching recommendations, not proof about a stranger at your table. 2 With A♠ Q♠ on the button , raising can remain attractive even if several worse aces, queens or suited hands call. With a marginal offsuit hand, the same callers may leave you making dominated pairs out of position or building a pot without a useful postflop plan. The number of callers alone does not decide either hand. Choose a size with an expectation about responses. If a larger raise gets nearly the same loose calls, strong value hands may benefit from charging more. That does not mean increasing every raise until somebody folds. Larger raises also reduce the stack-to-pot ratio and make mistakes more expensive. Ask what happens when you miss, face a limp-reraise or get called by three players. Overlimping can sometimes keep a playable speculative hand in a cheap pot. It also lets more players see the flop, can be punished by a raise behind and may produce costly second-best hands. “Suited” and “good pot odds” are starting observations, not sufficient reasons to enter. Include the actual cash-game rake or collection structure; cash-game costs explains why a small apparent edge may disappear after charges. There is no universal “raise this many big blinds per limper” solution here. An arithmetic sizing rule does not know the opponents, rake, remaining stacks or players behind you.

    Nut potential means being able to make the best possible hand on a given board. An ace-high flush draw can dominate lower flush draws. A small flush draw may complete and still lose. Even an ace-high flush can lose on a paired board to a full house or quads, or to a possible straight flush. Read the whole board. Domination risk appears when your likely pair loses to the same pair with a better kicker. Weak offsuit aces do not become automatic bargains because several people have entered. Making one pair can commit you to decisions against ranges containing better kickers and stronger made hands. Robust equity is a useful description for a hand that retains meaningful ways to win when opponents continue. A strong pair with a nut-flush draw is a different asset from a weak one-pair bluff-catcher. It still needs to be evaluated against actual ranges and the price of continuing. Vulnerability asks how often later cards or further action make a currently good hand difficult to play. Top pair may justify a value bet in one configuration and a check in another. A label such as “overpair” does not establish a willingness to play for a deep stack. When describing a bet, name hands rather than adjectives: “I expect calls from QJ, QT and some spade draws” is more useful than “I am betting because I am strong.” Then ask whether those holdings actually reach this point and choose this response.

    Here is an intentionally artificial model. A pure bluff wins only when every opponent folds; if anyone continues, the bettor loses the bet and has no later equity or betting decisions. Assume each opponent independently folds 55% of the time. Independent 55% folds: an artificial model Opponents who must fold Chance everyone folds One 55.0% Two 30.3% Three 16.6% Four 9.2% The calculation is 0.55 multiplied by itself once per opponent . It does not estimate any live player’s behavior. Real responses depend on cards, sizes, ranges and earlier actions. More generally, multiply conditional probabilities: the chance A folds, times the chance B folds given A folded, and so on. Do not assume independence because multiplication is convenient. In this simplified model, betting $50 into $100 needs everyone to fold more than 50 / (100 + 50) = 33.33% of the time to show a positive immediate return. Against two independent 55% folders, the joint fold rate is 30.25%. The modeled return is 0.3025 × $100 − 0.6975 × $50 = −$4.625 , about a $4.63 loss per attempt. A bluff can fail this test even though each opponent individually folds more than half the time. That calculation deliberately excludes draws, future play, rake, all-ins and side pots. It illustrates a burden, not a bluffing chart. A heads-up minimum-defense figure is not a quota that each opponent must separately meet. For the pot-eligibility and conditional-response details, continue to the multiway workshop . Check: are two 55% fold rates enough? Under the independent, zero-equity model above, does a $50 bluff into $100 profit against two such opponents?

    A continuation bet, or c-bet , is a bet by the preflop aggressor on a later street. Raising before the flop gives you no entitlement to win it afterward. Before betting into several opponents, ask who has the strongest hands on this board and what continues against your chosen size. One GTO Wizard study compared an eight-handed, symmetric 100bb chip expected value (chip-EV) setup where the lojack opener faced either the big blind alone or both blinds. Its weighted 20-flop subset used bets of 33%, 66% and 100% pot , with one raise size. Adding the small blind increased the opener’s checking by 11 percentage points ; pot-sized c-bets fell from 18% to 1.3% . The preflop response ranges also changed. These are results from a defined three-way model, not recommended frequencies for a four-way $1/$3 game. 3 Treat that as a reason to examine marginal bets closely. With a medium-strength hand, checking can retain the ability to reach showdown without building a pot against several strong continuing ranges. With a strong value hand, betting may have several willing customers. A smaller bet risks less but also offers a better calling price; it does not make a weak bluff good by itself. Do not read every check as weakness. Andrew Brokos’s three-way turn-probe study considers a 100bb cash, big blind–cutoff–button single-raised pot . The cutoff, with the button still behind, has reason to check strong hands. The study finds board-dependent turn aggression rather than a simple permission to attack after everyone checks. A range is capped when it excludes, or is short of, the strongest possible hands; one check does not establish that. 4 The useful adjustment is specific: remove a proposed bluff if its required folds are implausible; reconsider a value bet if worse hands do not call; keep strong hands in an opponent’s checking range when the action supports them. “Never bluff multiway” and “always bet small” skip the same analysis.

    Setup: two early-position players limp for $3. You hold A♠ Q♠ on the button , start with $450, and raise to $18 total . The small blind folds. The big blind and both limpers call to $18. All three opponents started with at least $450. No straddle, ante, rake or promotional drop is included in this illustration. The size is an example, not a prescribed isolation size. Four players contribute $18, plus the small blind’s dead $1: 4 × $18 + $1 = $73 . You have $432 behind . Your stack-to-pot ratio is about 432 / 73 = 5.92 . Every opponent can cover your remaining stack, but that would change if one had started short. The flop is Q♦ 9♠ 6♠ . All three opponents check. You have top pair, top kicker and the nut-flush draw. You can be behind a set or two pair, and a flush completing later will not guarantee victory on every runout. Still, this is much more resilient than a weak queen without a draw. Suppose you bet $25 . The big blind folds, the first limper check-raises to $90 total , and the other limper folds. The problem is now heads-up against the check-raiser , not four-way against all the original callers. The preflop and flop history still informs that opponent’s range. There is $188 in the pot: $73 + your $25 + the opponent’s $90. Calling costs another $65 , creating a $253 pot. With a free showdown and no deductions, the required expected pot share would be 65 / 253 = 25.69% . This is the flop, however. The turn can bring another bet, so that fraction does not prove a call is profitable. Now construct competing hypotheses. If this player check-raises sets, two pair and strong draws, your hand faces a different problem than if the range contains only sets. A♠ Q♠ removes ace-high spade draws and Q♠-containing combinations from the opponent’s possible holdings. It does not remove every other spade draw. Do not count blocked combinations as potential bluffs. Before choosing call, raise or fold in a review, write the candidate hands, their plausible frequencies and what happens on several turns. A shove needs a case about worse calls or better folds, not only “I have a big draw.” No exact action is solver-certified by this incomplete range description. The useful output is a decision whose reasoning changes coherently when the opponent assumption changes. Check: what changed after the check-raise?

    Keep tournament chips separate from cash-game dollars. Earlier in a conventional event, a chip-EV model can be a useful approximation, but it is a choice with limits. Antes, shorter stacks and possible reshoves change the preflop tree before anyone sees the flop. A cash-game isolation range is not automatically a 25bb tournament strategy. At shorter depths, the 10–20 BB lesson separates opening, re-jamming, calling and small-blind completing. Its examples show why a restricted push/fold model cannot answer every one of those questions. Fictional earlier-stage example: you have 40bb and A♣ J♣ on the button after two limps. If the blinds rarely reshove and the limpers call worse hands, raising can have a clear value case. Change the big blind to an aggressive 16bb stack and you must plan for a shove. You cannot conclude “raise-call” or “raise-fold” from the hand label alone; size, ranges and the other players’ responses matter. Near a bubble or final table, add the payout structure, remaining field, other stacks, who covers whom and any bounty. ICM , the Independent Chip Model, estimates tournament prize equity from stacks and payouts. It is a model of the prize situation, not a forecast of your personal future results. Folding can preserve or change prize equity while others continue to contest a pot. GTO Wizard’s September 2026 documentation explicitly includes nonzero fold values in multiway ICM and asymmetric three-way postflop incentives. 5 Fictional payout-pressure example: a 25bb middle stack is covered by a chip leader while another player has 7bb. Losing to the leader can eliminate the middle stack before the short stack. That risk can make a chip-profitable confrontation unattractive in prize equity. It does not establish an automatic fold: exact payouts, ranges, coverage and other stacks are missing. Satellites and bounties require their own objectives too. See tournament equity . If someone ignores payout pressure or calls much wider than the model, state that as a read. Do not describe a population guess as an ICM result.

    “Solvers cannot model multiway poker” is outdated. GTO Wizard’s February 2026 release documents custom preflop solving for up to nine players, with adjustable stacks, sizes, rake, antes and opponent strategies. Nodelocking means fixing part of an opponent’s strategy to test a stated assumption. It does not verify that the assumption matches a real person. 6 The September 2026 release adds custom preflop ICM and three-way postflop ICM. Crucially, the reviewed documentation says its preflop trees allow at most three players to reach the flop ; a fourth overcaller or overlimper is not supported. A nine-player starting table therefore does not imply a nine-player postflop solve. Recheck this boundary when using the product because capabilities can change. 5 A nearby three-way solve can help investigate a principle in a four- or five-way hand. It cannot certify the exact action in the fictional four-way example above. Record the simplification and compare more than one reasonable range assignment instead of importing a percentage with false precision. Multiplayer equilibrium also lacks the same defensive payoff guarantee as two-player zero-sum equilibrium. One opponent’s deviation can transfer value among the others. That is a limit on the guarantee, not a reason to discard model-based study. 7 For a useful study record, keep the game type, pot and stacks, rake or payout objective, starting ranges, available sizes, locked behavior and excluded actions. Distinguish the provider’s published experiment from a solve you personally ran. This article reports linked experiments and illustrative arithmetic; it does not claim a new solver run or a tested low-stakes winning strategy.

    Choose a hand you can reconstruct. First count the pot and action order. Then write one range hypothesis and one alternative that could reverse the decision. Change one input at a time: remove a caller, shorten one stack, give the check-raiser more draws or introduce payout pressure. Explain why the preferred action changes, or why it does not. Download the blank multiway hand-review sheet , or copy the same text below. Keep completed notes private; mark uncertain cards and amounts rather than filling gaps from the result. Check: does a three-way solve settle a five-way hand? Use recording hands to capture a real session and poker under uncertainty to separate a sound decision from one result. Winning a pot does not validate every range assumption; losing it does not prove the plan was wrong.

    GTO Wizard: 10 Tips for Multiway Pots in Poker , February 13, 2023. General concepts about position, hand quality and shared defense. Its older software discussion is superseded by the dated product sources below; independence must not be assumed when multiplying fold probabilities. Upswing Poker: Limps in Poker , updated April 21, 2025. A coaching framework conditioned on limper tendencies, aggression behind and effective stacks. This guide does not adopt a blanket judgment about every limper. JonnyLaw / GTO Wizard: Playing In Position Against Two Callers , March 9, 2026. The defined 100bb, eight-handed chip-EV, 20-flop comparison summarized above; the quoted percentages belong to that model. Andrew Brokos / GTO Wizard: Probing in 3-Way Pots , March 17, 2026. A 100bb cash BB–CO–BTN study of checking ranges, board texture and turn probes. GTO Wizard: Now Live: Preflop ICM Solving , September 15, 2026. ICM and three-way postflop functionality, fold-value accounting and the stated three-player-to-the-flop limitation, checked October 15, 2026. GTO Wizard: Introducing Multiway Preflop Solving , February 3, 2026. Custom preflop inputs and nodelocking. Its launch roadmap is superseded by the September ICM release. GTO Wizard: Quirks of Nash Equilibrium in Multiway , August 5, 2025. Why multiplayer equilibrium has different payoff guarantees from two-player zero-sum equilibrium. Published October 15, 2026 . Adapted, edited and fact-checked from a supplied research essay with AI assistance. Sources checked on that date. Worked hands are fictional; no personal session, original solve or beginner usability result is claimed.

    On this site · Section overview

    Practice the next poker idea.

    Learn six beginner poker ideas through worked examples, 18 varied questions, mixed practice and a private review of what to revisit.

    Read matching section

    Searchable article text, without exercise answers

    Learn one idea, see it worked through, then try a different example. This practice room supports the Poker Foundations free course . Start with one skill; return for mixed practice after you have studied several. There are six worked examples and 18 fixed questions, three per skill. Say your answer and reason before revealing the choices. Examples repeat after three mixed sets. These are fictional exercises in standard 52-card no-limit Texas hold’em, with enough counters for the stated actions. They teach mechanics and reasoning, not recommended betting lines. Still learning which cards make a hand? Start with card basics and the hand-building lab . Select the strongest five cards yourself before returning to these decisions.

    Six skills, with one worked example and three questions each.

    Blinds are 1/2. You posted the big blind of 2. The button raises to 9 total. You have enough counters to call; no one else changes the wager. How many additional counters does a call cost? Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices. 9 more. 11 more. 7 more. Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

    On the flop, you bet 5. Your one opponent raises to 17 total on this round. You have enough counters to call. How many additional counters would a call add? Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices. 17 more. 12 more. 22 more. Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

    You paid 12 on the flop. On the turn, you have paid nothing yet and your opponent bets 6. You have enough counters to call. How much does a turn call add now? Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices. 6 more. Nothing; your earlier 12 covers it. 18 more. Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

    Six seats in initial preflop order are: first seat, next seat, cutoff, button, small blind, big blind. The first two fold. You are the cutoff. After your initial action, which seats still have initial decisions? Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices. Only the small blind and big blind. Button, small blind and big blind. Nobody; two folds end the round. Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

    This hand began with six players. After preflop action, only the button and big blind remain. The flop has just been dealt and nobody has acted on it. Who acts first on the flop? Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices. The big blind. The button. The player with the stronger cards. Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

    Only the big blind and button remain. On the flop, the big blind checks, the button bets 3, and the big blind raises to 9 total. Both have counters remaining. Whose decision is next? Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices. Nobody; the button already acted. The big blind again immediately. The button, facing the raise. Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

    These are your two private cards and the three shared flop cards. Your private cards Shared board Which description fits your cards now? Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices. A pair of queens and a heart-flush draw. A completed heart flush. A draw with no made pair. Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

    Use your two private cards with this flop. Your private cards Shared board What do you have now? Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices. A pair of aces. A completed club flush. Ace-high and a club-flush draw. Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

    Use your two private cards with this flop. Your private cards Shared board Which made hand can you build? Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices. Only a pair of eights. Three eights. A heart flush. Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

    The river is dealt. Use these seven available cards. Your private cards Shared board Which is your best five-card hand? Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices. 9-9-K-K-Q. K-K-Q-Q-9. K-K-K-Q-Q. Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

    The button holds the first private hand; the big blind shows the second. Compare both players on this completed board. There are no other players or side pots. First private hand Second private hand (shown) Shared board Who has the better five-card hand? Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices. The button because it has a pocket pair. The big blind because its private cards are higher. Neither. Both play the board and tie. Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

    Choose from your two private cards and this completed board. Your private cards Shared board Which five-card hand can you make? Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices. An ace-high heart flush: A♥ K♥ 8♥ 6♥ 3♥. Only ace-high, because just one private card is a heart. A jack-high straight. Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

    Your opponent checks. Consider only which exact private cards are physically possible, not how likely they are. Your private cards Shared board Which opposing hand is still possible? Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices. K♠ A♣. Q♥ Q♦. Q♦ Q♣. Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

    Your one opponent checks on this flop. No other information about that player is supplied. Your private cards Shared board Which statement is an observed fact? Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices. The opponent checked; their hidden hand is not revealed. The opponent has no ace. Every possible hand is equally likely. Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

    In one fictional river hand, an opponent bets, is called and reveals a bluff. No previous hands or population data are supplied. What does this single ending establish? Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices. The opponent always bluffs when betting the river. This bet was a bluff; its frequency across other hands remains unknown. Every earlier call against this player was correct. Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

    Nothing is owed on the river. In a hypothetical response model, some worse pairs call your proposed bet and no better hand folds. Your stated aim is to get called by those worse pairs. Which description matches that stated aim? Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices. Bluffing to make better hands fold. Seeking value from worse callers, while still needing to compare alternatives. Proving a bet is best just because you hold a pair. Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

    On the river, your draw has missed. Nothing is owed. Your proposed bet is intended to make an opponent fold a better made hand. Whether they will do so often enough is not supplied. What is the stated purpose? Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices. A bluff intended to fold out a better hand. A value bet to get paid by worse hands. A guaranteed profitable bet because a bluff is possible. Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

    In one fictional hand, your river bet makes the opponent fold and you receive the pot. The opponent's hidden cards and response frequencies are not supplied. Which conclusion is supported by this ending? Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices. Every worse hand would have called. The bet was certainly better than checking. You won this pot; the ending alone does not grade the bet against checking. Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

    Keep one mistake and its lesson link on the private study card . At your next study visit, explain that idea before looking at an example. Then try a different mixed set or the beginner checkpoint , which has separate questions and changed retries. These short questions sample six ideas. Their answers are not a grade for the full course, a measure of profitable play or a qualification to play for money. Answers and review notes stay in this tab and disappear when it reloads. The practice script does not send or save them. Ordinary site pageviews are described in the privacy notice .

    The IES learning and study practice guide recommends alternating worked examples and independent attempts, asking for explanations and revisiting material after a delay. Those general findings inform this design; they do not validate this course, these questions or a particular poker-study schedule. Mechanics were checked October 15, 2026 against PokerStars’ Hold’em rules and hand rankings . External publishers may advertise gambling. Every example here is original and fictional, not a recorded Nolan hand or a solver output. Prepared with AI assistance.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    BB / big blind

    A forced live wager; also the unit used to compare stack sizes. BB can label a seat.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    SB / small blind

    The forced wager immediately before the big blind in the seating order.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    BTN / button

    The marker defining nominal dealer position, not a guarantee of last action preflop.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    UTG

    The first preflop acting position after the blinds at a table with more than two players.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    CO / cutoff

    The seat immediately before the button.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    HJ / hijack

    The seat two places before the button.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Effective stack

    For two players, the smaller relevant stack, limiting what they can contest against each other.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    IP / OOP

    In position means acting after an opponent on a street; out of position means acting before.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Check

    Pass without adding chips when there is nothing to call.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Call

    Match the outstanding wager, or call all-in for the amount available.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Fold

    Give up the hand and any claim to its pots.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Raise to / by

    “To” gives the new total wager; “by” gives the increment over the previous wager.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Three-bet / 3-bet

    A reraise. Preflop the big blind counts as bet one. Not a three-times sizing rule.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Jam / shove

    Informal terms for betting or raising all-in.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Limp

    Call the big blind preflop instead of opening with a raise.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Check-raise

    Check, then raise a bet when the action returns.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Hole cards

    The two private cards dealt to a hold'em player.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Board

    The shared community cards.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Street

    A betting stage: preflop, flop, turn, or river.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Suited / offsuit

    Hole cards with matching suits / different suits. AKs means suited; AKo means offsuit.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Kicker

    An unpaired side card used in comparing the best five-card hands.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Set / trips

    Both are three of a kind; a set uses a pocket pair, trips uses a board pair and one matching hole card.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Overpair / top pair

    A pocket pair above every board rank / a pair matching the highest board rank.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Rainbow / two-tone / monotone flop

    Three different suits / two cards of one suit / all three cards of one suit.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Draw

    A holding needing further cards to complete a combination such as a straight or flush.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Gutshot / open-ended

    A straight draw missing an internal rank / one with either end available. Winning outs still need checking.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Range

    Possible holdings assigned to a player, often with weights. It is a model, not hidden-card knowledge.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Equity

    The expected share of a pot under specified hands or ranges and future cards, including ties.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Pot odds

    The price of a call relative to the pot; a simple break-even percentage uses call ÷ final pot.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Blocker

    A known card that removes some otherwise possible opponent holdings.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    C-bet / continuation bet

    Commonly a flop bet by the preflop raiser. The label does not establish hand strength.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Value bet / bluff

    A wager seeking calls from worse hands / seeking folds from better hands; some bets serve multiple purposes.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Ante / BBA

    A forced pot contribution separate from live blinds; BBA means big-blind ante.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Bubble / ITM

    The boundary before a payout threshold / in the money, qualifying for a payout.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Pay jump / min-cash

    The increase between payout levels / the smallest scheduled cash award.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Re-entry / bullet

    Another permitted paid entry / informal language for an entry or attempt.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Freezeout

    An event allowing no re-entry or rebuy.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Satellite

    A tournament awarding entry or tickets to another event under its prize structure.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Bounty

    An elimination-related prize; eligibility and award mechanics depend on the format.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Bagging

    Recording and securing a stack for a later stage; not proof of a payout.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Hero / villain

    Analysis labels for the focal player and opponent. “Villain” is not a character judgment.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Showdown

    Comparing remaining eligible hands after betting ends.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Main pot / side pot

    Separate pools contested by players with different matched contributions.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Runout

    The remaining community cards as they are dealt.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Double-up

    Informal description of approximately doubling a stack, often through a called all-in.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Cooler / bad beat

    Informal labels for strong-hand collisions / losing after being favored. Neither proves correct play.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Tank

    Take time over a decision. An edit does not establish how long the actual decision took.

    Glossary · Hold’em terminology

    Reconstructed hand

    An account rebuilt from notes, memory, or footage; estimates should remain identified.

    About this search

    What this search covers

    90 on-site pages, 146 external resources and 48 glossary entries. Guide prose and section headings are searchable; exercise answers, navigation and external article bodies are excluded. An overview or glossary entry is not an additional guide.

    Common abbreviations are expanded. Guide results include matching passages and section links. Only topic, source type and free-access filters appear in shareable link fragments. Search ranks text matches, not strategic quality or product performance. With no query, on-site pages appear first, then external sources and glossary terms. “Free” describes the listed resource, not every product its publisher sells. Ordinary pageview analytics remains covered by the privacy notice.

    Browse the topic map or choose a guided reading path. Use study material away from play. An empty search is not proof that no useful source exists.

    Always available

    Support is not a search result to earn.

    Gambling-support resources remain available regardless of your filters. For a procedure or disputed hand, use the rules and fair-play guide to find the appropriate authority. For a site error, send a correction.
